#5625. Nuclear power at sea: Seattle startup targets Norway for ships and floating power plants

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Oct 27, 2026 at 7:06 amOctober 27, 2026 at 7:15 am

Emerald Nuclear today announced a $2.1 million award from The Research Council of Norway to support its efforts to bring nuclear energy to the shipping industry and offshore power. The Seattle-based startup is developing high-temperature gas reactors that use an encapsulated fuel designed to resist meltdowns.

“This award will enable Emerald Nuclear to work directly with our marine partners to validate integration of our technology with their state-of-the-art marine power distribution and control systems,” said Wesley Deason, co-founder and CEO.

The funding supports Norway’s Marine Nuclear Propulsion System Pilot project, which is being led by Emerald Nuclear’s Norwegian subsidiary.

Shipping accounts for roughly 3% of global carbon dioxide emissions, making it a significant target for lower-carbon energy solutions. Some ferries serving shorter routes are adopting hybrid-electric propulsion. Shipping companies are exploring methanol, ammonia, biofuels and other alternatives to heavy fuel oil, but their climate benefits depend on how those fuels are produced and used.

Nuclear reactors have powered U.S. Navy submarines for more than 70 years. Now, a new wave of companies is working to expand nuclear power’s role in commercial shipping and other marine applications.

The award supports an early development step for Emerald Nuclear, with substantial work remaining before commercial deployment. The company has yet to build its first reactor, and its plans will require additional financing, regulatory approvals and a reliable fuel supply. The startup has previously received an undisclosed amount of funding from angel investors.

Emerald Nuclear has five employees, most of them in Norway, and is targeting two applications: offshore ships that help construct facilities like oil platforms and wind turbines and lay deep-sea cables, and floating power plants for remote communities. Each reactor is designed to produce 5 megawatts (6,705 horsepower), according to the company.

Bringing nuclear to the marine environment poses several significant challenges. They include safety issues, regulations for vessels traveling internationally, management of nuclear fuel and waste, and the way shipping companies frequently buy and sell vessels.

Deason said the company’s approach helps address those concerns:

Emerald Nuclear is designing its technology “to integrate with the unique power needs of the ship, but also to meet the ways that the maritime industry does business,” Deason said.

Other companies pursuing nuclear ship propulsion include Core Power, newcleo and Blykalla. Core Power, Westinghouse, Saltfoss Energy and Prodigy Clean Energy are also developing floating nuclear power stations. Russia’s state-owned Rosatom already has nuclear-powered icebreakers and a floating nuclear power plant in operation.

Prior to launching Emerald Nuclear, Deason, a nuclear engineer, worked for Ultra Safe Nuclear Corp. (USNC) developing reactors for space-based applications.

During his tenure at the Seattle company, a professor from the Norwegian University of Science and Technology approached USNC about applications for the maritime sector. USNC declared bankruptcy in October 2024 and the deal wasn’t pursued. But the idea interested Deason and Hallgeir Juliebø, a Norwegian entrepreneur who had been a consultant with USNC. The two co-founded Emerald Nuclear in 2024 and Juliebø serves as chief commercial officer.

Emerald Nuclear has signed a lease for an engineering center in Norway, where it’s designing and building its first prototype, a non-nuclear thermal device that will be used for the Marine Nuclear Propulsion System Pilot project.

Other partners for the project are VARD Group, Vard Electro, Island Offshore, Norwegian University of Science and Technology, Imperial College London and Maskindynamikk, bringing together nuclear technology, ship design and integration, vessel operations and academic research.

The startup will build its first nuclear reactor, named the Gem Microreactor, at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology, with 2030 as its goal for completion. Emerald Nuclear will integrate equipment from Peregrine Turbine Technologies in Maine to convert the reactor’s heat into electricity.

The target for the first commercial deployment is 2031, on a Norwegian offshore vessel.

Deason is hoping to open a manufacturing site in the future in Western Washington on Puget Sound with an initial focus on floating nuclear power systems that replace diesel generators. That phase of growth is roughly targeted to the early 2030s.

#5624. Mortgage Rates Above 7% Are Testing Home Buyer Engagement

Mortgage rates are a key factor in the home-buying process, and online shopping activity suggests consumers are paying close attention to borrowing costs. With rates around 7.5%, Zonda’s Homebuyer Outlook Clicks Index, which tracks NewHomeSource online new-home shopping activity, has fallen to its lowest level since 2022.

Of course, the relationship between rates and shopping activity is not one-to-one. The job market, broader economy, stock market, geopolitical uncertainty, and consumer confidence can all influence whether prospective buyers start searching for a home. The stability of mortgage rates can matter as well.

Still, the Homebuyer Outlook data suggests 7% may represent an important psychological threshold for consumers.

When mortgage rates first moved above 7% in 2022, online shopper activity weakened noticeably. Another significant pullback occurred as rates climbed well above 7% in late 2023. The latest data shows a similar pattern, with the Clicks Index dropping in September as mortgage rates approached 7.5%.

That relationship matters because online shopping often represents an early step in the purchase funnel. Fewer consumers browsing new-home options can translate into a smaller pool of prospects moving toward community visits and eventual purchases.

Importantly, Zonda’s Homebuyer Outlook shows that the right communities can still outperform even in a challenging market. For builders, that puts the focus beyond simply generating traffic and toward understanding which buyers remain engaged, what they can afford, and how closely a community’s location, product, and price point align with those consumers.

#5623. BRUNT Workwear Pledges $1 Million of Work Boots for Trade Students in 2027

BRUNT Workwear connects with a trade school student during a previous boot donation event. Since its founding in 2020, BRUNT has donated approximately 25,000 pairs of work boots to students pursuing careers in the skilled trades.

Work boot and apparel brand BRUNT Workwear has announced a commitment to donate $1 million of work boots to trade school students nationwide in 2027, as demand for skilled workers continues to grow. The commitment expands BRUNT’s longstanding pledge to donate 100,000 pairs of boots to trade school students by 2030.

“America needs the next generation of builders, electricians, plumbers, and skilled tradespeople more than ever,” says Eric Girouard, founder and CEO of BRUNT Workwear. “These are the people who will build our homes, maintain our infrastructure, and keep this country running. We want to do our part to make sure they’re equipped to succeed. We’ve already donated approximately 25,000 pairs of boots to students across the country, and this $1 million commitment is another step toward our goal of donating 100,000 pairs by 2030. As BRUNT grows, our commitment to the trades is only going to grow with it.”

Taking a boots-on-the-ground approach to putting the people who wear its products at the center, BRUNT often names products after real tradespeople and incorporates direct customer feedback into product development. The gear brand shares workers’ stories through its Bucket Talk podcast and brings the trade community together through weekly BRUNT Garage events.

Through the existing trade school boot donation program, BRUNT strives to help ease an upfront expense, while welcoming them into a community that understands, supports, and celebrates this workforce.

“BRUNT Workwear’s boot donation program is truly changing the face of vocational education in Massachusetts one pair of boots at a time,” says James Hachey, director of the Center for Career & Technical Education at Somerville High School.

“Particularly for students in high-need communities, having the proper and safe work boots can mean the difference between opportunity and exclusion. Students not having the same access to required safety gear can create an immediate barrier to hands-on career and technical learning. Donations like BRUNT Workwear’s help remove that barrier, thereby ensuring all students can safely participate, build the necessary skills, and prepare themselves for lasting careers.”

Starting January 1, 2027, trade schools nationwide can find more information and apply for work boot donations at bruntworkwear.com. Selected schools will receive boots throughout 2027.

#5622. Philadelphia Renters Win Record Settlement Over Unsafe Conditions and Illegal Rent Collection

A group of Philadelphia renters has reached a settlement in one of the largest per-tenant recovery class action suits in the city’s rental law history.

A preliminary approval of the settlement, which requires Odin Properties LLC to provide the tenants at Bentley Manor apartments with rent forgiveness and refunds for wrongly collected rent, was finalized by a Philadelphia judge last week.

The aggregate settlement amount exceeds $140,000, and individual renters will receive varying amounts based on their payment history, with the average refund estimated at about $1,200.

Three residents of Bentley Manor, located in West Oak Lane, filed a class action suit in March 2025 against Odin Properties and related companies for allegedly illegally collecting rent after the building was designated “unsafe” by the Philadelphia Department of Licenses and Inspections (L&I), according to The Public Interest Law Center.

Philadelphia law prohibits a landlord from collecting rent if a serious L&I violation if not corrected within 30 days. However, the plaintiffs alleged that Odin Properties continued to charge, demand, and collect rent each month, even as the building remained in unsafe status.

Odin Properties will now be required to forgive all unpaid rent and associated fees, estimated to be $66,891, and provide $75,000 in cash refunds for any rent collected, for a total of $141,891 in relief.

“This case sends a simple message: Landlords cannot collect rent while ignoring serious safety violations,” Madison Gray, the staff attorney at the Public Interest Law Center, tells Realtor.com®. “We hope it becomes clear that collecting rent while ignoring serious safety violations is a losing business model in Philadelphia, and we hope it encourages every landlord in the city to fix dangerous conditions promptly and comply with the law before tenants are forced to go to court.”

Realtor.com reached out to Odin Properties for a statement, but received no response.

Bentley Manor, which has approximately 71 sets of renters, was constructed in 1962. Between November 2021 and February 2024, L&I issued several violations related to fire safety, electrical hazards, and nonlatching building doors, all of which were resolved, according to the complaint.

On Nov. 14, 2024, L&I issued another notice of violation declaring the building an “unsafe structure,” citing “loose and missing bricks” and a “leaning parapet” as dangerous conditions. At the same time, multiple previous violations continued to resurface.

When the class-action complaint was filed four months later, in March, Odin Properties had allegedly still not made the building safe to the satisfaction of L&I, which made it ineligible to collect rent.

“Nevertheless, the Odin Defendants charged and collected rent from Plaintiffs and other tenants in December 2024, and in January, February, and March, 2025,” the complaint reads.

Three tenants were named as plaintiffs in the complaint: SEPTA transit operator Porter Grant, who paid $1,274 in monthly rent; Philadelphia police officer Casey Allison, who paid $1,352 in monthly rent; and a grandmother with mobility impairments, Dawn Colbourne, who paid $317 in monthly rent with the Philadelphia Housing Authority paying a monthly $968 subsidy.

“Without admitting or conceding any wrongdoing, liability, or damages, the Defendants have agreed to settle the Action to avoid the substantial expense, inconvenience, burden, and disruption of continued litigation,” the settlement document reads.

In between the lawsuit being filed in March 2025 and the settlement, the defendants made the necessary repairs to Bentley Manor.

Tenants will receive individualized amounts of the $75,000 settlement pool based on how much they paid during the non-compliance time period. On average, tenants will receive more than $1,200 per refund check, according to Gray.

“We also hope this sends a message to tenants. Philadelphia's housing laws only matter if they're enforced, and they don't enforce themselves,” says Gray. “This settlement shows that when landlords break the rules, tenants can fight back and win. Ultimately, we hope this settlement shows that tenants can hold even large landlords accountable when those laws are broken.”

#5619. How Making Daylight Saving Time Permanent Affects Homeowners

Most homeowners change their clocks twice a year: forward by one hour on the second Sunday in March and back by one hour on the first Sunday in November.

However, this longstanding ritual may come to an end, thanks to the Sunshine Protection Act, which was passed by the U.S. House earlier this year and aims to make daylight saving time permanent year-round.

If passed by the Senate and signed into law, the act would lead to lighter evenings and darker mornings. And whether it’ll work in your favor depends on where you live.

Homeowners in Alabama, Florida, and Texas, for example, would enjoy more usable daylight while those in Maine, Michigan, and Wisconsin could see much later sunrises and limited daylight hours.

However, at the moment, the bill has stalled, and during a recent campaign rally in Mississippi, President Donald Trump weighed in, calling the twice-yearly clock change "stupid" and urging the Senate to pass the measure.

Regardless of where you live, it’s important to understand how permanent daylight saving time might affect your home and lifestyle. That way you can prepare for the changes if the legislation becomes law.

With more daylight in the evening, you’ll be less reliant on artificial indoor lighting when you’re awake and active. And this could slightly reduce your electricity use.

However, any savings may be offset by increased heating and cooling demands.

“The dark, cold winter mornings that stem from permanent daylight savings would mean that your furnace will need to work harder before sunrise,” says Brandon Young, CEO of Payless Power in Fort Worth, TX.

In the summer, the additional sunlight can keep your house warmer later into the evening, forcing your air conditioner to run when energy use is the highest.

“As for the landscaping, additional sunlight can allow you to take care of your lawn in the evening rather than wait for the weekend. You might also have to adjust when you water and maintain your lawn,” Young explains.

More sunlight can also improve the security of your home as most perpetrators commit their crimes at night when it’s dark outside.

Lastly, if you plan to list your home in the future, the extra daylight could help you out.

“Since most buyers look at homes in the evenings, you’ll have more opportunities to show your home in the winter months,” Young says.

Plus, the natural lighting can provide a better view of your home’s exterior, landscape, and overall curb appeal.

There are several ways you can prepare for the darker winter mornings you’ll face if permanent daylight saving time becomes law.

“Allow it to preheat your house 30 to 45 minutes prior to your alarm clock going off—not all night long,” explains Young.

Marcus Griswold, founder of Little Green Myths in Vallejo, CA, suggests closing the doors and turning off the heat in rooms you’re not using.

“Some smart systems also help you isolate unused rooms by sensing when someone is present. This is known as zoned heating,” Griswold explains.

Also, take advantage of smart shades that can stay open during the day to heat your home and close with the sunset to hold in the warmth in the winter.

Additionally, use the gradual sunrise option on your smart bulbs, which will mimic the increase in brightness. Place the smart bulbs in bedrooms, bathrooms, and hallways to help enhance alertness as you wake up and ease into your routine.

Don’t forget to be patient with yourself as it might take some time for your body to get used to the change.

“In our survey, 84% of Americans claim it takes at least one day to adjust to a new time after the time change, while 29% say it takes at least one week. Setting your smart home devices like thermostats and lighting to automatically adjust can make the transition easier,” Young explains.

And if you use time-of-use pricing from your utility company, schedule the dishwasher and the laundry to work outside of peak hours. Doing so can lead to cheaper rates and potentially save you some serious cash.

#5617. Real Estate or Stocks? Risk Tolerance, Markets Key Most Decisions

There’s always been a question about which is the better investment long term, real estate or stocks? Opinions vary, but there is one thing for sure: You can’t reside in your stock portfolio. Another thing for sure is if you ask real estate pros for opinions, you pretty much get the same answer.

Those willing to accept a fair amount of risk will likely do better in the stock market over time. The 10-year annual S&P 500 performance breakdown from 2016 to 2025 wins hands down, or palms up if collecting profits. Within that decade were four gains in the mid-20% range, with only two negative return years. Of course, what happened in the past has no bearing on the future.

Real estate properties have historically increased in value over time. In 1970, the average price of an American house was $27,000. A comparable investment property now would be worth approximately $500,000, according to Federal Reserve Economic Data. That appreciation could represent a meaningful source of retirement funding if the property were eventually sold.

According to the Zillow Home Value Index, the average United States home value is $366,157, up 1.2% over the past year, and homes go to pending in around 27 days. Stock returns can be volatile due to several factors. Economic events such as recessions, interest-rate fluctuations and geopolitical tensions can significantly impact stock prices. Few would probably be shocked if the continuing war with Iran cratered the stock market at some point.

Stocks now account for more than a 30% share of total U.S. household assets, versus real estate at closer to 25%, according to TD Securities. That wasn’t always so. In the mid-2000s, real estate represented more than 30% of total household wealth, while stocks were around 15%.

So what would you as a real estate pro tell clients if the stocks vs. real estate subject arose?

“Your first investment property is the home you live in,” asserts Pam Rosser Thistle, with Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices Fox & Roach, Realtors® in Philadelphia, while admitting the stock market numbers win right now. “Over time, it appreciates. And you enjoy it. Win, win! Right now I am bullish on happiness, and owning a home is part of that. Appreciation is not like it was during COVID. But over time, your home will make you money when you sell in most cases as long as you stay in it for five to seven-plus years.”

Josh Jarboe, principal broker/owner of RE/MAX Empire in Mount Washington, Kentucky, has never believed real estate should be viewed as a guaranteed investment. But he firmly believes it remains one of the strongest, proven paths for long-term wealth creation.

“Unlike the stock market, homeownership offers something beyond financial returns: stability, utility, leverage and the opportunity to build equity while enjoying the asset itself. Higher home prices and mortgage rates have undoubtedly changed the equation, especially for first-time buyers. However, I remind clients that real estate and stocks aren’t necessarily competing investments. They serve different purposes, and a well-diversified financial strategy can include both.”

Leslie Hirsch, a broker at Christie’s International Real Estate New York, admits that many of her clients have been questioning whether to keep their money invested in the stock market, which has been performing so well, or purchase real estate.

“In New York City, this is driving a very strong rental market, with record prices being paid, as would-be buyers opt to rent instead of tying up cash in real estate,” she says. “Financial advisors/portfolio managers are encouraging clients to stay in the market and not buy real estate. On the flip side, there is chatter about the stock market being too good to last. People need housing, and they also want to diversify investments, maximize returns and mitigate risk.”

Hirsch tailors her advice depending on a client’s personal situation, but admits that generally speaking, the anticipated timeline to hold onto property and see appreciation has shifted.

“I cannot tell someone that we would expect to see ‘x’ amount of appreciation per year, as we have not seen predictable appreciation in Manhattan for 10-plus years,” she says. “Instead of a five-year property value growth cycle, we are now seeing 10-year-plus cycles, and the key is to buy property during the down cycle and sell when it’s up.

“For clients that I know plan to move cities, expand their family or upgrade in three to five years, I try to manage expectations and sometimes suggest they look at renting instead of buying while saving up for the bigger purchase down the road. Some people who would only ever consider being homeowners (never renters) will now consider it.”

Hirsch knows that housing is a fundamental need, and thus is not worried about mortgage rates and the market because the market will ultimately adjust to meet the climate of the day.

“If housing prices become unaffordable, then prices will come down,” she explains. “If the rents go too high, then purchasing becomes the better option again. What I do worry about is the affordability of housing for first-time homebuyers and people starting out in their careers.

“The second home market is where I see even more dramatic fluctuation happening because that is a ‘want’ and not a ‘need.’ When we see home values decrease enough, we eventually see investor buyers swoop in to purchase them. Then, when the stock market stops performing as well, we will see people pivoting back to real estate again, and the prices will stabilize.”

Jarrod Duncan, also with Christie’s International Real Estate New York, has a take as a real estate investor, feeling that while stocks may be booming, real estate is still a strong long-term investment.

“I own many properties in the Southeast that have increased in value exponentially since purchasing them,” he says. “I am also invested in the stock market, as I feel like it’s important to have multiple vehicles for wealth building. I do agree that the stock market has been a good place to be the last few years. So has real estate in certain places, especially in the Southeast, where people are moving for tax advantages, etc.

“I also think that investing in real estate can be even better in an elevated rate environment. Higher rates keep prices down, and you can always refinance, but an attractive deal may not come around again for years. There are some potential tax advantages to investing in real estate, such as the ability to take advantage of accelerated depreciation and ongoing costs to offset other sources of income. I remain committed to investing in real estate and recommend it to others if the fit is right for their long-term goals.”

Jarboe echoes the sentiment that the concern isn’t people choosing stocks over real estate, but the growing number of Americans being priced out of homeownership altogether.

“The longer affordability remains a challenge, the greater the potential wealth gap between those who own real estate and those who don’t,” he says. “Ultimately, I encourage clients to focus less on timing the market and more on whether purchasing a home aligns with their financial position, lifestyle and long-term goals. Real estate isn’t a guaranteed investment, especially in ‘boom-towns/cities’, but historically, patience and responsible ownership have rewarded those who take the long view.”

Michael Catarevas is a senior editor for RISMedia.

The Arlington, Texas-based builder closed 22,915 homes during the quarter, down 2% from the prior year period. Home sales revenue declined 2% to $8.4 billion.

Net sales orders fell 7% to 18,619 homes, with the value of those orders declining 9% to $6.6 billion. The cancellation rate was 23%, compared with 20% a year earlier.

“We expect incentives to remain elevated in fiscal 2027, the extent of which will depend on market conditions throughout the year,” he said.

D.R. Horton also pulled back sharply on starts as it worked to align inventory with the slower sales environment. The builder started approximately 13,100 homes during the September quarter, down 45% sequentially, according to the earnings call.

D.R. Horton enters fiscal 2027 expecting affordability constraints and elevated mortgage rates to continue influencing buyer demand.

Avante, the maker of an AI platform to help companies manage employee health care and other benefits, has landed a $30 million Series A round.

Frist Cressey Ventures led the round, with participation from Sorenson Capital, Hearst Ventures, Morgan Stanley Next Level Fund and existing investor Fuse. The new funding, announced Tuesday, brings Seattle-based Avante’s total raised to $40 million, following a $10 million seed round led by Fuse in 2024.

The startup plans to use the cash to expand internationally and develop more AI agents, building on a beta release of its “Ava Agents” last week.

Avante says it now has more than 70 customers, including Samsung Semiconductor, Real Chemistry, Zscaler and News Corp, and that bookings grew nearly fivefold over the past year. The platform reaches more than 385,000 employees and family members, according to the company.

Avante was founded in 2023 by CEO Rohan D’Souza; Carly Eckert, a physician and epidemiologist who serves as head of innovation and impact; and executive chairman Kabir Shahani, the co-CEO of Amperity.

D’Souza and Eckert previously worked as executives at health care automation company Olive AI, which shut down in 2023. The startup emerged from stealth in early 2024 and launched publicly in April 2025.

“Benefits teams are responsible for one of the largest and most consequential investments their companies make, yet they’re still operating with outdated information, archaic spreadsheets, and technology built for another era,” D’Souza said in a statement.

Avante is pitching its software as employers face rising health care costs. Large employers are projecting a median 9.2% increase for 2027, the company said.

The startup competes with benefits and HR software providers such as Workday, ADP, Deel and Rippling. It has also signed partnerships with benefits advisory firms including Gallagher, OneDigital, Segal Benz, Howden and USI Insurance Services.

#5613. Inside Legacy Hills’ Strategy for Reaching a Broad Range of Buyers

Developed by Centurion American, the Legacy Hills master-planned community (MPC) spans over 3,000 acres in Celina, Texas, and is planned for up to 7,000 homes at full buildout. The community opened in April 2024 and includes a diverse mix of builders, lot sizes, and floor plans. Pricing generally ranges from the $300,000s into the mid-$500,000s.

Importantly, Legacy Hills is not relying on a single buyer profile. Its product strategy creates multiple entry points into the community, with housing choices that can appeal to buyers at different price points and stages of life.

That product diversity is paired with a layered amenity program. Plans call for seven amenity centers throughout Legacy Hills, along with a 27-acre sports park and a 3-mile walking and biking trail. The planned 1876 Country Club adds a destination component with an 18-hole championship golf course, clubhouse, driving range, putting green, and short game facilities.

For families moving to Legacy Hills, children in the broader community attend Celina ISD, while future school sites are planned within the development. The community also broadens its reach further through Del Webb’s dedicated 55+ neighborhood, which adds to Legacy Hills’ family-oriented offerings with age-targeted homes and amenities.

The strategy is unfolding against a strong demographic backdrop. Celina’s population and household base are projected to more than double between 2020 and 2029, expanding the potential pool of buyers around the community.

At the same time, the broader housing environment remains competitive. The Zonda Market Ranking for MPCs characterized Dallas as slightly underperforming per August data, yet Legacy Hills stood out. In the Q2 2026 Master Plan Outlook report, the MPC recorded the largest year-over-year percentage increase in last 12-month sales among qualifying MPCs with at least 200 sales in the previous 12 months.

Legacy Hills illustrates the value of creating several paths into a large-scale community rather than building around a narrow customer profile. Differentiated housing, offerings for multiple life stages, and amenities ranging from everyday recreation to destination experiences give the development multiple ways to appeal to buyers.

The insights in this article were taken from a more in-depth case study in Zonda’s Master Plan Outlook subscription.

Eva Beeth is a data analyst within Zonda's economics department, where she supports housing market analysis through data modeling, forecasting, and market-level insights. She contributes to national and local research reports and analytical initiatives.

#5612. These State and Local Elections Will Hinge on Housing Policy—What Voters Need To Know

In this year's midterm elections, housing affordability has emerged as a central flashpoint in three high-profile races: the California gubernatorial contest and the mayoral races in Los Angeles and Washington, DC.

At both the state and municipal levels, voters face major structural and economic constraints, from scarce buildable land and a sluggish pace of new construction to restrictive zoning, drawn-out permitting timelines, high inflation, and mortgage rates topping 7%.

On this year's Realtor.com® State-by-State Housing Report Card, part of the Let America Build campaign, California was among six states to earn an F grade because of a dismal housing affordability score. Washington, DC, fared only marginally better, earning a D+.

Meanwhile, Los Angeles ranked dead last on the Realtor.com Metro Report Cards among the 100 largest U.S. cities, posting the lowest combined score measuring both affordability and homebuilding metrics.

Statewide and local candidates appearing on the Nov. 3 ballot have spent months pitching their proposed solutions to the housing crisis.

On the eve of the vote, here is where each of the contenders for these key gubernatorial and mayoral races stands on housing.

Former Secretary of Health and Human Services Xavier Becerra, a Democrat, and Fox News contributor Steve Hilton, a Republican, are the front-runners vying to replace termed-out California Gov. Gavin Newsom.

If elected governor, Becerra pledges to declare a housing-shortage state of emergency on his first day in office and appoint senior staffers across state agencies to tackle the crisis.

His agenda also includes implementing "shot clocks" to clearly communicate permit wait times to developers, overhauling and lowering impact fees statewide, standardizing and streamlining reviews for modular construction, and simplifying affordable housing financing.

"California should be a place where the carpenter who builds a home can afford to buy one," he said in a speech this summer.

According to a new Realtor.com analysis of the latest available housing and American Community Survey data, the typical household in California earns 49% less than the income needed to finance a median-priced home—a shortfall of $98,292—making it the second-most unaffordable state in the nation behind Montana.

Becerra has voiced support for building "missing-middle" multifamily housing, especially near transit hubs, and expanding first-time homebuyer down payment assistance programs to put homeownership within reach of more renters.

On the issue of homelessness and homeless encampments, which has become a lightning rod for political candidates in California this election cycle, Becerra is laser-focused on prevention.

At an event in the East Bay last week, Becerra argued that keeping at-risk people housed after a medical emergency or a sudden job loss is far less costly to the state than rehousing them from the street, reported ABC 7 News (KGO).

"We have to do everything we can to prevent them from falling into homelessness," Becerra said.

His strategy includes bolstering tenant protections, expanding funding to organizations that have proven effective in addressing the homelessness crisis, and holding accountable those who have failed to act.

The Donald Trump-endorsed GOP hopeful for governor of California has been aggressively pushing for the clearing of homeless encampments, vowing to rid the state of every single one by Dec. 31, 2027.

Similarly to his Democratic rival, Hilton has highlighted the need to cut through red tape constraining residential construction, though his approach hinges on capping fees, permits, and regulation costs at $50,000 per new home to make it cheaper for developers to build.

"We have to get rid of the regulations that make it two or three times as expensive to build the exact same home in California as in neighboring states," said Hilton during a televised debate in May.

His housing platform also includes utilizing over a million vacant lots to build starter homes, and creating 10 new municipalities across California to expand housing supply instead of trying to shoehorn multifamily developments into single-family communities.

“We have to stop trying to force housing into suburban neighborhoods where people don't want it," he proclaimed during the debate.

Despite their contrasting platforms, Hilton and Becerra are united in their fierce opposition to the California Billionaire Tax, officially known as Proposition 40, which Gov. Newsom had unsuccessfully tried to keep off the ballot.

Championed by a coalition of labor unions, the measure would impose a one-time tax of up to 5% on the worldwide assets of more than 200 Californians with a net worth of $1 billion or more who resided in the state as of Jan. 1, 2026.

Opponents of the initiative across the political spectrum have warned that it will accelerate an exodus of high-net-worth residents and tech innovators from California, diminishing the state's tax base.

Speaking on "The Steve Hilton Show" in January, Hilton criticized Proposition 40 as the epitome of what he called the "stupidity and the failure of 16 years of one-party rule" in California that, if adopted, will "drive business out of state."

On his part, Becerra dismissed the proposal as a "sketchy policy" and instead threw his support behind an alternative measure that would extend temporary tax rate increases on the ultrawealthy to reliably fund healthcare and public schools.

At the municipal level, incumbent Mayor Karen Bass, a Democrat, is seeking reelection for a second term. She is being challenged by L.A. City Councilmember Nithya Raman, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America.

Since taking office in 2022, Bass has made fast-tracking affordable housing construction and tackling homelessness the twin pillars of her agenda.

One of Bass' signature initiatives was Executive Directive 1, which streamlined approval for roughly 50,000 units of fully affordable housing. About 6,000 of those units are currently under construction.

In an email to Realtor.com last month, the mayor's office said that under Bass' leadership, the city has carried out a historic rezoning program to create the capacity for half a million new homes and bring more housing to transit corridors and commerical centers.

"After decades of inaction, Mayor Bass has been laser-focused on slashing red tape and accelerating the building of affordable housing in Los Angeles," a mayor's representative said.

Beyond construction permitting, Bass used her executive power to update the Rent Stabilization Ordinance for the first time in 40 years to lower the maximum allowable annual rent hike from 10% to 1%–4% for rent-controlled units, expanded the Adaptive Reuse Ordinance to convert vacant office buildings and parking lots into housing, and streamlined the building application process.

That last action, according to Bass' camp, was in direct response "to the barriers that applicants, developers, and contractors have identified as impediments to building in L.A."

Bass' plan to solve homelessness is anchored by her Inside Safe program, which clears encampments and moves unhoused people into motels and hotels on a voluntary basis with the goal of helping them secure permanent housing.

Councilmember Raman, who is seeking to unseat Bass, has been sharply critical of her record on housing, arguing in a statement to Realtor.com last month that her administration has not done enough to address L.A.’s housing crisis, leaving tens of thousands of residents "struggling to afford rent."

Responding to the Realtor.com Metro Report Cards' findings, that named L.A. the nation’s least affordable large city, Raman said she was not surprised.

"We’ve made it too difficult, time consuming, and costly to build homes in Los Angeles," said the candidate.

To lower costs, Rama’s platform outlines a plan to triple annual housing production by accelerating permitting through strict "shot clocks" for approvals, overhauling inspections, updating codes, and eliminating additional fees to create more starter homes for working families, and pressuring state lawmakers to pass reforms that wold incentivize developers to build more for-sale homes.

Citing results in 4th District, where her office recorded a 49% drop in street homelessness, Raman has made a campaign promise to cut the citywide population of unhoused people in half by the 2028 Summer Olympics through rental subsidies and the expansion of low-cost housing.

Raman and Bass share common ground on the issue of L.A.'s controversial Measure ULA, colloquially known as a Mansion Tax, which they both want to see reformed.

Enacted in April 2023, the measure imposes a 4% tax on property sales of $5.4 million to $10.9 million, and a 5.5% tax on sales exceeding $10.9 million. These rates apply on top of Los Angeles' standard 0.45% base real estate transfer tax.

Contrary to its nickname, the tax applies not only to luxury homes but to all real estate priced at over $5.4 million, including apartment buildings.

A recent report from the nonpartisan global policy think tank RAND Corporation found that the tax cost the city over 9,000 new housing units, 16,500 construction jobs, and $452 million in lost revenue.

Earlier this year, Raman unsuccsefully proposed a ballot measure to exempt newly built multifamily, commercial, and mixed-use buildings from Measure ULA for 15 years, arguing that it was suppressing much-needed housing production.

In Washington, DC, three candidates are striving to succeed three-term Mayor Muriel Bowser: Janeese Lewis George, a Democratic Socialist and member of the Council of the District of Columbia; Rhonda Hamilton, a veteran and community advocate running as an independent; and Robert L. Gross, representing the DC Statehood Green Party.

The cornerstone of Lewis George’s platform is the "Homes for All" plan, which includes provisions for rent stabilization, a coordinated affordable housing development system, stricter code enforcement, and expanded down-payment assistance.

Additional planks in her platform include amending the city’s zoning restrictions to add more homes and mixed-income housing, especially closer to transit lines.

"Increasing supply, paired with policies to protect residents, really is critical to stopping further displacement and making housing more affordable for all," she wrote in an op-ed.

The latest ACS numbers from the Census Bureau reflect the urgent need for change. Buyers in DC have to contend with a 25% gap between earned income and the minimum required income to afford a home.

Her long-term goal is to add 72,000 new housing units throughout DC within five years.

Lewis George has secured the backing of several pro-housing development groups, but President Trump does not count himself among her supporters.

Trump said in June that he "wouldn’t like" having Lewis George as mayor and floated the prospect of overseeing a federal takeover of DC.

"Maybe we’ll take back Washington, run it on a federal basis," he said. "We won’t put up with it. We’re not going to lose our businesses."

Rhonda Hamilton, who grew up in DC, is focused on building deeply affordable housing and requiring all new residential development to include this type of units. Her other major project aims to audit underperforming agencies, including the Housing Production Trust Fund and the District of Columbia Housing Authority (DCHA) waitlist.

"We’ve got to do something about the high rents," said Hamilton, per DC News Now. "We’ve got to make sure that our citizens are not being pushed out of the city."

Like L.A., the nation's capital is dealing with high levels of homelessness. Hamilton's agenda looks to put an end to street encampment clear-outs and partner with local churches to temporarily shelter unhoused residents.

Robert Gross, an information technology engineer by trade, wants to harness the power of artificial intelligence to speed up housing approvals and streamline zoning permits as part of his broader agenda to modernize city government.

Gross’ platform hinges on his "Human Life Standard" framework, which has as its goal to establish green infrastructure standards and reform the housing voucher structure by creating two distinct tracks for families with children and for single, unhoused individuals.

Snejana Farberov is a reporter at Realtor.com covering the U.S. housing market and the latest domestic real estate trends. She has worked as a general assignment journalist in New York City and Long Island for 16 years, writing for New York Post, Daily Mail, and News 12. Snejana earned bachelor's degrees in journalism and Italian from St. John's University, followed by a master’s degree from Columbia University School of Journalism.

#5611. 8 Resilience Moves Builders Can Make Before Extreme Weather Hits

When extreme weather hits, small construction details can make a big difference in how well a home performs.

According to Fred Malik of the Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety (IBHS), research continually points to roofs, openings, and structural connections as potential failure points. Damage in these areas can allow wind and water into a home and trigger larger, cascading losses.

For builders, stronger construction can also help reduce disruption for homeowners, limit warranty-related costs, and protect a company’s reputation for delivering durable homes.

“Resilient, durable buildings are usually the result of making several intentional decisions,” Malik says.

Here are eight steps builders can take to improve resilience ahead of severe weather:

Rather than approaching roofing as a collection of individual products, Malik recommends treating the entire roof as one interconnected system. The goal is to keep the roof intact and prevent an initial failure from creating a pathway for additional wind or water damage.

A sealed roof deck creates an additional layer of protection beneath the primary roof covering. If shingles or other roofing materials are damaged or blown off during severe weather, this secondary layer can help limit water intrusion into the home.

Small details can have an outsized impact on performance. Builders should carefully install and inspect flashing at roof edges, roof-to-wall transitions, vents, chimneys, and other penetrations. These areas can become pathways for water if they aren’t properly protected.

Windows, entry doors, and other openings need to withstand both wind pressure and wind-driven rain. Following manufacturer installation instructions and properly installing flashing are critical to maintaining the home’s building envelope.

Garage doors represent a large opening in the building envelope and need to withstand pressures generated by high winds. Malik notes that this is important even in inland markets, where tornadoes can cause significant structural damage.

In areas exposed to more severe winds, builders should consider a professionally designed continuous load path connecting the roof to the walls and ultimately the foundation. Strong connections throughout the structure help transfer wind forces safely through the building instead of allowing individual components to fail.

In flood-prone areas, elevate or otherwise protect mechanical, electrical, and utility equipment. Keeping critical systems above anticipated flood levels can reduce damage and make it easier for homeowners to return to their homes after an event.

Programs such as IBHS’ FORTIFIED standards provide builders with a framework for putting resilience measures into practice. FORTIFIED goes beyond minimum code requirements with an emphasis on keeping the roof on, keeping water out, and tying the structure together.

The program also requires third-party documentation of critical resilience measures, including construction details that may no longer be visible once finishes and other materials are installed.

Overall, resilience isn’t dependent on a single product or construction technique. It’s the cumulative result of getting multiple details right, Malik says.

Leah Draffen is a senior editor at Builder. She earned a B.A. in journalism and minors in business administration and sociology from Louisiana State University.

#5608. Jenny McCarthy Is Living in a Tent and Considering a Move to Las Vegas After ‘Serious’ Mold Problem

Jenny McCarthy is opening up about her unusual living situation as she’s moved into a tent in her yard while she deals with the effects of a “mold and mycotoxin poisoning” diagnosis.

During the Oct. 28 episode of “The Jenny McCarthy Wahlberg Show,” the actress explained the health-related challenges she’s faced over the last two years, which have included multiple surgeries and rounds of antibiotics.

Eventually, medical professionals tested “The Masked Singer” judge for mold, and she was diagnosed with mycotoxin poisoning.

McCarthy, 54, believes she was initially exposed to mold at her “very, very old” dressing room that “had a dampness to it,” as the makeup artist who exclusively works with her “in that dressing room also wound up getting mold poisoning.”

After the diagnosis, McCarthy embarked on a “mold protocol” in January 2025, following a routine of taking vitamins and undergoing treatments. She also took on the costly experience of remediating her home—which she said can cost anywhere from tens of thousands of dollars to “a hundred grand.”

“Remediation costs are so high because it takes a specialist to be able to move the mold without ruining your entire house,” she said, noting that the process was not covered by her insurance.

After remediation, McCarthy explained she had to hire contractors to “come in and rebuild” the home.

“You have to get rid of all your furniture. You have to get rid of all your clothes. I’m like, ‘Oh my god, that’s crazy!’” she said of the advice she received. “So, we remediated and because I am paranoid now about basically sleeping anywhere, I live in a tent. And I’m not even joking.”

McCarthy shared a look at the tent she’s been living out of, noting that it has a rain-proof cover for safety.

“I don’t have to worry about rain in California, but I do worry about chemtrails. And sprinklers,” she said.

She also added that she “won’t even go into an RV” because she is concerned about “chemicals.”

The podcast host went on to explain that she feels “a little bit crazy sometimes,” noting a “paranoid” state of mind, “like the walls are caving in.” She called the situation “really, really hard,” and confirmed that her husband, Donnie Wahlberg, 57, is not living in the tent with her.

“Donnie is working in Canada, and he is safe inside of a building,” McCarthy said. “Does he think I’m crazy? Yes. But he completely understands it.”

McCarthy also said that in the wake of the ordeal, she’s considering a relocation.

“I am so paranoid that I’ve even talked to Donny about moving out of the Midwest, where it’s humid, and going to a dry location like Vegas or Arizona or something, because my body just can’t detox mold very well,” she said.

While it appears that the tent McCarthy is residing in is located in California, it’s unclear whether the home she had remediated is the St. Charles, IL, residence she and Wahlberg listed for $2.799 million in September of this year.

In a recent Instagram comment, McCarthy indicated that the couple was “Going to Vegas. Not Cali.” following the listing of their longtime home.

The couple have owned the property for over a decade, and purchased it for $1.1 million in 2015.

“This isn’t an extravagant home, but there’s no greater symbol of our love for each other than this house and how much love has gone into it,” Wahlberg told People magazine of the dwelling in 2019.

The four-bedroom, 5.5-bathroom home was built in 1996. Spanning 7,236 square feet, the abode sits on 1.26 acres. Based on the contingent status on the property’s listing, it appears the couple has found a buyer.

#5606. Seattle’s Kivo Health raises $10M to bring lung disease rehab into patients’ homes

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Oct 27, 2026 at 10:19 amOctober 27, 2026 at 10:52 am

Seattle-based Kivo Health today announced $10 million in funding to help increase access to its services, which target older adults with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). The Series A round brings the startup’s total funding to more than $16 million.

Kivo ships equipment to patients’ homes and provides a nine-week program of therapist-led, live video sessions focused on exercise, breathing techniques and disease management. The company provides ongoing support following the program and says it uses AI to handle administrative tasks and communicate with patients, supporting its clinicians.

“We’re using the funding to build our AI health coach to blend AI-led care with human-led care,” Dr. Victor Sadauskas, Kivo’s co-founder and CEO, said via email. That pairing, he added, will help patients manage their chronic disease over the long term.

The company has approximately 50 employees, including clinicians.

COPD is an incurable lung disease in which damaged airways and air sacs make breathing difficult and can worsen over time. Common symptoms include shortness of breath, a persistent cough and fatigue. COPD is the third leading cause of death globally and the fifth in the U.S.

However, there are effective treatments to improve the condition, though many patients are not able to easily access care. A study of Medicare beneficiaries with COPD found that only 3.7% received pulmonary rehabilitation in 2012.

Kivo reports that a peer-reviewed study of its program found improvements in participants’ symptoms, physical function and mental health. The company also funded an analysis that estimated its model could reduce annual health care spending by $8,245 per member through fewer hospitalizations, ER visits and time in nursing homes.

Kivo says its program is covered by Medicare, Medicaid and private insurers including UnitedHealthcare, Humana, Blue Cross, Aetna and Priority Health.

“By thoughtfully combining high quality clinical care with AI, we can now scale proactive, accessible care to every senior, improving symptoms and reducing avoidable costs,” Sadauskas said in a statement.

Sadauskas launched Kivo in 2023 with co-founder and Chief Technology Officer Vaughn Koch. Sadauskas previously was an emergency medicine physician for Kaiser Permanente and a senior investment fellow with Life Science Angels. Koch is a serial entrepreneur who sold his startup Movity to Trulia in 2010.

While its current focus is COPD, Kivo aims to expand into other costly chronic conditions affecting older adults.

Allumia Ventures led the round, with participation from Corewell Health Ventures, Y Combinator, Heuristic Capital and MassMutual Ventures.

#5605. Mortgage Rates Dip as AI Jitters Boost Bonds Ahead of Fed Decision, GDP Data

In A Nutshell: Rates have mellowed a bit coming into a big week with a Fed meeting and the first read of Q3 GDP data.

Last Week’s Highlights: Oil prices continued to increase last week, but rates came down, as doubts about the AI narrative battered stocks, sending money into the bond market. On the housing front, the increase in mortgage rates has sent builder confidence down to its lowest level in 14 years. Permits for single-family homes also fell to a multiyear low.

Upcoming Attractions: The biggest event of the week is the Fed decision and press conference Wednesday afternoon. The committee is not scheduled to update its forecast (the “dot plot”) this time. Markets believe the Fed will hold and then hike on December 9th for an every-other-meeting hike cadence, so the attention will be on clues for the next meeting rather than the outcome of this one. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh will hold a press conference but is likely to stick to his usual practice of not foreshadowing upcoming decisions. Fed watchers may get more color out of SF Fed President Daly and St. Louis Fed President Musalem’s remarks on Friday.

Apart from the Fed, there are also a couple of important data releases this week. The first look at Q3 GDP is coming on Thursday morning. Part of the thesis for rates increasing so much these last few months is a belief that the economy is growing faster. At one point, estimates had Q3 GDP growing as fast as a 5% annual rate. Forecasters are expecting this advance estimate to land around 3.2%, which would be a meaningful pick-up from 2.2% in Q2. And finally, the September durable goods report will be released on Tuesday with forecasters expecting a solid reading of 2.0% month-over-month growth. This report tracks new orders, shipments, and inventories of long-lasting manufactured products, which is a signal of how confident businesses and consumers are about the future.

Chen Zhao is the head of economics research, where she produces research on the housing market for public and internal audiences. Previously, she was an executive director leading housing finance and financial markets research at the JPMorgan Chase Institute. Prior to joining JPMCI, Chen was an economics consultant at Analysis Group, Inc., where she worked on financial litigation cases and led teams conducting health economics and outcomes research on behalf of pharmaceutical companies. While in graduate school, Chen was with the Center for Economic Studies and the Social Economic and Housing Statistics Division at the US Census Bureau, where she conducted applied microeconomics research using large scale restricted-access linked survey-administrative data. She started her career at the White House Council of Economic Advisers, where she focused on labor and health economics.

#5604. Houston’s Historic Kirby Mansion Is Demolished To Make Way for Convenience Store

Preservationists in Houston are up in arms after a historic mansion dating back to 1894 was demolished to erect a convenience store.

On Friday, demolition on Kirby Mansion began but was quickly halted by Houston Public Works after it was discovered that a demolition permit had been applied for but not approved.

Dozens of locals held a candlelight vigil on Sunday to protest the demolition, but the permit was approved over the weekend. Demolition resumed and was completed on Monday morning.

The Kirby Mansion was named after lumber baron and industrialist John Henry Kirby who purchased the small home that was originally on the site in 1896 and expanded it into a 36-room Tudor Revival mansion.

Among the many unique features of the home was a library with hidden panels and a “thunder room”—a sound-insulated room built because Kirby's wife, Lelia, had a severe fear of thunderstorms.

The Kirby family sold the property in 1947, and the mansion served as the headquarters for the Houston-Harris County Red Cross for 30 years, though it had not been occupied in recent years.

Over its 132-year history, the mansion hosted presidents Franklin D. Roosevelt, Herbert Hoover, and George H.W. Bush, as well as British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher.

This past September, OB Texas Properties LLC, a company owned by Omair Bashir, purchased the property for more than $9.3 million. Bashir and his brother, Usman, are the owners of Brake Time Corner Market, a fast-growing convenience store and gas station chain.

In September 2025, Brake Time announced it would be opening 35 new convenience stores across Texas, Arizona, Arkansas, Colorado, and Kansas through the end of 2026, with three planned for Houston.

This past June, OB Texas Properties filed a plan for a 13,254-square-foot, one-story commercial building at an address within the mansion’s property boundaries. The filings included a hemp registration—indicating consumable hemp products would also be sold at the location.

Local preservationists had rallied to save the mansion, but because it lacked local, state, or federal historic designation, there was little they could do.

Over the weekend, Preservation Houston tried to contact Bashir’s company about removing some of the historic details from the site, including the mansion’s hand-carved oak staircase and imported tiles, but received no response.

“We wish the owner had been transparent and honest about the plans for this property and willing to discuss preservation options,” Jennifer Kapral, the executive director of Preservation Houston told Realtor.com in a statement. “We offered to explore ways to give this building a future. We also asked for the opportunity to document it and discuss salvaging irreplaceable materials if demolition went ahead. We received no response. Houston deserves better than this.”

“What’s so sad is the people that did buy this, and again, it’s their private property they can do with it as they choose. It just seems like not the best place for a vape store and gas station when there are numerous gas stations within a three-mile radius,” local resident Jason Fuller told the Houston Chronicle.

This isn’t the first time the Kirby Mansion was scheduled for demolition. In 2018 Central Houston Auto Properties LLC purchased the property, with the intention of turning it into a car dealership, though those plans never came to fruition.

Realtor.com has reached out to Brake Time for comment.

Julie Gerstein is a writer and editor based in Philadelphia. She previously worked at Business Insider as an executive editor covering news, entertainment, and digital culture, and was the company's founding Singapore bureau chief. She was also a senior editor at BuzzFeed, covering lifestyle, fashion, and beauty. She earned a B.A. in women's studies from the University of Pennsylvania and an M.A. in media and cultural studies from the University of Sussex.

#5603. Microsoft earnings preview: Employee buyouts, AI spending and a new financial scorecard

by Todd Bishop on Oct 27, 2026 at 10:50 amOctober 28, 2026 at 3:02 pm

Update, 10/28: Microsoft’s Azure cloud business brought in $33.2 billion in revenue in the September quarter, up 48% from a year earlier, blowing past the company’s own forecast and beating Wall Street’s expectations. Read the full story.

Microsoft’s earnings report Wednesday will come two days after the company offered buyouts to about 60,000 people, roughly a quarter of its employees. The call gives executives their first chance to say what the offer will cost, and to explain how it fits with the company’s long-term view of its workforce.

Whether or not they go into those details, it’s one of several issues to watch in Wednesday’s report, the first under Microsoft’s new reporting structure. Anthropic’s IPO filing on Monday adds another storyline, showing how much the Claude maker has agreed to spend on Microsoft’s cloud.

Coming into the report, Microsoft’s stock is near its high. Microsoft closed Monday at $532.60, about 2% below its record close of $543.45 on Oct. 13, after gaining roughly $1.4 trillion in market value since late June.

Here are the key numbers and issues heading into Microsoft’s results for the first quarter of its 2027 fiscal year, ended Sept. 30.

Core numbers: Analysts expect revenue of $90.75 billion, up nearly 17% from a year ago, and earnings of $4.72 per share, up 14%, according to Yahoo Finance. Microsoft’s own forecast was $89.85 billion to $90.95 billion, so Wall Street is looking for a result near the top of that range.

In July, Microsoft reported $90 billion in revenue for the June quarter, well above the $87.7 billion analysts expected.

A new scorecard: Microsoft announced in September that it would sort its business into two groups instead of the three it had used since 2015. This is the first quarter under the new setup.

The first, dubbed Agents and Infra, includes Azure, Microsoft 365, Dynamics, LinkedIn’s recruiting and sales tools, and server and productivity licensing. It brought in 81% of Microsoft’s revenue and 88% of its operating income in fiscal 2026, based on figures Microsoft recast under the new structure.

Microsoft expects Agents and Infra revenue of $75.15 billion to $75.75 billion this quarter, which would be growth of about 22% to 23%, by GeekWire’s calculation.

The other group, Devices and Consumer, includes Windows, Xbox and search advertising. Microsoft expects it to bring in $14.7 billion to $15.2 billion, down 5% to 8% from a year earlier.

Azure, in dollars: Microsoft started disclosing Azure’s annual revenue last year, when it passed $75 billion, and topped $100 billion in fiscal 2026. Starting this quarter, it reports the figure every quarter. It also changed what counts as Azure: GitHub’s cloud business and Security Copilot now fall under Microsoft 365, and its healthcare cloud moved to a new industry unit.

Counted that way, Azure brought in $29.4 billion in the June quarter, up 42%. Microsoft expects growth of 44% to 45% this quarter, not counting currency fluctuations, which would put Azure at roughly $32 billion, by GeekWire’s calculation. That compares with the roughly 45% Microsoft projected in July, under the old definition.

Hitting that forecast may not be enough. Investors are looking for about 46%, BNP Paribas analyst Stefan Slowinski wrote in a note Monday. In January, Azure beat Microsoft’s own forecast and the stock still fell 10%, because investors had privately expected more.

“Azure moves the stock, but the read that matters is whether capacity is absorbed as fast as it lands,” wrote Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives in a note last week.

Capital spending: Microsoft expects capital expenditures of more than $50 billion for the quarter, which would be a record. That’s up from $41 billion in the June quarter and $34.9 billion a year earlier.

An accounting change reduces what Microsoft reports as capital spending, without reducing its planned investment. Microsoft now assumes its data center buildings will last 25 years instead of 15. As a result, more of its data center leases will be classified in a way that doesn’t count as capital spending, CFO Amy Hood said on the July earnings call.

That change alone lowered Microsoft’s capital spending estimate for calendar 2026 to about $175 billion, from the roughly $190 billion it projected in April. Hood said the company’s actual spending plans hadn’t changed.

Cloud margins: Microsoft Cloud gross margin came in at 65% last quarter, better than expected but down from a year earlier. Microsoft said it expects the figure to be relatively stable this quarter. It also expects operating margins to be roughly flat with a year ago.

Workforce: The new “voluntary exit” offer, announced Monday by Chief People Officer Amy Coleman, covers participating teams in the U.S., Canada, the U.K. and India. It has no age or tenure requirement and extends to some vice presidents. Employees have until the first week of December to decide, and Microsoft hasn’t said how much the offer will cost or when it will record the charge.

For the spring retirement program, Hood disclosed the cost on the April earnings call: about $900 million, with roughly $350 million in cost of revenue and $550 million in operating expenses. The charge showed up in the following quarter. About 30% of the 8,750 eligible employees accepted.

The new offer is less generous. It matches Microsoft’s standard severance, without the extended healthcare of the spring program, and the company expects a much smaller share of people to take it. But the pool of eligible employees is nearly seven times larger.

Microsoft says the offer doesn’t mean it needs fewer people. Coleman said in July that the company was studying whether to make voluntary exits a regular part of managing its workforce. It has told investors to expect operating margins roughly flat this quarter and down less than a point for the full fiscal year, even with record capital spending.

Nadella has addressed this before. In a July 2025 memo to employees, after Microsoft laid off about 15,000 people, he acknowledged the “uncertainty and seeming incongruence” of thriving financially while cutting jobs. “This is the enigma of success in an industry that has no franchise value,” he wrote.

In his annual shareholder letter last week, he focused on Microsoft’s spending on AI infrastructure. “Based on the demand we see and the efficiencies we are driving, I am confident in the long-term returns on our investments,” Nadella wrote. “We are building against a growing book of business tied to this secular shift.”

Microsoft had about 223,000 employees as of June 30, before it cut 4,800 jobs in July and more in September. The Information reported this month that Azure President Girish Bablani told leaders in his group to find ways to cut costs by at least 20%. Microsoft called the report inaccurate and said Azure leadership had not directed teams to develop cost-cutting plans.

Copilot: Microsoft said in July that businesses were paying for more than 30 million Microsoft 365 Copilot seats, up from 20 million in April. That’s still only about 7% of the more than 450 million commercial Microsoft 365 seats.

The bigger change is in how Microsoft charges for Copilot and its other AI tools. In July it added usage-based billing alongside per-seat pricing. It’s also pushing customers toward E7, a new premium bundle that includes Copilot. Microsoft expects Microsoft 365 commercial cloud revenue to grow about 17% this quarter, not counting currency swings, a number that now includes GitHub.

The BNP Paribas analyst Slowinski, who attended Microsoft’s Frontier Tour event in London last week, wrote that partners are seeing more customers roll out Copilot company-wide. Partners also told him that Microsoft now ties 35% of E7 sales incentives to how much customers use features like Cowork.

Anthropic and OpenAI: Anthropic’s S-1 filing shows the company has committed to spend at least $44.9 billion with Microsoft from November 2026 to May 2033, up from the $30 billion Azure commitment announced last November. That’s well below its minimum commitments to Amazon ($110 billion) and Google ($114.5 billion).

Microsoft agreed last year to invest up to $5 billion in Anthropic. Its results for the June quarter included a $3.2 billion gain on that investment.

OpenAI remains the bigger factor. Microsoft’s commercial remaining performance obligation (RPO), the measure of signed contracts it hasn’t yet delivered on, reached $678 billion last quarter, up 84% from a year earlier. Without OpenAI, the backlog grew 25%. OpenAI told investors its annualized revenue approached $50 billion at the end of September, The Information reported, lower than earlier reports of about $70 billion.

Windows: Microsoft expects revenue from Windows licenses sold to PC makers, along with its own devices, to fall a little more than 20%. Higher memory prices are making PCs more expensive, and PC makers are still working through extra inventory.

What’s next: Alphabet also reports Wednesday afternoon, and Amazon reports Thursday, setting up a side-by-side look at Azure, Google Cloud and AWS.

Anthropic is aiming to go public the week of Nov. 16, according to the Wall Street Journal.

Check back Wednesday afternoon for coverage.

#5602. The Holiday Season Is the Best Time For Homebuyers to Score a Deal in These 7 U.S. Metros

Early November is the best time for homebuyers to score a bargain in three U.S. metro areas: Milwaukee, Riverside, CA and Tampa, FL.

In Detroit and three Florida metros–Fort Lauderdale, Miami and West Palm Beach–house hunters may benefit from holding out a little longer. Mid-December is typically the best time of year to get a deal in those places.

This is according to a Home Economics and Redfin analysis of housing market data; the analysis was originally completed in April. The analysis identifies the time of year when discounts off a home’s original asking price–through price drops and/or negotiations between buyer and seller–typically approach their seasonal peak.

Nationwide, discounts tend to peak in early fall before plateauing or shrinking as winter approaches. But housing is local, and in these seven metros, peak discounts typically arrive later. Homebuying slows as the holidays approach, leaving sellers with fewer potential buyers–giving the buyers who remain more room to negotiate. And some late-year listings have been sitting for months, making sellers more motivated to strike a deal before the end of the year.

“There’s a tradeoff to shopping for a home late in the year: Buyers may have fewer fresh listings to choose from, but they also face less competition, and many sellers are ready to make a deal,” said Redfin Senior Economist Asad Khan. “A seller who has been waiting months for an offer may be more willing to negotiate on price or other costs than they were in the spring. Buyers shouldn’t purchase a home just because the calendar says it’s a good time for deals, but those who find the right home may have room to negotiate.”

In Florida, the best deals for buyers typically arrive in November or December, partly due to weather. South Florida’s biggest wave of buyers–retirees and seasonal residents–often show up after the new year, when the weather is sunny and comfortable in Florida but cold in the Northeast.

“Local buyers have a good shot at getting a deal in November, mainly because it’s just before the snowbirds arrive,” said Todd Edwards, a Redfin Premier agent in Tampa. “House hunters have a window of opportunity to negotiate on listings that have been lingering on the market since summer: Sellers want to close a deal before the new year, and there’s often not much competition from out-of-towners yet.”

Hurricane season, which runs through early fall, also keeps some house hunters away and leaves lingering listings ripe for discounts once it passes. Additionally, Florida’s high concentration of luxury homes tend to sell below asking price, especially late in the year when sellers are eager to get those properties off their books.

The story is a bit different in Milwaukee and Detroit. Those northern metros have a fairly short selling season: Cold-weather markets compress the window for touring and closing on homes; sellers keep at it later into fall, trying to close a deal before the depth of winter hits and buyers hibernate.

That delays the usual seasonal slowdown until November in Milwaukee and December in Detroit, later than in most of the country.

The November and December discount windows in Milwaukee, Riverside, Detroit and much of Florida aren’t a one-time event; they show up as a recurring pattern each year, regardless of whether the broader market favors buyers or sellers.

But the seasonal advantage could be particularly useful to buyers this year. The U.S. housing market is already firmly tilted toward buyers, with 63% more sellers than buyers—the biggest imbalance in Redfin records dating back to 2013. A jump in listings coupled with sluggish homebuying demand has given house hunters in many parts of the country more options and more negotiating power. Miami is one of the strongest buyer’s markets in the nation, with more than twice as many sellers as buyers. Tampa, West Palm Beach, Fort Lauderdale, Riverside and Detroit are also buyer’s markets.

Milwaukee is one of just five seller’s markets in the country. With more buyers than sellers in Milwaukee, deals aren’t commonplace–so buyers there may want to pay extra attention to seasonal patterns.

The best time to buy a home is more complex than the week when buyers are most likely to score a discount.

There’s typically a tradeoff between selection and savings. New listings generally peak months before the best deals arrive. For instance, Milwaukee typically has the most new listings in mid-May and the most fresh inventory in mid-July,then its best deals arrive in early November. Detroit’s new listings typically peak in early August and fresh inventory in early September, months before its mid-December dealmaking sweet spot.

That means buyers who wait until November or December may have fewer homes to choose from. But those who prioritize price—and are flexible about their timing—may find sellers more receptive to negotiations. Ultimately, buyers should balance price, selection and their own circumstances.

Please note that this table includes 3 key moments for buyers; it’s important for buyers to balance what’s most important for them–choice or price

To identify the best time to buy, this Home Economics and Redfin analysis focuses on the seasonal indexes for three metrics: new listings, fresh inventory, and the average discount.

As a data journalist at Redfin, Dana Anderson writes about the numbers behind real estate trends. Redfin is a full-service real estate brokerage that uses modern technology to make clients smarter and faster. Asad taught urban economics as a Research Fellow at the University of Wisconsin-Madison and earned a PhD in economics from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. His research has focused on the economics of city structure and zoning policy.
