#5601. Tech Moves: Xbox COO’s sudden departure; SeekOut leadership shakeup; Fred Hutch names VP

Tech Moves covers notable hires, promotions and personnel changes in the Pacific NW tech community. Submissions: [email protected]

by Lisa Stiffler on Oct 27, 2026 at 2:08 pmNovember 2, 2026 at 1:05 pm

— Xbox Chief Operating Officer Helen Chiang has suddenly left Microsoft after 21 years with the company, just months after landing the role in July. Her past roles include leading Mojang and the Minecraft franchise.

Verge first reported the news on Friday, citing a memo from Xbox CEO Asha Sharma that did not disclose the reason for her departure.

An Xbox spokesperson was likewise mum on details. “We don’t discuss individual personnel matters. We’re grateful for Helen’s years of service and wish her well,” the company said in an email to GeekWire.

In response to speculation around her departure, Chiang offered a LinkedIn post on Nov. 2 refuting rumors that she left because of leaks to the media, to take a role with a competitor, for poor behavior or because she was passed over for a larger role.

“My story is about staying true to your core values, especially when it is hard. That’s the legacy I hope to leave behind,” Chiang wrote, without providing specifics.

Xbox has undergone a massive reorganization that included Chiang’s appointment, roughly 3,200 job cuts through the fiscal year — about 20% of the Xbox workforce — the spinoff of four game studios and a plan to dramatically flatten management.

— Seattle-based tech leader Philip Su has joined Anthropic as a member of technical staff on beneficial deployments. The management role focuses on AI applications in global health, life sciences, economic mobility and education.

Su started his tech career with 12 years at Microsoft and later worked for Facebook. He has launched multiple ventures, including Audere, a global health software nonprofit, and Superphonic, a podcast player. In 2021, he worked at an Amazon fulfillment center to experience the holiday rush.

Su also created and leads an annual course for University of Washington computer science students on how to maximize their personal and professional growth.

— More leadership changes are underway at SeekOut, a Bellevue-based recruiting startup launched in 2017. The company announced Monday that co-founder John Tippett is now president, moving from his role as chief client officer.

In April, SeekOut CEO and co-founder Anoop Gupta retired and passed the reins to enterprise software veteran Sean Thompson. In August, co-founder and chief technology officer Aravind Bala took over as CEO. Thompson is now listed as an adviser to the board.

Tippett will lead day-to-day operations and work with Bala “on the company’s direction,” according to a press release. SeekOut said it wants to integrate AI tools into customers’ operations to reduce recruiters’ workload.

SeekOut is No. 68 on the GeekWire 200, a ranked index of the Pacific Northwest’s top startups.

— Fred Hutch Cancer Center has appointed Michael (Mick) Merritt as vice president of strategy and partnerships, effective Dec. 7.

Merritt joins from Penn Medicine, where he was chief operating officer of Penn Signature Services. He has more than 25 years of experience in academic medicine, consulting, strategy, business development and operations.

— Industrial wastewater treatment startup Membrion has named Alexander Demihovsky as director of applications engineering. He joins the Seattle-based company from Xylem. His past employers include Evoqua Water Technologies and Bechtel National.

“Alex helps turn customer needs into viable project plans, mitigate execution risks and develop competitive proposals,” the company said.

— Marine geothermal energy startup Endurance Energy has named Marty Calvert as the director of turbomachinery. Calvert joins the Seattle startup from Blue Origin. He was previously a turbomachinery engineer at NASA for more than 13 years.

Endurance completed its fifth deployment to the ocean floor last month, testing Adélie, a 100-kilowatt geothermal generator named for a penguin.

#5600. Rocket Beats Expectations in Q3 Earnings Report Amid Stressed Mortgage Market

Despite operating in “one of the hardest mortgage markets in a generation” that’s “punishing” for American families as described by its CEO, Rocket Companies reported Q3 adjusted earnings above Wall Street expectations, with shares rising about 3% in after-hours trading Oct. 29.

Rocket reported a GAAP (Generally Accepted Accounting Principles) total revenue of $3.28B, up 18% from Q2’s $2.78B in total revenue; and adjusted revenue of $2.57B, down almost 7% from Q2’s adjusted revenue of $2.76B, but a notable 200%-plus increase in net income of $709M this quarter from last quarter’s net income of $229M. Adjusted net income and adjusted EBITDA were both down slightly from last quarter to $419M and $748M, respectively.

But looking at Rocket’s year-over-year earnings shows a total top-line turnaround. Its GAAP total net revenue increased over 94% from $1.69B; adjusted revenue up 37% from $1.87B; adjusted net income up 165% from $158M; adjusted EBITDA up 114% from $349M and most notably, a net income increase from a $124M loss swinging to that $709M profit.

In a release, Rocket Companies CEO and Director Varun Krishna attributed the numbers coming in against a backdrop of mortgage rates at three-year highs, to gains in both purchase and refinance.

“Rocket gained market share in both purchase and refinance, quarter-over-quarter and year-over-year, and delivered our highest profitability margin in nearly five years, even as mortgage rates climbed to a three-year high,” said Krishna. “We didn’t spend the last three years waiting for rates to fall. We acquired distribution, connected real estate and mortgage, and invested heavily in technology. We changed the economics of our business. Rates went up. We took share. Profits grew. That’s not a coincidence.”

In an investor call following the release of the data, Krishna attributed Rocket’s turnaround to a company rebuild three years ago that’s “built for any cycle,” which today is experiencing historic housing market hardships—from the 10-year Treasury rising to its highest point in 24 years to mortgage rates rising to their highest point in three years, to declines in existing-home sales and refinance applications.

“Here’s the truth about tough markets: they don’t lie,” he said. “They strip everything down to what’s real—who has the capital to keep investing, whose model works in any cycle, who can win their clients back, and who can move fast when it counts. This quarter did all of this. This was our highest margin in nearly five years and our fourth straight quarter of expansion since we closed the Mr. Cooper transaction. Adjusted net income of $419 million; $0.15 of adjusted EPS.

“So why does Rocket win?” he continued. “It’s no accident. Three years ago we made a decision: Rebuild this company at every single level. An ecosystem that serves clients from home search through servicing. A technology platform built for scale, speed and efficiency. Distribution that reaches homebuyers and homeowners everywhere. And a fortress balance sheet, now over $11 billion in liquidity, so we can keep investing while others pull back.”

On the investor call, Rocket Companies’ Chief Financial Officer Brian Brown walked through the Q3 numbers in more detail.

“We expanded adjusted EBITDA margin to its highest level in nearly five years, and we ended the quarter with record liquidity,” he said, noting that the $2.6B adjusted revenue was near the midpoint of its guidance range (an estimate of the company’s future financial performance). He said the company generated $40.4 billion in net rate lock volume and $43.6 billion in closed loan volume and that based on its estimates, purchase market share approached 6.5% and refinance market share was 15.5%. That’s compared to the 6.2% and 14.3% reported in the second quarter, he added.

Brown also commented that Rocket Local, its team of in-market loan officers who work directly with real estate agents, also grew volume more than 30% year-over-year, and now includes 400 loan officers across several major metro areas. He said the company’s partnership with Redfin and Compass extends that reach, with one in five of its purchase clients represented by a Redfin or Compass agent.

On the wholesale and partner lending side, he said over the last few months, the company has added around 200 new Rocket Pro partners to its platform, representing $12 billion in potential annual volume. Refinance volume set a record, Brown noted, saying cash-out refinance volume remained healthy, supported by another step up in recapture.

“Recapture rates on the combined portfolio reached an all-time high, the fourth consecutive quarter of improvement. Gain on sale margin, excluding correspondent, was 333 basis points, up from 311 basis points last quarter,” he said.

Krishna said that more than 70% of the company’s revenue this year is coming from recurring or less rate-sensitive sources, such as servicing fees, subscriptions, purchase, cash-out refinance and home equity. He said because of the firm’s integration with Redfin, mortgage buyers are brought into their ecosystem early, creating a path to Rocket from the beginning of their home-search journey. He said as of this earnings report, visitors who click through to start a purchase mortgage transaction are up 50% year-over-year.

“Redfin’s contribution to our refinance leads also more than doubled this quarter from a year ago,” Krishna said. “Compass simply extends that same playbook and delivers what buyers want most—homes and the agents who sell them. Cumulative unique listings are now nearly 40,000, up from roughly 25,000 last quarter. Homes you cannot find anywhere else. Rocket Pro net rate lock volume through Compass has passed $3 billion since February, up 50% from last quarter. Then there’s servicing—our ballast. More than $1 billion a quarter in servicing fees. More than $4 billion a year. That’s triple where we were three years ago. That’s recurring cash flow in any rate environment, revenue that shows up whether rates are 4% or 8%. And here’s what makes it compound: Because we know these clients; we’re first in line when they’re ready for their next loan. In Q3, recapture across the combined portfolio hit the highest level in our history.”

Rocket has a three-year agreement with Compass to provide national exposure to its private and coming-soon listings via Redfin.

Krishna said advances in AI in mortgage lending are a game-changer for Rocket, citing four segments of the process: Credit pulls, digital refinance, voice agents and the future of agentic AI.

On nearly 20% of its direct-to-consumer volume, AI completed the credit pull step on digital purchase and refinance leads before the client spoke to a loan officer, he said.

On refinance loans, he said clients can choose to pull their credit, see their loan options and lock their rate without having to speak to a loan officer. In Q3, he said digital was more than 40% of all direct-to-consumer refinance applications, and digital leads converted at four times the rate of every other channel.

Rocket’s AI voice agents now handle 65% of inbound servicing calls and resolve more than half of them on their own, Krishna added. On the future of agentic AI, he said consumers are starting to shop with their own AI agents to compare price, speed and ratings across lenders. Over the past 18 months, Rocket has built the APIs and protocols those agents need to complete the mortgage process with Rocket end to end, he noted.

Looking ahead, Brown said he expects the economic headwinds that have hammered the better part of this year to continue in Q4 and beyond, especially in the refinance sector.

“The MBA Purchase Application Index is down nearly 20% year-over-year, and refinance applications are down more than 50%,” he said. “The fourth quarter is seasonally low for our industry, and this year that slowdown comes at a time where mortgage rates are reaching highs we haven’t seen in two decades.”

Brown added that Rocket expects the refinance market to decline by almost half from the third quarter, “which would leave the overall mortgage activity near multi-decade lows.”

With that context, in the fourth quarter, Brown said they expect adjusted revenue to be between $2.1B and $2.3B with their guidance reflecting continued share gains. For expenses, they expect total expenses of $2.05B, including $110M of intangible amortization, $80M of stock-based compensation and $10M of one-time integration costs. Excluding these items, Brown said they expect expenses of $1.85B, a decline of $165M from the third quarter.

“Tough markets drive separation,” Brown said in his closing remarks. “This quarter, rates rose, volumes fell, and the industry felt it. Rocket Companies grew share, expanded margin, delivered synergies ahead of plan and ended the quarter with record liquidity. The fourth quarter will be harder still. We’re ready for it.”

Beth McGuire is RISMedia’s vice president of online editorial.

#5596. How To Deal With Noisy Upstairs Neighbors: 8 Clever Tricks To Keep The Peace

Shortly after they were married, Brittany H. and her husband moved into an apartment in Chicago’s Irving Park neighborhood. With Victorian houses and vintage flats dotting the tree-lined streets, they assumed their new home would be a peaceful spot to build their life together.

But the couple got more than they bargained for. At all hours of the night, they heard strange, loud sounds coming from the neighbors upstairs.

“It was midnight, and the loud upstairs neighbors sounded like they were dropping bricks on the floor," Brittany says, vividly recalling her first night in the unit. "Our ceiling light fixture rattled from the loud, noisy pounding.”

When their lease was up, the couple promptly moved to the top floor of a different apartment building. Brittany was so scarred by her experience with noisy neighbors, she says she'll never live anywhere but a top floor again.

As a renter, you have to be ready for some day-to-day noise—that's just part of living in close quarters with other people. So, how can you reduce noise from upstairs neighbors?

If you've lived below noisy upstairs neighbors like Brittany has, you know the sound: the relentless stomping, dropped objects that seem to ricochet off every surface, the mysterious midnight furniture rearranging. Beyond frustrating, it can feel inescapable.

In many apartments, especially older buildings, this kind of noise is more than a nuisance: It's a feature.

Many vintage units were built before modern soundproofing standards were a thing. That means there might be little to no insulation between floors, allowing every footstep, conversation, or clattering object to echo directly into your living space.

While some level of noise is part of communal living, chronic disruptions can wear on your nerves and your sleep cycle.

But you're not powerless to deal with it. Whether you have noisy upstairs neighbors stomping around at odd hours or sudden loud thuds overhead, these renter-friendly tips can help restore your peace and quiet.

Say what now? Ceiling clouds are acoustic panels that hang from the ceiling and can reduce noise and echoes. (Science!) Take that, noisy upstairs neighbors.

You've probably seen them before in auditoriums, atriums, and restaurants. They can do wonders for cutting down noise in your home, too.

Just make sure to check with your landlord before installing them since they need to be securely mounted to the ceiling.

If your landlord isn't on board, there are other less invasive approaches to dissipate sound, including acoustic light fixtures that claim to absorb sound.

Have you ever lived next to a neighbor who plays the piano (or worse, an amped-up electric guitar) well past bedtime?

If the neighbor won't knock it off, you don't have to move (or file a complaint with the landlord or police). Just put some stuff between you and the pandemonium next door.

Start by placing bookcases or other heavy furniture against the dividing wall, covering as much of the wall as possible.

"The more mass between you and the neighbor, the less sound that will come through,” says Zach Ziskin, a recording engineer in Fort Lauderdale, FL.

Then, rearrange fabric-covered sofas or chairs so that they're close to windows and doors. And for more quiet, use lots of decorative pillows and throws.

“The heavier and denser the textile, the greater the absorption,” says Heather Humphrey, owner of the interior design firm Alder & Tweed, in Park City, UT.

If you can hear your neighbors flush the toilet, they can probably hear you, right? That’s because open spaces with tile and hard surfaces, such as a bathroom, amplify sound.

Short on space? Fill the bathroom with wall coverings and soft goods such as rugs and towels, which is a pretty easy way of dealing with noisy upstairs neighbors and their sounds.

“The same principle goes," she says. "The more you cover your walls, the greater the barrier to sound created."

Sometimes, the outside noise you hear in your apartment can be just as irritating as noise from your neighbors. And closing your windows isn't always a cure-all—those sounds can trickle in regardless.

One way to dial it down? Make sure the window casings and frames are fully caulked and sealed. (You'll want to call your landlord about this one.) Or use a window insert to make the seal more airtight, Ziskin says.

Even easier? Just hang some heavy curtains, which will help muffle any noise from outside.

You'd be surprised by how much noise can seep in through the cracks around your door and ruin your quiet. Your best soundproofing efforts will be futile unless you address them.

Make sure there's high-quality weatherstripping between the door and door frame to create a seal when closed, Ziskin says.

Likewise, if there's an air gap between the bottom of the door and the floor, attach a heavy-duty door sweep or draft blocker to create a seal.

Because wall hangings and tapestries are porous, they can absorb sound and excessive noise.

If you're conjuring up images of your college dorm room, don't worry—there are tons of options these days that are beautifully on trend.

For instance, the heavy knotting in macramé makes it perfect for buffering noise and giving your place stylish flair.

Canvas wall art can also help absorb sound; consider adding a layer of foam to the hollow inside for an extra buffer. Or try sound-absorbing felt panels—you can even use one to make a DIY bulletin board.

"It will add a decorative touch and keep you organized, while reducing noise levels," says Dayna Hairston, interior designer at Dayziner in Cary, NC.

If you have wood floors, do yourself and your neighbors a favor and throw down some area rugs. (Heck, if you have carpet, go ahead and do this, too—the more padding, the better.)

When buying a rug, seek out thick-pile material or something with a rubber backing to muffle sound, Humphrey suggests.

Of course, it just isn't always possible to completely soundproof your apartment. If you're still fighting the urge to grab a broom and bang on the ceiling, it's probably time to talk to the neighbors.

"If all else fails, invest in high-quality earplugs or a white noise machine,” Ziskin says.

Sometimes, your noisy upstairs neighbors aren’t just annoying—they’re violating local laws. Most cities have noise ordinances, which define quiet hours, typically between 10 p.m. and 7 a.m. (These can vary by location.) If your neighbors are consistently blasting music late into the night or stomping around at 2 a.m., you might have legal grounds to act.

Start by documenting the disturbances. Note the time, duration, and type of noise. Audio recordings and written logs can help if you need to escalate the issue down the line.

Next, try to resolve the problem directly. Politely let your neighbor know the noise is disruptive. If that doesn't work, reach out to your landlord or property manager.

Still no improvement? Then it's time to contact your local nonemergency number. Don’t dial 911 unless it’s an emergency—for everything else, most municipalities have a nonemergency line for noise complaints.

If you're unsure about your city’s laws, search “[your city] noise violation hours” or visit your city’s website to understand when and how to file a formal legal noise complaint.

It might be tempting to fight noise with noise by blasting your own music, banging on the ceiling with a broom, or leaving a snarky note taped to their door. But while getting back at your neighbors might sound like a dream, these passive-aggressive tactics rarely work—and often make things worse.

Instead, aim for constructive solutions. Communicate clearly, keep things civil, and involve your landlord or building management when needed. If all else fails, rely on renter-friendly soundproofing upgrades and consider investing in a white noise machine or noise-canceling headphones.

Allaire Conte contributed to this report.

Jenny Lelwica Buttaccio is a writer living in Chicago. Her work has appeared in HuffPost, Prevention Magazine, Reader's Digest, and more.

#5595. Savannah Chrisley Reveals How She and Jason Galanis Pulled Off Their Secret Cayman Islands Wedding

Savannah Chrisley has opened up about her secret wedding to her 56-year-old husband, Jason Galanis, to whom she said "I do" in the Cayman Islands months before announcing they were expecting their first child.

The 29-year-old real estate agent, who shot to fame alongside her parents, Todd and Julie Chrisley, on their reality TV show, "Chrisley Knows Best," announced on Oct. 27 that she was both pregnant and engaged to Galanis, who is 27 years her senior and served time behind bars alongside her father.

Days later, it was revealed that they are actually married, with People reporting that they said "I do" on July 14—just one year after beginning their romance.

Although the TV personality has stayed tight-lipped about the details surrounding their nuptials, she has now spilled on the special day while appearing on "The Golden Ticket."

Savannah Chrisley admitted that the couple avoided filing their marriage paperwork in the U.S. so that they could keep the news to themselves.

“I’m not public about anything. We ended up getting married in the Cayman Islands in July. So we did everything there, but we haven’t filed [in the U.S.] because then it will be public record, right?" she said.

Despite having already tied the knot, she revealed that they plan to have another celebration in May.

“The wedding is in May. The wedding was supposed to be in January, [but] I have a real-life wedding crasher,” she said as she motioned toward her baby bump.

It was previously revealed that the couple began putting roots down for their family home months before she announced her pregnancy, with the soon-to-be parents picking up a $2.2 million pad in February, as first reported by TMZ.

The 5,207-square-foot property was built in 2023 and comes with five bedrooms and 5.5 bathrooms. It includes two fireplaces, chic wood and marble flooring, walk-in closets, and a chef's kitchen with state-of-the-art appliances.

It also features a patio, balcony, and two-car garage.

The home was listed for $2.9 million in June 2025, meaning the expectant mother got over a half-million dollars off.

After her husband's identity was revealed, Chrisley opened up about their romance on her podcast, "Unlocked," telling her fans that she doesn't pay any mind to their large age gap.

"Yes, there is a huge age gap there, OK? And that’s probably part of the reason why I kept a lot of it quiet, because I know how brutal the public can be. But I genuinely do not care," she insisted.

"I have always said, ‘I would rather [have] 20 phenomenal, unbelievable years with someone than 50 ‘meh’ years.' Like, the amount of love and respect that we have, we have so many dreams, and we dream together, we work together ... we want to have life experiences with each other. And I think that’s when you know you have the right person, when you don’t feel like you have to escape them at times. We do everything together. ... And it’s just such an amazing, fulfilling feeling to finally find your person. And I’m there. So, yes, the age difference. So what?"

Chrisley also shed some light on his proposal, which came a mere five months into their relationship.

"When he gave me the ring, he was like, ‘Before I open this, I just want you to know that this is just an expression of love to you. This can be whatever you want it to be. This can be an engagement ring, a promise ring, a cocktail ring for all I care. I just want you to know how much I love you,'" she said. "And there was no pressure ever put on me to, like, ‘You have to accept this as this.'"

Although she acknowledged that the engagement took place fairly early in their relationship, she added, "timing means nothing."

Chrisley announced the news of her pregnancy on Oct. 27 an adorable Instagram post.

“I’ve prayed for this life. I’ve cried for this life. And there were moments I truly wondered if this life would ever be mine. And just when I thought my heart couldn’t hold any ›more love, God gave us our sweetest blessing yet ... we’re having a BABY!," Chrisley said in the social media post announcing the news, which saw her cradling her baby bump while sitting on her kitchen island and kissing Galanis.

“The past few years have taken me through fires I never imagined I’d have to walk through. Seasons of heartbreak, loss, and moments when I didn’t know if I would ever make it to the other side. I wondered if I would ever find my forever ... if I would ever feel safe enough to truly breathe again. And then God sent me J," she added.

“My protector. My fiercest fighter. My most loyal person. My lover. My safe place. A man with the patience of Job (and Lord knows he needs it). The one who makes me laugh even on my hardest days. For the first time in a long time, I feel safe. I feel fulfilled. I can finally exhale. I found my forever in you," Chrisley said.

The TV personality then took a moment to praise her partner for how caring he has been during her pregnancy: “J, watching the way you already love and protect our baby before he/she has even entered this world has made me fall in love with you in an entirely new way. Not a single doctor’s appointment missed. Constantly caring for me, talking about our baby, and reminding me how beautiful my growing bump is. I thank God every day that this baby gets to call you Daddy."

“I once prayed just to make it through another day. Now I get to spend forever with the love of my life, carrying a little miracle we already love more than words. From heartbreak to healing. From surviving to living. From praying for my forever to building a family with him. Only God could have written this story. Here’s to forever, J ... and the sweetest little blessing we can’t wait to meet," she added.

Chrisley had kept the identity of her partner under wraps until now, having previously revealed on her podcast, "Unlocked with Savannah Chrisley,"  that she wouldn't share his name "until after I'm married."

In the latest episode of her podcast, she revealed she and Jason began their romance last July, branding it a "dream relationship."

She revealed that Galanis proposed five months into their relationship when they were in the Cayman Islands. "The ring is insane and it’s everything I ever wanted."

She then revealed that the couple connected after Jason reached out to her to praise her for her efforts to get her parents out of prison.

Todd and Julie Chrisley were found guilty in 2022 of conspiring to defraud Georgia banks out of more than $36 million in personal loans and tax evasion, before being pardoned by President Donald Trump in May 2025.

Savannah Chrisley has frequently spoken out about the toll of her parents' incarceration.

Todd, 57, was sentenced to 12 years (later reduced to 10 years) in the Federal Correctional Institution Pensacola in Florida. Julie, 53, was sentenced to seven years in the Federal Medical Center in Lexington, KY.

Following her parents' incarceration, Savannah took on the care of her brother, Grayson, 19, and her niece, Chloe, 13, while also assuming responsibility for the care and maintenance of her parents' opulent dwelling.

At the same time, the burgeoning real estate agent was tirelessly campaigning for Todd and Julie's release, issuing public pleas for government support, while alleging that her parents were being subjected to "beyond inhumane" conditions behind bars.

On May 27, her prayers were answered when Trump revealed to her in a personal phone call that he planned to pardon her parents. Just a few days later, they were released from prison.

At the time, Savannah revealed she was ready to return the hefty upkeep of their home to Todd and Julie.

#5594. Redfin Celebrates 250 Years of American History Through the Places We Call Home

From today, Redfin is celebrating America’s 250th anniversary by spotlighting the stories of iconic homes of America. Featured alongside millions of homes for sale or rent on Redfin.com, these historic properties offer a unique window into the people, pivotal moments and enduring spirit that have shaped America.

With immersive tours, detailed photography and stories of the people who lived within the walls, the franchise will bring the past into the present. Each property will also host a free in-person event, complemented by virtual experiences that make these remarkable stories accessible to people nationwide.

Each property will debut separately and remain on Redfin through the end of 2027.

“America’s story isn’t just written in history books. It’s written in the homes where people have dreamed, created, persevered and changed the course of our nation,” said Jonathan Mildenhall, Chief Marketing Officer of Rocket. “As we celebrate 250 years of American independence, Redfin Presents Iconic Homes of America is an invitation to rediscover the extraordinary stories behind these front doors, and to recognize that every home, in its own way, is part of the American story.”

Built around 1740, the Betsy Ross House offers a glimpse into the determination, ingenuity and entrepreneurial spirit of a working woman during America’s founding.

The Philadelphia home is associated with Betsy Ross, the upholsterer, entrepreneur and Revolutionary-era flag maker whose story became intertwined with the creation of the first American flag. While historians continue to debate parts of the familiar legend, records show Ross was an accomplished tradeswoman who made flags for the government for decades.

The home’s remarkable story extends beyond the Revolutionary era. When it faced demolition in the late 19th century, Americans from across the country came together to preserve it, contributing through 10-cent memberships. It was an early demonstration of the collective pride and community spirit that continue to give historic places their meaning.

Its Redfin listing-style page looks beyond the legend to explore Ross as a business owner, working mother and survivor who built an extraordinary life within two small, rented rooms.

Built between 1887 and 1892, Bishop’s Palace was designed by Nicholas J. Clayton, Galveston’s most influential architect, for lawyer and congressman Walter Gresham, his wife, Josephine, and their seven children. The home spans 52 rooms and 19,086 square feet. It became the residence of Bishop Byrne after the Catholic Church purchased it in 1923.

Each detail of the home was custom-chosen, from hand-carved woodwork throughout to a dining room ceiling mural painted by Josephine herself. At the heart of the home, an octagonal mahogany rotunda staircase rises beneath French stained glass, surrounded by finishes from Venice, Holland and North Africa.

The property also includes a few conversation pieces, among them Josephine’s china collection, the original bed, Walter’s desk and Bishop Byrne’s player piano. It sits in Galveston’s East End Historic District, a neighborhood of colorful historic homes and lush landscaping, with the Gulf only a few blocks south.

Today, Bishop’s Palace stands as a one-of-a-kind blend of elaborate craftsmanship, Texan influence and Gilded Age ambition.

Anthropic filed to go public on Monday under the ticker ANT, and you may end up owning the stock soon even if you never buy it directly, because index funds and ETFs will be required to buy it within weeks of its debut.

Anthropic’s bankers are reportedly valuing Anthropic between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion. Below is a simple, interactive tool to help you form your own opinion of what’s an appropriate valuation for Anthropic.

Disclaimer: this is highly simplified, and I’m not an investment advisor.

The whole IPO debate comes down to two numbers nobody knows: how much revenue Anthropic will have in 2028, and how much of it will be profit. Pick yours.

Your number = revenue × margin × profit multiple. The IPO valuation is $2 trillion, the top of the reported range. The arithmetic ignores two things that roughly cancel: a 2028 profit is worth about 17% less today than the same profit earned now, and Anthropic’s $132 billion in cash adds about 7% to any result. Big Tech multiples are market value divided by the latest quarter’s operating profit, annualized; margins are operating margins from the latest quarter. #5592. Mortgage Rates Drop From September Highs as Midterms and Jobs Data Loom

In A Nutshell: Rates have fallen about 30–40 basis points since the peak at the end of September and there’s little reason to believe the volatility will slow down.

The Fed meeting last Wednesday was the highlight of the week, with the committee voting to hold rates steady as expected. There were two dissents, with one coming from a surprising source, Governor Lisa Cook, who is usually seen as someone who favors lower rates. The statement and press conference reiterated a desire to keep hiking, making a December hike more likely than not if the economic data comes in as expected.

The Fed has been highlighting elevated inflation and strong economic growth as its reason for hiking. And Q3 GDP, in fact, came in at a brisk 3.4% annual rate. Real business fixed investment spending grew at a 12.7% annual rate thanks to rapid growth in AI spending. And real consumption grew at a 3.8% annual rate as people spent out of savings and wealth increases rather than income growth. The question now is what happens to growth in Q4. Real-time data is pointing to a potential slowdown as consumers pull back.

It’s another big week with both the midterm election tomorrow and employment data arriving throughout the week. Democrats are expected to comfortably gain a majority in the House of Representatives with control of the Senate also favoring Democrats, but less certain. Expectations for government spending, which has been a factor for rates, could certainly change with a more divided government. But the near term economic impact might be felt most acutely as we near government funding and debt limit deadlines. The closest budget deadline is December 11, which might get pushed to Q1. And we’re likely to hit the debt limit again in Q1 at which point the Treasury will take “extraordinary measures” until we truly run out of options sometime before October 2027.

Since it’s the first week of the month, we’ll also get the typical employment reports, including job openings and turnover on Tuesday and the official jobs report on Friday. With the Fed squarely focused on inflation, the jobs report mostly serves as a check on whether the Fed needs to turn its attention back to recession risk, which would reduce the need for the rate hikes that markets have priced in. So far this year, the answer has been “no,” with the labor market on solid enough footing and that is not expected to change with this week’s data.

Finally, Fed officials are out of their blackout period following last week’s FOMC meeting. With Chairman Warsh typically reluctant to offer much forward guidance, markets have been relying more on surrogates to forecast the outcome of the next meeting. There are numerous speaking engagements on the calendar, including Cleveland Fed President Hammack and Dallas Fed President Logan on Thursday, and New York Fed President Williams on Friday. Forecasters will be looking for clues to support the “hike every other meeting” thesis.

#5590. Tiger Woods Sets Plans for a Private Golf Destination With Member Cottages on Long Island’s Gold Coast

Golf legend Tiger Woods is heading up a new private golf destination on the North Shore of Long Island in Brookville, NY.

In collaboration with private golf club and lifestyle company the Armchair Collective and TGR Design, the 11-time PGA Player of the Year recipient will redevelop the former Tam O'Shanter Country Club, which was shuttered in 2021, according to Golf Course Architecture.

The project will feature a brand-new 18-hole course with practice facilities, a performance center, a clubhouse, and private member cottages.

"The opportunity to create a new golf experience in the heart of Long Island's Gold Coast, a region steeped in rich history, is tremendously exciting for our team," Woods said.

The golfer explained the location's significance, citing the "great memories" he has from competing in the area, "especially at Bethpage."

"This region has an extraordinary golf course architecture tradition, and we look forward to contributing to that legacy with a course that players can ejoy for generations," he continued.

While fans will have to wait until the beginning of 2027 for the name and conceptual renderings to be revealed, work is already underway. Demolition has begun, and construction is slated to begin next year.

"Bringing Tiger Woods and TGR Design to this beautiful and historic part of Long Island is a remarkable opportunity," said Brookville Mayor Dan Serota. "Combining the Gold Coast's longstanding golf tradition with Tiger and his team's skill and attention to detail makes this an exciting project for Brookville and the broader region."

In October, another Woods-spearheaded project was announced. The golfer is part of a luxury residential golf community in Fort Worth, TX, called Bluejack Ranch.

The $2.5 billion community and private club is a 914-acre resort-style development. The community will feature 500 custom and semicustom homes, ranging in size from 1,282 square feet to sprawling mansions spanning more than 19,000 square feet.

Pricing begins at $775,000 for half-acre lots to build on, whereas residential products begin at $1 million and average between $2 million and $4 million.

"You live on 900 acres with every form of entertainment imaginable," developer Andy Mitchell tells Realtor.com®. "You don't need a big home, necessarily. It's like going to a resort, you don't have to build your own game room."

Bluejack Ranch is Woods' second project of this nature and is the followup to his first, Bluejack National in Montgomery, TX.

When it comes to his own private residence, Woods is no stranger to exclusive community living. He currently resides in a $60 million Jupiter Island waterfront estate.

Woods purchased the 12-acre plot—which overlooks the Indian River—for $40 million in 2006. He razed the existing residence to build his own custom 9,700-square-fooot megamansion.

In addition to the striking structure, the estate includes a sizable swimming pool and a separate lap pool, a tennis court, a running track, and, of course, a private golf course.

#5589. Beyond the books: Real-time data is driving a small-business lending surge

Small businesses have long treated cash flow management as an afterthought, tallying expenses after the money is gone. Now, financial platforms are folding payments, payroll, credit and lending into one system that can see money moving both ways — and predict where it is headed.

That shift puts software providers in direct competition with banks for small-business credit. Intuit Inc. says its view of both sides of the ledger, paired with AI pushing finance toward automation, gives it an edge traditional lenders cannot match, according to Todd Denbo (pictured), senior vice president of lending and commercial leader of Money at Intuit.

“We can see the expenses you’ve got queued up,” Denbo said. “For us, we can effectively predict that you’re going to have a cash flow shortage. That’s why we’ve got our lending businesses as well, so we can proactively offer lines of credit or a term loan to bridge that gap.”

Denbo spoke with theCUBE’s Alison Kosik and Christophe Bertrand at Intuit Connect, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how Intuit uses real-time financial data and AI to help small businesses manage cash flow and automate financial tasks. (* Disclosure below.)

Intuit lent about $400 million a year four years ago and almost $7 billion in its most recent fiscal year, according to Denbo. That growth reflects data averaging 625,000 data points per small business across the 10 million companies already on the platform. Because those businesses manage their finances on Intuit’s platform, the company can see money coming in and going out as it happens.

“Most lenders in this space rely on outdated trends that are from the commercial credit bureaus or the personal credit bureaus, or they’re trying to infer data that is just very challenging to infer,” Denbo said. “All of that is real-time.”

Intuit has also added spending data through its QuickBooks-integrated business credit card, which lets owners control employee spending before money leaves. The company has extended QuickBooks into Claude and ChatGPT as well, though automation still stops short of moving money on its own, Denbo explained. AI can handle the financial groundwork while business owners retain the final say over actions involving their money.

“We are gathering the data, we’re analyzing the data, we are packaging a response or a draft,” Denbo said. “But when it comes to anything that is moving money or sending a draft out, that’s where we’re waiting for, effectively, a human intervention.”

#5588. A new pal for Pluto? Rubin Observatory finds its first dwarf planet candidate

by Alan Boyle on Oct 27, 2026 at 7:54 pmOctober 27, 2026 at 8:23 pm

Astronomers sorting through data from the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile have found an icy world that has a good chance of joining Pluto in the solar system’s retinue of dwarf planets.

University of Washington astronomer Mario Jurić joined the astronomer who made the discovery, Matthew Holman of the Harvard & Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics, to announce the findings today at a meeting of the American Astronomical Society’s Division for Planetary Sciences in Spokane, Wash.

Jurić, the Rubin team’s solar system lead scientist, said the observatory’s capabilities made it possible to detect and characterize the new dwarf planet candidate, known as 2026 ED138.

“Rubin is giving us an unprecedented capacity to explore the sky through a combination of speed, depth, and precision,” Jurić said in a news release. “And the discovery is just the beginning: Once we identify a new object, we can search back months, and sometimes even decades, finding it in images where nobody knew to look. This ability to both discover and ‘precover’ objects is transforming how quickly and accurately we can determine their orbits and understand the distant solar system.”

2026 ED138 traces a tilted orbital path that takes it well beyond Pluto, the solar system’s best-known dwarf planet. It’s currently at a distance of 46 astronomical units, where 1 AU equals the average distance between Earth and the sun. Pluto, by comparison, is currently about 40 AU from the sun.

Astronomers suspect ED138 formed billions of years ago closer to the sun before being flung into a wider orbit by gravitational interactions with Neptune.

Based on an analysis of its distance, brightness and assumed composition, ED138 is thought to be somewhere between 600 and 1,500 kilometers (373 to 932 miles) in diameter. At that size, an icy object should possess enough gravity to pull itself into a round shape — satisfying the primary physical criterion for a dwarf planet.

ED138 may be Rubin’s first dwarf planet candidate, but it almost certainly won’t be the last. Thanks to the observatory’s Simonyi Survey Telescope — named after the family of Seattle software billionaire Charles Simonyi — the Rubin team detected more than 11,000 new asteroids even before June’s official start of a 10-year survey of the southern sky.

Rubin’s researchers analyze the data from those scans to find objects of interest — ranging from asteroids to gamma-ray bursts — and track them over time. On Oct. 13, Holman was running data through a search code that he developed with Kevin Napier, a colleague at the Center for Astrophysics. ED138 stood out due to its exceptional size and brightness.

“My first reaction was one of excited disbelief,” Holman said. “Objects like this are very rare, so I immediately started checking whether I or the code had done something wrong.”

To confirm the discovery, Holman, Jurić and their colleagues found 30 archived observations of ED138 dating back to March 4. The Asteroid Institute’s ADAM Precovery service found still more images of the object, going back to 2016, in the archives of a different astronomical survey.

The precovery data confirmed that ED138 was a special case.

“Finding an object this big, roughly 1,000 kilometers across, is something that happens maybe once in a generation,” Jurić said. “It’s the largest trans-Neptunian object found in about 20 years, and Rubin turned it up while we were still commissioning the telescope.”

In 2006, the International Astronomical Union defined dwarf planets as planetary objects that are big enough to crush themselves into a roundish shape — technically speaking, into a state of hydrostatic equilibrium — but not big enough to clear their orbital neighborhood.

So far, the IAU has classified five solar system objects as dwarf planets — including Ceres in the main asteroid belt, plus Pluto, Eris, Haumea and Makemake in the region beyond Neptune. 2026 ED138 joins a host of other celestial objects that are thought to be dwarf planets but haven’t yet been added to the IAU’s official list.

“The official list hasn’t moved since 2008,” Jurić told GeekWire in an email. “I’m not sure if there’s an active process that reviews candidates, and what are the timelines.”

Jurić and his colleagues hope additional observations will boost ED138’s chances of attaining true dwarf planethood.

“The next step in building the case would be to prove it’s round (in hydrostatic equilibrium),” he wrote. “The means to do that would be directly through occultations (and there’s a good chance of that, given it’s in a dense stellar field), and then thermal measurements plus modeling and light curves (or the absence of variability).”

#5586. Intuit targets the mid-market ERP gap with AI

Growing companies that outgrow entry-level accounting software face a hard choice: Stay put or gamble on a mid-market ERP that promises automation but often brings cost and disruption. Artificial intelligence is now giving financial software providers a way to close that gap without forcing businesses through a risky migration.

Intuit Inc. is pushing finance toward automation, and its mid-market strategy targets companies caught between small-business tools and legacy systems. Those businesses face the problems of success, such as more customers, more entities and more currencies, and need technology to help them scale, according to Ashley Still (pictured), executive vice president and general manager of mid-market at Intuit.

“Actually, 50% of mid-market ERP implementations fail,” Still said. “So, 50% of businesses that leave their existing financial platform to go to what they think will be a better platform for them actually fail in that implementation. It typically costs $60,000 and six months.”

Still spoke with Alison Kosik and Christophe Bertrand at Intuit Connect, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed why mid-market ERP migrations fail, how Intuit Enterprise Suite fills the gap and how AI agents are taking on routine finance work. (* Disclosure below.)

Intuit’s answer is Intuit Enterprise Suite, which lets growing companies scale on the platform where their data already lives instead of starting over. Intuit has added industry-specific editions for construction, manufacturing and nonprofits. Still described the product as the CFO’s command center.

“First, they actually can see a complete view of the business for the first time ever, all of their entities in one place, consolidated financials,” she said. “That really is game-changing because it gives them the ability to make real-time decisions.”

Accounting firms are central to the plan, since 70% of mid-market businesses work with an accountant or advisor, according to Still. Intuit is automating routine work such as categorizations and reconciliations, while its new Agent Studio lets a business or firm build a customizable agent just by describing what it needs. Accounting firms Citrin Cooperman and Sorren have already put agents into production through the tool, she noted.

“The point is the expectation is that more and more of the tedious work is done for a finance team or done for a firm rather than them having to do everything themselves,” Still said.

#5584. The hidden threat in Anthropic’s prospectus: diseconomies of scale

GUEST COLUMN by Jason Bloomberg

As potentially the largest IPO in history, Anthropic PBC is breaking new ground. Its prospectus lists 88 risk factors covering 93 pages alone. From artificial intelligence posing an existential threat to humanity to the possibility AI will blackmail people, the company lists a litany of risks that should make any potential Anthropic investor wary.

One potentially company-sinking risk factor, however, does not explicitly appear in the prospectus: diseconomies of scale.

Diseconomies of scale occur when a company’s average cost of producing each unit of output increases as the company grows.

You would think that given the time and effort that Anthropic devoted to ensuring its list of risk factors was complete that they would have included this one. There is a reason, however, that they missed it, despite the fact that diseconomies of scale is the elephant in the room.

We’ve been down this road before with cloud computing. The fundamental economic driver of the hyperscaler clouds was economies of scale: the larger they became, the lower their cost of each unit of output, leading to massive growth and profitability over time.

Since the AI boom requires massive data center buildouts just as cloud computing does, it might be reasonable to assume that AI will experience the same economic benefits of massive growth that cloud computing enjoyed.

This assumption, however, is likely to be false. To understand why, we must take a look at how the software and cloud businesses scale – and why AI is so different.

Throughout the history of enterprise computing, software has benefited from its negligible marginal cost.

With physical goods, from automobiles to chicken nuggets, every unit has a raw materials and production cost. The more widgets you make, the more those costs add up.

Software is fundamentally different. Once a vendor has spent the money to build an application, it can sell that application to as many customers as it can find, where the cost of delivering additional copies of that application is negligible compared to the original cost of developing it.

This negligible marginal cost enables software vendors to become immensely profitable as their business scales.

Computer hardware, in contrast, is nothing more than more widgets – the more you deploy, the greater your materials and production costs.

Cloud computing combines both software and hardware in its offerings. The software may have negligible marginal cost, but each cloud provider must shell out money for each physical server.

To address this cost challenge, cloud providers take advantage of economies of scale.

The hyperscalers built their clouds by deploying massive numbers of commodity servers. As each firm expanded its business, the cost of each unit of output – say, the cost of providing a server instance or a unit of cloud storage – decreased.

As a result, the cost of servers went down as they scaled, and the cloud computing firms became increasingly profitable as they grew, despite the fact that their business models depended on hardware as well as software.

Back to Anthropic and the rest of the frontier large language model providers: Ostensibly, AI is just a type of software, and Anthropic is running its software in hyperscaled data centers that are essentially clouds. This underlying assumption is implicit in the company’s prospectus.

This assumption, however, is flawed. Frontier model vendors require graphics processing units and other premium, expensive hardware from day one – and their specialized processor requirements continue to accelerate as they rapidly innovate their software.

This advancing specialized processor requirement didn’t impact the rise of the cloud. True, each cloud provider eventually added various specialized hardware instance types as they grew, but those instances didn’t change the fundamental economics of the cloud business.

Anthropic, in contrast, doesn’t have the luxury of deploying commodity hardware to achieve economies of scale. Instead, it must build out expensive servers that only get more expensive as LLMs’ processor requirements continue to advance.

There are also diseconomies of scaling the human side of the AI boom that contrast with the growth of the cloud.

The hyperscalers certainly require an experienced workforce with deep expertise to deploy their clouds and keep them running. But as they grew, they were able to leverage such personnel more efficiently. An admin who managed a thousand physical servers could easily manage 10,000 or a million as the underlying cloud platforms matured.

Unlike the cloud providers, however, Anthropic and the other frontier model vendors must continually scale up the expertise of their teams. New LLMs aren’t simply scaled-out versions of older ones. Each one requires new expertise from expert humans.

Anthropic is battling its competitors to innovate quickly and roll out increasingly powerful models on unprecedented timeframes. As a result, frontier LLM vendor teams experience diseconomies of scale that the hyperscalers never had to face.

Anthropic and the rest of the frontier LLM vendors suffer from a fundamentally novel economic reality, because they must continue to increase their hardware capabilities while upskilling their workforce so they can competitively innovate their software.

They can’t simply run increasingly powerful models on commodity hardware – or even the same hardware they ran the previous generation model on. They must increase their investments in hardware at a pace that keeps up with the pace of software innovation.

The end result is a diseconomy of scale the technology industry has never seen before. We are so used to the negligible marginal cost of software and the massive economies of scale of the cloud, that we are simply unprepared for the diseconomies of scale that frontier LLM vendors like Anthropic must negotiate.

Even though the frontier model marketplace is still quite new, we’re already seeing the impact of its inherent diseconomies of scale as token costs become an increasingly significant expense for consumers of AI.

As LLMs become more powerful and the hardware they require becomes an increasingly expensive bottleneck, it’s just a matter of time until token costs become prohibitively high for a range of AI-based applications.

Anthropic and the other LLM model vendors can try to respond by increasing the efficiency of their more powerful LLMs or rolling out less powerful, and thus less expensive models – assuming their customers buy into these moves.

We may also eventually reach a plateau where the models are sufficiently powerful and the hardware is sufficiently performant, thus enabling more familiar economies of scale to take over. However, no such plateau is in sight.

The question potential Anthropic investors must ask, therefore, is whether the company’s leadership position in the LLM market is a strength or a weakness? Just how far can it innovate and grow before its offerings are too expensive? And what does it do then?

Jason Bloomberg is founder and managing director of Intellyx, which advises business leaders and technology vendors on their digital transformation strategies. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE. All of Intellyx’s content is 100% human generated, including this article. Anthropic is not an Intellyx customer.

#5582. New York Knicks Star Josh Hart Takes Another Shot at Selling Florida Home for $5.7 Million

New York Knicks star Josh Hart has relisted his sprawling Florida mansion for $5.69 million—just one year after removing the home from the selling block.

The 31-year-old shooting guard and his wife, Shannon Hart, snapped up the palatial mansion in 2022 for $4.75 million.

Last year, they listed the property for $5.9 million, then cut the price to $5.8 million, before removing it from the market.

Now, the home has been relisted with Michael Martinez of ONE Sotheby’s International Realty, as first reported by The Wall Street Journal.

The five-bedroom mansion spans 5,800 square feet and features lush amenities.

Soaring ceilings and large windows flood the home with natural light. The chef's kitchen is equipped with stylish cabinetry, a large white island, and state-of-the-art appliances.

"Thoughtfully designed with an expansive open floor plan, the home showcases spacious living and entertaining areas, a charming breakfast nook, a beautifully appointed kitchen with designer appliances and walk-in pantry, and the convenience of second-floor laundry facilities," adds the listing.

The primary bedroom is the perfect place to relax thanks to its large balcony, which offers sweeping views of the property's lush setting.

"Designed for seamless indoor-outdoor living, expansive covered terraces provide inviting spaces for relaxation and entertaining, while a resort-style pool, summer kitchen, and private putting green create the ultimate setting for alfresco dining and year-round enjoyment," the listing notes.

The home offers a "remarkable opportunity to experience refined South Florida living in one of Pinecrest's most desirable neighborhoods," the listing continues.

Hart also installed a putting green and an outdoor sound system.

Although Hart spends the majority of his time in New York, during the basketball offseason, he relaxes in Florida.

“We will be back. We loved the location," he told the Journal, revealing that he would be buying another home in the area after he retires.

Speaking about the property, Hart revealed his favorite spot was the breakfast nook: “The ability to go down there, make coffee, hang out with the boys, watch a little TV, kick it by the breakfast nook—that was the highlight.”

In 2024, the couple splashed out an undisclosed sum on a property in New York, which he purchased from local Compass real estate agent Kim Arenas.

“We are thrilled to have had the opportunity to help these amazing clients find their home! From searching off-market homes, exploring the plans to adding the final touches, it was a wonderful journey building their new home.

"We can’t wait for their family to create lasting memories here. And of course, go Knicks!” wrote Arenas.

Little is known about where the property is located or its amenities.

#5581. As Anthropic finally files for its IPO, rising risks aren’t slowing the AI buildout – yet

THIS WEEK IN ENTERPRISE by Robert Hof

The other artificial intelligence shoe dropped this week, as Anthropic filed for what surely will be the second blockbuster AI initial public offering of stock this year.

Nearly 70,000 words in the filing list a ton of risks, but in short, it’s making unimaginably huge bets on buying computing power, it’s uncertain on how long customers will keep spending on AI in the face of dubious returns — and of course there’s the really-not-unusual “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.” And as Jason Bloomberg writes, the unmentioned risk is that AI as of today doesn’t have the economies of scale that made software so lucrative.

But it’s hard to imagine it won’t be crazily successful if and when it happens before Thanksgiving. They’ll join the 70% of Nvidia employees who are millionaires. Shed another tear for anyone looking for affordable housing in the Bay Area — we’re not building our way out of this, no matter what YIMBY folks hope.

One interesting wrinkle: SpaceXAI, the other AI IPO earlier this year, will be hoping Anthropic’s offering is successful, since it’s supplying a large chunk of that compute. Same with other AI partner/rivals such as Google and Microsoft.

And Anthropic isn’t alone in amassing cash to continue buying and building more AI infrastructure. Meta this week said it will issue $95 billion in nonvoting stock to build even more. Few, least of all universal backstop Nvidia, seem to think the AI and data center backlash will dent this investment. But that doesn’t mean everyone will win. As SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said this week, self-servingly but perhaps not wrongly (Gartner agrees), a lot of AI neoclouds are going to go belly-up.

Investor worry extends to the big cloud providers too. Despite a continued boom in its cloud business, Google parent Alphabet saw its stock swoon more than 12% Thursday, vaporizing more than $500 billion in market value as it reported a slow quarter for search and ads — perhaps because AI chatbots are siphoning off people’s attention. Microsoft fared better thanks to its resilient application layer on which it can apply AI. But despite strong cloud revenue growth, Amazon stock fell on concerns it could be spending too much on infrastructure. All that came to a head Friday, when the Nasdaq tanked, down almost 3%.

Seems like investors are just generally skittish. On a tear this year until now, Intel stock plunged almost 30% after its Thursday earnings report, on concerns the PC business is slowing. Fortinet also fell more than 20% following its report that included a slightly lower outlook.

For some wider perspective on the AI buildout and what’s needed to make it pay off, check out Dave Vellante’s Breaking Analysis, a late addition here Saturday, a conversation with analyst Crawford Del Prete.

Don’t relax yet. Next week there’s another earningspalooza, including Apple, AMD, Supermicro, Qualcomm, Arm and Palantir.

So an apparent Chinese spy for some time has been hanging around Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who evidently didn’t know she was more than a customer executive. Lordy. The New York Times laid out the bones of the U.S. government’s concern, but read it carefully and it sure seems like there are some missing dots throughout. Perhaps this kind of espionage is more common than we know where there’s a nexus of big money and geopolitics, but this may not be the last we hear of it, even if the Trump administration is shrugging.

Oh, and there’s an election next week that might change things… in unpredictable, not necessarily great ways for the economy. Fasten those seatbelts. And vote (but not for the wrong people, thanks).

#5580. Amazon earnings preview: AWS is booked up, and Wall Street wants to know what comes next

by Todd Bishop on Oct 28, 2026 at 8:11 amOctober 28, 2026 at 8:11 am

Amazon reports third-quarter earnings Thursday afternoon with more demand for its cloud services than it can serve, driven by AI labs such as Anthropic and OpenAI along with growth in its traditional cloud business.

One big question for Wall Street going into the report is what Amazon might signal about next year’s spending as it tries to keep up with that demand.

CEO Andy Jassy said on an Andreessen Horowitz podcast last week that AWS capacity is largely booked for this year and next, along with “a good chunk of ’28.”

Amazon has said it expects to spend about $220 billion on capital expenditures this year, largely on AI and cloud infrastructure, up from its earlier plan of $200 billion. Even at that level, Jassy said, Amazon is “leaving a meaningful amount of demand on the table.”

Past spending pushed Amazon’s free cash flow to negative $7.6 billion for the 12 months ending in June, as the cost to add data centers, chips and other equipment exceeded the cash its operations brought in. Jassy gave no indication of slowing down, saying the company “could invest a lot more and it wouldn’t be a bad use of capital.”

Core numbers: Analysts expect revenue of about $202 billion, up 12% from a year ago, according to Yahoo Finance. That’s at the top of Amazon’s own forecast of $197 billion to $202 billion.

Analysts expect earnings of $1.96 per share, about the same as a year ago.

Amazon’s sales growth will likely look slower this time, about 12%, down from 20% last quarter. A big reason is timing. Prime Day, the company’s biggest sales event of the year, fell in the second quarter this year, rather than the third quarter as it did last year, so this quarter is up against a tougher comparison.

Amazon estimated in July that the shift would take nearly 4 percentage points off its growth rate this quarter. It hits online store sales hardest: analysts expect them to grow only about 3%, according to Zacks.

AWS: Amazon Web Services, the company’s cloud business, generates the majority of its operating profit. AWS revenue grew 37% to $42.2 billion in the second quarter, its fastest pace since 2021 and the fifth straight quarter of faster growth.

Analysts expect AWS revenue of about $45.4 billion this time, up 37.5%, according to Zacks. Wedbush is more optimistic, projecting growth of about 41%.

AWS had $496 billion in signed contracts it hadn’t yet delivered as of June, more than double the year before. That means its growth depends largely on how quickly Amazon can bring new data centers online.

“Capacity, not demand, is the constraint,” Yorkville Ives analyst Dan Ives wrote of the industry in a note Sunday.

Jassy said on the a16z podcast that running AI models is still “an order of magnitude too expensive” for businesses to use them widely, and that Amazon’s custom chips, including its Trainium AI processors, are a big piece of bringing that cost down. Amazon said in July that its chip business was on pace for more than $25 billion in annual revenue.

Anthropic stake: Amazon’s reported earnings could look very different. That’s because its profit fluctuates significantly depending on the value of its stake in Anthropic.

Last quarter, $53.4 billion in pre-tax gains, mostly on Anthropic, pushed Amazon’s earnings to $5.75 per share, against expectations of $1.82.

Anthropic filed paperwork Monday for a planned IPO on the Nasdaq. Amazon’s stake in the AI company was valued at about $190 billion as of June 30, according to Amazon’s latest quarterly filing. That includes about $92 billion in gains on convertible notes, a form of loan that turns into stock, which haven’t yet been counted in Amazon’s profit. Those notes would convert to Anthropic stock when it goes public.

Anthropic is also one of Amazon’s biggest cloud customers. Its IPO filing shows commitments to spend at least $110 billion on Amazon’s computing capacity into the 2030s, behind the $114.5 billion it committed to Google, as GeekWire reported Tuesday. Anthropic also said in the filing that it has asked its cloud providers for more computing power than they were willing to supply.

Shopping agents: Amazon blocked Meta’s new Muse AI agent from its store last month, escalating a fight over who controls the customer relationship when software does the buying. Amazon said Muse broke its rule requiring agents to identify themselves.

Agents that shop on a customer’s behalf could bypass Amazon’s advertising business, which depends on people browsing its pages. Ad revenue grew 26% to $19.8 billion last quarter, and analysts expect about $20.8 billion this time, up 18%, according to Zacks.

“Investor questions remain on agentic commerce risk, particularly to advertising, but we see limited risk,” Wedbush analyst Ygal Arounian wrote in an Oct. 16 note, citing Amazon’s logistics advantage and its role connecting shoppers with sellers.

Amazon is trying to give shoppers fewer reasons to look elsewhere. It now lists 250 million products sold on other retailers’ sites, about 2.5 times as many as in March, The Information reported Wednesday. On the seller side, Amazon opened its tools to outside AI agents in September, starting with Anthropic’s Claude.

Cloud rivals: Microsoft and Alphabet report quarterly results Wednesday afternoon, a day before Amazon. Microsoft’s report is its first under a new structure that breaks out Azure cloud revenue every quarter.

Check back with GeekWire on Thursday afternoon for coverage.

#5579. Krafton-backed Ludo Robotics releases robot intelligence model designed around human intent

Ludo Robotics Inc., a subsidiary of major South Korean video game publisher Krafton Inc., today debuted Ludi 0.2, a robotics artificial intelligence system built to understand people and interact with them in the physical world.

Headquartered in Palo Alto, Ludo spun out of Krafton, a company that primarily publishes video games and is best known for the ultra-popular “PUBG: Battlegrounds.” Ludo also has a research and development lab in Seoul where it combines the efforts of researchers and engineers across robotics, machine learning and AI.

Krafton Chief Executive CH Kim also helms Ludo as CEO, with Krafton’s Chief AI Officer Kangwook Lee serving as its chief technology officer.

Why did a video game company form and back an AI robotics company? Krafton said it believes AI makes games more responsive and replayable. It also has strong roots in simulation, interaction and real-time systems, which have immediate applications in the bridge between the digital and physical, where the interaction between humans and robots lives.

“Robots are becoming increasingly capable of performing physical tasks, but understanding and responding to people remains a major challenge,” said Lee. “Ludi 0.2 represents another step toward our goal of bringing conversation, reasoning and physical action together so robots can better understand human intent, respond to feedback and adapt as situations change.”

The company introduced the first version of Ludi 0.1 in August 2026. It combines a vision-language model for reasoning and dialogue with specialized navigation and manipulation capabilities. Today’s next-generation model has advanced its capabilities, forming more natural human-robot interaction, including social intelligence, memory and reasoning, tool coordination, gesture interpretation, and physical movement.

The company said it’s working toward a final version of Ludi that will integrate perception, dialogue and physical action.

The objective is to integrate communication, reasoning and physical action into one “brain.” The model would watch what’s happening, listen to commands and speech, interpret those commands alongside human gestures and physical movements and reason about the environment. This would happen in real time, coordinating similarly to how another human decides on actions based on another person’s actions in their workspace.

This is the “Holy Grail” of physical AI, where intelligent robots can perform actions not just in industrial environments and warehouses, but also retail and domestic spaces such as restaurants, living rooms and kitchens.

Krafton said much of its work includes proprietary foundation models and co-playable characters developed in collaboration with Nvidia Corp., AI teammates designed to understand players in real time. Ludo builds on this foundation to develop the same kind of intelligence into real-world robots.

Startups are bringing the physical world to robots so they can see objects and grab and move them with increasing capability. Interpreting human intent and responding to social cues from people around the robot, however, remains elusive. Simulation makes it easy for physical AI to prepare robots to work with objects and around humans, but it doesn’t always prepare them to model human behavior.

#5578. Blue Origin leases former Bartell Drugs warehouse south of Seattle for new manufacturing site

by Kurt Schlosser on Oct 28, 2026 at 8:25 amOctober 28, 2026 at 12:33 pm

Blue Origin is taking over an industrial building in Des Moines, Wash., where the Jeff Bezos-founded space company plans a mix of lab, development and light production work, the company confirmed to GeekWire.

The 265,922-square-foot facility, known as Prologis Park SeaTac 3, was previously a Bartell Drugs distribution center just south of Seattle-Tacoma International Airport. Blue Origin said that at full capacity over the long term, the site is expected to support hundreds of employees.

KING 5 first reported the news Tuesday, citing a state environmental application filed in September that lists Blue Origin Manufacturing LLC at the building’s address, 21202 24th Ave. S. A pre-application under review by the city indicates the property could be used for research and development of commercial satellites, the station reported.

Commercial real estate firm Newmark announced a lease for the entire building last week without naming the tenant.

“The manufacturing project that will be using this property is cutting-edge and we are excited about the job growth and possibilities that it represents for our region,” Newmark Executive Vice Chairman Thad Mallory said in a news release.

With roughly 33,000 residents, the small city of Des Moines is becoming something of an aerospace hub.

Blue Origin’s new location is around the corner from where Shield AI is building X-Forge 3, a 420,000-square-foot facility that will make the company’s X-BAT autonomous fighter jet. Shield AI said last month it expects to have 4,000 workers in the region by the early 2030s, and that it’s looking for another 1 million square feet.

“It’s all about labor and access to power,” Mallory told KING 5, referring to the advanced manufacturing projects coming to the area.

Blue Origin is headquartered in nearby Kent, Wash., about 5 miles from the Des Moines site.

The company is working to get its New Glenn rocket flying again after one exploded during a ground engine test in May, which damaged its Florida launch pad. New Glenn is slated to carry Blue’s Blue Moon Mark 2 lander on NASA’s Artemis 3 mission, a test in Earth orbit planned for mid-2027 ahead of a crewed moon landing targeted for 2028.

#5576. Former T-Mobile CEO Mike Sievert exits board of directors, wraps up his run at the wireless giant

by Lisa Stiffler on Oct 28, 2026 at 9:51 amOctober 28, 2026 at 10:17 am

Former T-Mobile CEO Mike Sievert is hanging up his magenta hat, leaving the wireless giant’s board of directors and vice chair role effective Nov. 1.

Sievert will also leave the board’s Transaction Committee, according to a federal filing. His departure comes a year after he handed the CEO job to Srini Gopalan.

A company spokesperson said via email that the vice chair role was structured as a one-year term, adding that Sievert has “been a valued strategic advisor throughout the leadership transition, and we’re incredibly grateful for his contributions.”

T-Mobile said in the filing that his departure “is not the result of any disagreement with the Company on any matter relating to its operations, policies or practices.”

Sievert joined T-Mobile in 2012 as executive vice president and chief marketing officer, the same year John Legere became CEO. He later became president and chief operating officer and was mentored by Legere before succeeding him as chief executive in 2020. He served as CEO for about five and a half years.

Sievert was a central figure in T-Mobile’s campaign to brand itself the “Un-carrier.” During his time at the company, T-Mobile grew from fewer than 30 million customers to more than 130 million by September 2025, a period that included its merger with Sprint.

Once the scrappy outsider, Bellevue, Wash.-based T-Mobile currently ranks second among U.S. telecom companies by market capitalization, behind Verizon and ahead of AT&T.

Sievert previously worked at Microsoft, AT&T Wireless, E-Trade, IBM and Procter & Gamble.
