#5478. Enterprise architecture: Dell and Microsoft integrate hybrid AI

How can software and cloud giant Microsoft Corp. translate its platform vision into fully deployed enterprise architecture in the age of AI?

This central question has defined the next chapter in a decades-long partnership between Microsoft and Dell Technologies Inc. Dell provided some answers at this year’s Dell Technologies World by expanding its private cloud offering to deploy the latest Microsoft software implementations.

Since that event, Microsoft has worked to enable a disaggregated architecture, simplifying operations across Dell PowerEdge compute, Dell PowerStore storage and Azure Local. Flexibility is the key attraction for enterprise customers evaluating Dell and Microsoft’s joint solutions, according to Paul Nashawaty, principal analyst at theCUBE Research.

“Microsoft and Dell are moving beyond infrastructure partnerships to deliver a more integrated go-to-market strategy for enterprise AI, hybrid cloud and application modernization,” he said. “Since Dell Technologies World in May, the focus has been on connecting Microsoft Azure Local, SQL Server and hybrid-cloud capabilities with Dell’s automation platform and enterprise infrastructure to help customers deploy, govern and operate AI workloads wherever their data resides.”

This feature is part of SiliconANGLE Media’s exploration of the architectural shifts powering continuous, production-grade AI. Be sure to check out theCUBE’s “Dell AI Data Platform Event: From Ambition to AI at Scale,” and past coverage of this year’s Dell Technologies World. (* Disclosure below.)

The market opportunity for both Dell and Microsoft centers on the need to operationalize AI applications. Meeting this goal requires integration across the full AI deployment lifecycle.

Dell Automation Platform and Dell Private Cloud provide an operational backbone for deploying Azure Local on-premises and managing the hardware lifecycle, including firmware and updates. Azure Arc provides consistent management across environments. SQL Server can be run in virtual machines or Kubernetes containers without learning separate skill sets for cloud and on-premises environments.

“The key architecture for AI capabilities is integrating with things like embedding models for vector searching or chat completion models for AI agents, but we do it all inside … the SQL Server Engine,” Bob Ward, principal architect at Microsoft, told theCUBE. “We [formed a] partnership with Dell so that we can connect to anything on premises. I can connect to Azure Local, Dell [and] Nvidia Factory. We just got a framework built in. It doesn’t matter where you’re running these AI models; we can easily integrate with it.”

A central element of Dell and Microsoft’s partnership involves integrating database, automation and hybrid cloud capabilities into a stack that can feed AI the data it needs. Data fragmentation is often cited as a top blocker to scaling AI beyond pilots, and integrating the two companies’ services addresses a pressure point that surveys have identified across enterprise information technology.

Data fragmentation remains a barrier to scaling AI beyond pilots. Dell and Microsoft’s partnership brings database, automation and hybrid cloud capabilities into a common stack.

“From an AppDev perspective, that integration matters because the challenge is no longer simply building AI applications, but operationalizing them securely, consistently and at scale,” said Nashawaty. “TheCUBE AppDev Research highlights the execution gap: Approximately 88% of AI pilots fail to reach production, while 64% of enterprise AI teams identify integration complexity as a leading barrier to adoption.”

Dell’s partnership with Microsoft also extends to unstructured data storage. The two companies are bringing familiar storage capabilities into hybrid and multicloud environments.

Dell PowerScale for Microsoft Azure brings Dell’s OneFS file system software into Azure as a managed storage service. Customers can provision file storage directly from the Azure portal while retaining familiar PowerScale management capabilities.

The solution supports a wide range of production workloads across industries. These industries increasingly depend on high-throughput, low-latency file access to drive the next generation of agentic AI and advanced analytics. Media and entertainment firms can use it to handle massive video files, real-time editing and tight production timelines. Semiconductor and electronics design houses can accelerate simulation and modeling using large datasets.

“This isn’t really about running the software just in the cloud,” said Rachna Lalwani, senior consultant, director and product manager at Dell, in an interview with theCUBE. “It’s about creating a truly integrated experience that empowers businesses to do more with their data. What they really gain is the operational consistency across their entire storage landscape.”

A recent IDC analysis found that 95% of enterprises already run at least one AI agent workflow in production, and it predicted 2.5 billion agents by 2030. With the rise of agentic AI, Dell and Microsoft are collaborating on solutions designed to help enterprises deploy autonomous agents while controlling costs.

Managing the cost of tokens, the fundamental units of data processed by large language models, is one of AI’s financial challenges. To help address it, Dell introduced Deskside Agentic AI in May in collaboration with Microsoft and Nvidia Corp., providing a local environment for building and testing AI agents.

“What’s resonating with customers right now is that the cost of tokens is through the roof,” explained Jon Siegal, senior vice president of Dell portfolio marketing at Dell. “We know even though the cost of a token has come down pretty dramatically, the amount of tokens that are being consumed right now is just astronomical. The cloud costs are just pretty high right now. How do customers balance that out and run the right workload in the right place? We’re trying to give customers a place to start. The PC is a great place to start.”

In early October, Dell announced an expansion of its Windows PCs and workstations for agentic AI. In partnership with Microsoft, Dell broadened its AI development portfolio to provide creators, developers and enterprises with more choice in how they build, test and scale agentic AI on Windows.

This marked a key step in the evolution of Windows, where the platform has evolved into a broader resource for agentic AI. Tools such as Windows AI Foundry give developers a structured path to build, package and scale agents inside a governed environment.

“With Windows, we’re going beyond just it being an operating system — we’re thinking about it as really a canvas for AI,” said Mary Ann Anderson, worldwide marketing director of Dell partnerships at Microsoft. “Pretty soon there’s going to be a point where individual employees are managing their own agents, maybe a small army of agents. You have to do that in a way that is governed and is very secure.”

Dell and Microsoft see a significant market opportunity in closing the gap between AI development and production deployment.

“Microsoft and Dell have an opportunity to address that gap by simplifying deployment, automating infrastructure operations and giving partners repeatable solutions they can take to market,” said theCUBE Research’s Nashawaty. “The real measure of success will be whether their combined ecosystem helps enterprises move from AI experimentation to production-ready applications with stronger governance, predictable costs and measurable business outcomes.”

(* Disclosure: TheCUBE is a paid media partner for the Dell AI Data Platform Event. Neither Dell, the sponsor of theCUBE’s event coverage, nor other sponsors have editorial control over content on theCUBE or SiliconANGLE.)

#5476. Metal fabricator NIC Global to cut 103 jobs near Seattle, move production to Eastern Washington

by Lisa Stiffler on Oct 30, 2026 at 10:24 amOctober 30, 2026 at 10:25 am

Metal fabricator NIC Global plans to close its Woodinville, Wash., plant, eliminating 103 jobs. Declining business from local customers is prompting the company to shift production primarily to Eastern Washington to meet data center-related growth.

The layoffs are scheduled to begin Jan. 18, 2027, with final departures Aug. 31, 2028, according to a notice filed with the Washington Employment Security Department. Affected jobs include assembly, engineering, quality assurance, metal fabrication specialists, and forklift positions.

The building will be returned to its landlord when the lease ends in September 2028.

“This is a sad day for our company. Woodinville is where NIC was formed — three Seattle-area sheet-metal shops brought together under one roof in 2001 — and the people in that building built the foundation of everything NIC is today,” Troy Wood, company president and CEO, said via email.

The 100,000-square-foot site mostly served energy and medical device customers. Wood said the volume of work at the plant has declined while demand has increased in Eastern Washington for customers building power distribution technology needed by data centers.

“NIC is a supplier of sheet-metal fabrications and assemblies, and in our business, being close to our customers is what keeps us competitive,” Wood said.

While most of the work from Woodinville will go to Spokane, and a smaller portion will go to NIC’s Gallatin, Tenn., facility. The company also has manufacturing in Pullman; Chillicothe, Ohio; and Denton, Texas. The work outside of Washington is focused on the heavy truck sector. The company’s headcount is nearly 600.

Laid-off workers will be encouraged to apply for openings at other plants.

There are smaller fabricators remaining in the Seattle area, including JEMCO Components & Fabrications, which provides precision machining and sheet-metal fabrication for customers in medical, aerospace and defense sectors, and QUAL-FAB serving medical and dental customers.

NIC’s legal and financial headquarters will stay in the Woodinville area, where the company plans a new office for its finance, IT, sales and West Coast support teams.

Wood praised the quality and reliability of the Woodinville employees’ work.

“I am grateful to every one of them,” he said, “and especially to those who chose to stay with us through two and a half years of uncertainty and kept doing their jobs with integrity.”

#5475. Jupiter's Q3 Staking Rewards For All Wallets Opens Today, See Who Clears the 50 JUP Bar

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

50 JUP sounds like a threshold almost anyone can meet. It isn't, and today is when many stakers will find that out.

Jupiter's Active Staking Rewards (ASR) for July to September 2026 are now open to every wallet. That means a 50 million JUP pool can be claimed by anyone who qualified. The problem is that "qualified" doesn't mean what most people think. The rule isn't "have 50 JUP staked." It's "average 50 JUP across the whole quarter." Running the numbers this morning and a lot of wallets that look eligible at a glance aren't.

The round started quietly. According to the official Q3 campaign page, the campaign ran from July 1 until earning closed on September 30, and claims opened on October 12. That first week was reserved for Jupiter's own apps. Early access was limited to Jupiter Wallet and the Jupiter Mobile app, and other wallets can claim from 20 October 2026.

So if you stake from Phantom, Solflare, Backpack or a hardware wallet, today is your first real opportunity. Jupiter's documentation explains why the wallet matters. Rewards are linked to the wallet you staked from. If that wallet lives in another app, you either wait for the general opening or import the same recovery phrase into Jupiter Wallet or Jupiter Mobile.

There's no rush to the finish line yet. Reports put the claim deadline at January 12, 2027. Still, I wouldn't leave it to the holidays.

The campaign page states the rules plainly. 50M JUP will be distributed to stakers this period, ASR is calculated on a time-weighted average of your stake, and an average of 50 JUP or more staked during the quarter qualifies.

The words that matter are "time-weighted average." A wallet that held 50 JUP for all 92 days of Q3 averages exactly 50. A wallet that held 500 JUP for only a few days might average less than that. Jupiter designed it this way on purpose. The 7-day unstaking cooldown stops users from staking briefly around distribution periods to collect rewards without sustained participation.

One more detail surprised me, given the program's name. Voting has no effect on ASR, and you do not need to vote to be eligible. The "Active" in Active Staking Rewards now refers to keeping tokens staked, not to governance turnout.

Here's the simple math. It assumes the average is weighted day by day across the 92 days from July 1 to September 30. Jupiter hasn't published its exact snapshot schedule, so treat these figures as close estimates, not guarantees.

The edge cases are where people get caught. Suppose a wallet held 60 JUP from July 1 but started unstaking at the end of August. Its average comes to only about 40 JUP, so it misses. Another wallet held 40 JUP all quarter and added 30 more on September 1. It ends up at roughly 49.8 JUP, just under the line. Adding 31 instead of 30 would have qualified it.

The simplest check is to connect your wallet at Jupiter Rewards. The page will show the amount of ASR you're eligible to claim. If it shows nothing for an older address, the time-weighting is the most likely reason.

Now for the payout. As of mid-October 2026, total staked JUP topped 1.1 billion tokens, roughly 33% of circulating supply, spread across more than 357,000 wallets.

If you divide 50 million JUP by about 1.1 billion staked, you get roughly 4.5% for the quarter. A wallet that just clears the 50 JUP average would receive about 2.3 JUP. An average of 1,000 JUP works out to about 45, and 10,000 to around 455. The quarter's average total stake may have been a bit below the October figure, so actual allocations could come in slightly higher. Your campaign page shows the real number.

Don't expect the tokens to show up as spendable JUP. ASR is paid in JUP and added to your staked balance, which increases your governance power over time.

Three problems come up again and again in Jupiter's support notes:

Squads multisig users have a more manual process. The ASR documentation covers it in detail, including checking that the claim uses the Jupiter Merkle Distributor program, DiS3nNjFVMieMgmiQFm6wgJL7nevk4NrhXKLbtEH1Z2R before you approve anything.

Missing the deadline has real consequences. According to the Jupiter DAO portal, unclaimed ASR goes back to the community treasury once the claim period ends. Jupiter also says that no transfer is made on your behalf after the support deadline.

The bigger picture is a pool that's getting more crowded. Every quarter, 50M JUP goes to eligible stakers, and that figure doesn't change. With staked JUP now above 1.1 billion, each new staker gets a smaller slice of the same pie.

ASR is also the main reward Jupiter is still paying out. The Jupiter DAO voted in February 2026 to postpone Jupuary and send its 700 million JUP back to a community multisig. That leaves this quarterly distribution as the core reason to keep JUP staked.

My advice is to claim this round now and then look ahead. The October to December period is already more than halfway through. The same math applies, and each week you wait raises how much JUP you need to reach a 50 JUP average.

Comparative figures refer to July-September 2025

Comparative figures refer to January-September 2025

Following a challenging year, I am very pleased to report that the third quarter marks a strong sequential recovery across all our revenue streams, signaling a return to growth. Our consistent focus on shifting our revenue mix towards recurring revenues is delivering clear results, while our advertising business has improved significantly on the back of our successful reset of the business.

Net sales for the quarter amounted to SEK 464.0 million, representing an 18 percent sequential growth compared to Q2, and an increase of 3 percent in constant currencies year-on-year. Compared to Q2, ad revenues grew 23 percent.

Following our shift to a multi-partner model, message volumes for Business Messaging are now structurally higher than at the same point last year, while our core Verified Business offering continues its stable development. Net sales for TfB grew 15% compared to Q2 and are back to growth Y/Y.

Our consumer Premium subscription business delivers robust growth, with revenues growing 32 percent year-on-year. An area of continued focus for us.

The acquisition strengthens our group's product offering and is laying the groundwork for accelerating growth in the US market. text+ is now promoted inside Truecaller, with further integrations in both directions under way. Over time we see text+ extending TruecallerÂ´s protection into everyday calling and messaging in the US, as well as other regions.

During Q3, we experienced a deceleration in user growth, primarily driven by a global contraction in smartphone sales alongside some product issues on our platform. Smartphone shipments have dropped 20-22% globally in Q3 alone, the lowest in more than a decade. In our own device pre-loads initiative, we observe a similar trend where we OEMs are pre-loading Truecaller less in the recent quarters due to the lack of device shipments.

While the product issues are being addressed with highest priority, we expect these external growth challenges to continue in many regions in the short term as rising RAM prices make smartphones more expensive. This deceleration is anticipated to be more evident in highly price-sensitive and well penetrated markets, such as India, Nigeria and Egypt, where a larger share of growth comes from new-to-mobile users. #5471. iPhone sales lifted Apple to record September-quarter revenue of $114.5 billion

Free daily briefing on global business news.

iPhone revenue set a September-quarter record and Services reached an all-time high, while iPad revenue missed estimates

Apple $AAPL reported record September-quarter revenue of $114.5 billion on Monday, up 12% from a year earlier, thanks to soaring iPhone revenue and an all-time record in Services revenue.

Fiscal fourth-quarter revenue beat analyst expectations of $113.39 billion, according to Reuters. The quarter ended Sept. 26.

Apple stock barely moved in after-hours trading.

Diluted earnings per share were $2.10, up 14%, including a $0.05 benefit from tariff refunds. Gross margin was 47.9%, including a benefit of about 1 percentage point from the refunds. Analysts expected earnings of $1.99 per share and a gross margin of 47.5%, according to Reuters.

iPhone revenue was $57.58 billion, Mac revenue was $10.79 billion, and iPad revenue was $6.23 billion, the company said. Analysts had estimated $56.54 billion, $9.61 billion, and $6.70 billion, respectively, according to Reuters.

The iPhone figure covers eight days of iPhone 18 Pro sales and excludes the iPhone Duo, which reached stores after the quarter ended, according to CNBC.

"Apple delivered September quarter records for net income and EPS," CFO Kevan Parekh said in a statement. Apple generated $28 billion in operating cash flow during the quarter and returned $28 billion to shareholders. Revenue for fiscal 2026 reached $479 billion.

Apple's board declared a cash dividend of $0.27 per share, payable Nov. 16 to shareholders of record as of Nov. 12.

Apple raised prices on some iPhone and MacBook models while memory-chip costs climbed, according to Reuters.

"We did see higher memory costs as compared to the June quarter, which was partially offset by the benefit of carrying inventory and lower costs on certain non-memory components," CEO John Ternus told Reuters. "These price increases provided some offset."

Ternus told Reuters that supply of the iPhone Duo trails demand. "Duo is constrained as of today," he said. He said a "very small percentage" of Duo devices were sent back over screen defects, and that Apple is swapping those out for new ones. He added that Apple is "not able to predict when supply and demand will be in balance."

Apple had reported June-quarter revenue of $109.4 billion, up 16% from a year earlier, in the last quarter under Tim Cook as CEO. Ternus took over on Sept. 1.

#5470. Spotify’s founder wants to scan you

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Neko Health brings AI-powered body scans to the U.S. for $499, but its expansion raises a bigger question

A version of this article originally appeared in Quartz’s members-only Weekend Brief newsletter. Quartz members get access to exclusive newsletters and more. Sign up here.

Two decades ago, Daniel Ek got people to pay for music they used to pirate. Now the Spotify $SPOT co-founder is asking them to pay $499 to get a look at their own bodies.

Neko Health, the startup Daniel Ek co-founded in 2018, opened its first U.S. clinic in New York on Sept. 24. More than 50,000 New Yorkers had joined the waitlist before the doors opened, and the company said more than 350,000 people worldwide had signed up for a scan or a place in line.

The hour-long visit includes a 53-marker blood panel, more than 6,000 high-resolution photos of the skin, a look at heart and circulation, and a grip strength test. AI flags suspicious moles for a human clinician to review.

Insurance does not cover it, though the scans are eligible for health savings accounts. Ek said Miami and Washington, DC would follow, with more cities over the next one to two years. Until then, the waitlist is the closest most people could get.

Neko arrived in a crowded health tracker market, and not a particularly successful one. Fitbit launched its first tracker in 2009, and Jawbone, once valued at $3 billion, followed with the UP band in 2011. Jawbone liquidated in 2017, and Google $GOOGL later bought Fitbit for $2.1 billion.

Still, the wearable refused to die — a 2024 JAMA study found that 40 percent of Americans wore a tracker — whether or not it ever made the money its makers wanted.

Even the latest AI-backed attempt with Oura, a ring that tracks 50 health metrics and is backed by Salesforce $CRM chief executive Marc Benioff and Dell $DELL founder Michael Dell, had to postpone its IPO last month. Even with a reported 5.7 million paying customers, it cited market uncertainty after planning to go public at a valuation near $15 billion.

Lab tests have been an even harder sell. Theranos promised answers from a finger prick and 23andMe promised health insights from a tube of spit, and both collapsed. Newer companies tried again, with Function Health selling annual blood panels for $365 and landing $450 million in growth financing in July, while Superpower charged $199 a year for more than 100 biomarkers.

Then came the whole body. DEXA scans, X $TWTR-ray tests that measured fat, muscle and bone, had been sold in gyms and offices for about a decade, with BodySpec charging around $50. Prenuvo charged $2,499 for a whole-body MRI that took it further, and Kim Kardashian posted about hers in 2023. Neko’s scan is not an MRI, but it sold for a fifth of the price.

American healthcare was built to treat infectious disease, Ek told the All-In podcast, so it rewarded fixing people once they were sick. Employer-based insurance made it worse, he said, because workers changed jobs every few years. Why would an insurer pay for a prevention bet that took 10 or 20 years to come good?

Neko’s answer was to skip the insurer and ask the individual to pay. But the company’s own numbers showed the limits of that bet.

After more than 100,000 scans, Ek said about 1% of members had a serious undiagnosed condition. The company presented that as evidence the product worked. But finding a condition is not the same as demonstrating that the scan improved someone's health.

Some of that 1% were real saves. The founder of the meditation app Calm said the scan caught a malignant mole on his back, and catching skin cancer early is a good outcome for anyone who can afford the visit.

For a worse result, the earlier catch was only the beginning. Neko's U.S. clinic provides screening and clinical review, but members who need further diagnosis or treatment may have to seek additional care. The $499 bought a head start on a system where the costs could dwarf it.

The harder problem was what happened after the scan. Heart disease remained the leading cause of death in America, and spotting risk was only one part of preventing it. People also needed regular access to doctors, affordable medication and the time and resources to follow medical advice.

A primary care doctor who works in a clinic for homeless patients said none of her patients wore trackers. She told the New York Times that data only mattered if someone had the agency and money to act on it. Her patients lived in circumstances “so out of their control” that more information would not help them.

That was the gap the quantified self movement keeps stepping over. Measuring was the cheap part. The follow-up, the medication and the time off work stayed out of reach for the people with the most to gain.

#5469. CertiK Verified 40.68M TPS for Sui, Here Is What It Means

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The biggest throughput figure a blockchain security firm has ever signed off on is sitting on CertiK's homepage right now: 40.68 million transactions per second.

It isn't CertiK's own number, and it isn't an on-chain number either. If you read the 2,000-word report behind it, you'll come to become more interested in what CertiK chose not to verify than in what it did.

Scroll past the client logos and media mentions on CertiK and you'll find it in the "Latest Research And Market Insights" strip. One card says CertiK independently verified Sui's Mainnet Tunnel performance campaign, which recorded more than 15.2 billion off-chain transactions across 7,680 tunnels at a peak of 40.68 million TPS.

Most readers will see "CertiK" next to "40.68 million TPS" and stop there. Crypto social media mostly did the same. Sui's own post described the figure as set live on stage at Sui Basecamp 2026 and certified by CertiK, and added that the network now clears in under 20 seconds what Visa processes in a day.Walking through CertiK's verification method when the report first came out. Now that the number has been promoted to CertiK's front page, it's worth looking at exactly what it represents.

According to CertiK's announcement, Sui ran a live Mainnet performance campaign on October 7, 2026, during Sui Basecamp Day. It recorded 15,241,348,297 tunnel transactions across 7,680 tunnels, and every tunnel was opened and settled on chain.

A Sui Tunnel works roughly like a private room. A small group of participants carries out many application actions without sending each one to the blockchain. Sui records the starting terms when the tunnel opens and the final result when it closes. Everything in between happens off-chain as signed receipts. CertiK compares the design to Bitcoin's Lightning Network but notes that tunnels can handle more than payments.

The test was more varied than a single payment loop. The campaign ran 10 runs across five workload types: simple payments, flash, blackjack, tic-tac-toe and battleship. Payments still made up most of the activity. Its 6,144 tunnels committed more than 12 billion transactions, or 78.98% of the total.

This is the part of the report I respect most. The peak came from the busiest complete second, between 08:46:17 and 08:46:18 UTC, when 40,682,328 qualifying tunnel transactions were committed. The highest 60-second rolling average was 40,339,143.65 TPS.

Doing the math on the gap between those two figures. It's about 343,000 transactions, or roughly 0.84%. In other words, the network held near-peak throughput for a full minute rather than spiking for one second.

CertiK also avoided the easiest way to inflate a number like this. For concurrent tunnels sharing the same time window, it added up their transaction counts once and divided by a single shared duration. It did not add individual per-tunnel rates together or multiply one tunnel's rate by the number of tunnels.

The checking itself was thorough. All 7,680 executions and all 960 slots reached VERIFIED status, and the 15.24 billion committed transactions matched the full-history admitted receipts exactly. The work ran on dedicated AWS infrastructure with 128 vCPUs and 247 GiB of RAM.

There's also a small correction in the story. Sui's first announcement reported 40,614,180 TPS. CertiK's audited peak came in about 68,000 higher, a 0.17% difference. A verifier landing slightly above the project's own claim is unusual, and I think it reflects well on the method.

The homepage card doesn't mention any of this, but the full report is clear about its limits.

First, this isn't on-chain throughput. CertiK states that Tunnel TPS measures off-chain tunnel transactions and is not a measurement of Sui's on-chain capacity.

Second, the data came from the project being tested. The Sui team supplied the campaign data and executed all test scenarios, and CertiK examined the retained evidence and recalculated the totals.

Third, the cryptographic checks were not exhaustive. CertiK reconciled the arithmetic, receipt counts and timestamps, but it did not re-run individual signatures or do a fresh cryptographic replay of every receipt.

Fourth, the report can't speak to how the system would behave in normal use. The records don't establish clock accuracy, failure rates, latency percentiles or results across repeated runs. The sustained figure is the best 60-second window observed, not a guaranteed minimum.

Put simply, CertiK verified that the accounting is correct. It did not verify that Sui can handle 40 million real users' actions every second.

The number that's most telling isn't the TPS figure. More than 15.2 billion off-chain transactions were anchored to Sui through just 1,920 on-chain lifecycle transactions: 960 openings and 960 settlements.

By simple calculation, that's about 7.9 million off-chain actions for every on-chain transaction. That ratio is what the tunnel design is built to achieve. It's an impressive engineering result, but it measures how well Sui compresses activity, not how fast its base layer runs.

This isn't the first speed record CertiK has signed off on, and the earlier ones show why comparisons are tricky. In its earlier TON verification, CertiK worked from per-minute transaction count data and arrived at 104,715 TPS for TON's testnet. In April 2025, Qubic announced 15.52 million TPS verified by CertiK, measured over 10 peak ticks on its Layer 1 mainnet.

On paper, Sui's tunnel figure is about 2.6 times Qubic's and nearly 390 times TON's. But these were three different kinds of tests: a sharded testnet, a base-layer burst and an off-chain channel network. They don't belong on the same leaderboard.

My view is that the 40.68 million figure is real, well documented and carefully bounded. It's also a measure of what an off-chain system can process, not what Sui's blockchain itself handles. CertiK's report is honest about that, even if the one-line homepage card isn't.

#5468. These Millionaires Have the Cash to Buy a Home. Here’s Why They’re Renting Instead.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

For a growing number of wealthy households, renting is a choice to seriously consider.

More millionaires are renting, despite being able to afford homeownership. This group of wealthy renters is choosing a different path on purpose.

According to a recent report from apartment search website RentCafe, millionaire renters are growing at a faster rate than millionaire homeowners. The report qualified individuals from households that have a total annual household income of $1 million or more as millionaires.

From 2020 to 2024, the number of millionaire households renting their homes surged 229%, more than tripling in five years, compared with a 193% increase among homeowners in that same time period, according to RentCafe’s analysis of American Community Survey estimates.

Choosing to rent contradicts a long tradition of treating homeownership as a defining symbol of the American Dream, especially for affluent Americans.

“For a growing number of millionaires, renting is now a deliberate choice,” the report said. “That’s because many prioritize mobility without the commitment of owning a home, as well as the ability to relocate without going through the lengthy process of selling a multi-million-dollar house.”

The report also pointed out that many wealthy renters would rather keep their money accessible and pursue returns in a strong stock market rather than lock their funds into a home.

Most millionaires reach that status with two incomes. According to the report, couples with high earnings account for 75% of these households, while individuals make up the remaining quarter.

RentCafe found that millennials represent the largest share of millionaire renters at 49%. However, Gen Z is the fastest-growing group, with its count rising 46-fold from fewer than a dozen households renting in 2020 to more than 400 in 2024. The report revealed that despite that jump, Gen Z still comprises just 2% of millionaire renter households.

Gen Z “was barely entering the workforce in 2020,” Adina Dragos, RentCafe writer and research analyst, said in an interview with USA Today. She noted that “by 2024, the oldest Gen Zers were approaching 30.”

“Many who struck it big early — through the creator economy, crypto or startup equity — were choosing to rent precisely because their wealth isn’t tied to a traditional career ladder,” she said. “With no employer anchoring them to one place, they have little reason to put down roots.”

According to RentCafe, millionaire renters typically hold lucrative white-collar jobs as chief executives, technology professionals and senior financial managers. These roles offer flexibility about where they live and work.

The group also includes less obvious high earners, such as professors and operations managers. It’s “a sign that the millionaire renter isn’t always who you’d expect,” per the report.

New York, San Francisco and Los Angeles remain major hubs for millionaire renters, but their numbers are climbing rapidly in Texas and Florida.

Houston recorded the fastest growth of any major metro, with millionaire renter households rising from 18 in 2020 to 232 in 2024, a 1,189% increase.

“Granted, 232 households is still a tiny fraction of the Houston metro’s roughly 2.7 million households, but the growth rate far outpaces any other major metro,” RentCafe noted.

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Oct 30, 2026 at 11:30 amOctober 30, 2026 at 3:35 pm

Powerlattice, a Vancouver, Wash.-based startup developing chips that cut the power demands of AI processors, has raised $86 million, according to an SEC filing on Friday.

The new funding is nearly triple the $31 million the company had raised when it emerged from stealth last November with a $25 million Series A led by Playground Global and Celesta Capital. Board members include former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger, a general partner at Playground, and Steve Fu of Celesta. The filing also lists Wen Hsieh, founding managing partner of Matter Venture Partners, as a director.

The filing shows Powerlattice is seeking $111 million, with 18 investors participating so far. It does not name the investors or the round. The company declined to comment.

AI chips are drawing so much electricity and throwing off so much heat that data center operators are running into limits on available power and cooling.

“AI is not constrained by capital, it’s constrained by power,” Gelsinger said last year when Powerlattice announced its Series A.

Powerlattice makes what it calls a power delivery chiplet, a small component that sits inside the processor package. Conventional setups route current over long paths to the processor, wasting energy along the way. The company says shortening that path can cut energy use by more than half and boost performance. Powerlattice said last year it was providing engineering samples for GPUs, CPUs and custom accelerators.

CEO Peng Zou, Gang Ren and Sujith Dermal founded the company in 2023. The three are semiconductor veterans whose backgrounds span Qualcomm, Intel and NUVIA, a startup Qualcomm acquired in 2021. Powerlattice also has offices in Chandler, Ariz.; San Jose, Calif.; and Hsinchu, Taiwan.

Earlier this week, Powerlattice announced it had demonstrated what it calls the industry’s first monolithic integrated voltage regulator chiplet, which packs the controller, power transistors and inductors onto a single piece of silicon.

In the test, the chiplet powered a device Powerlattice built to mimic the fast-shifting electrical loads of next-generation AI accelerators. The company says multiple chiplets can be linked to work as one, letting chip designers match the setup to their processors.

“Breaking through the AI power wall requires us to rethink how power reaches the processor,” Zou said in the announcement.

#5466. Madrona Prize goes to UW research on agents that shrink AI models to run on small chips

by Todd Bishop on Oct 30, 2026 at 3:13 pmNovember 2, 2026 at 11:53 am

A University of Washington project that uses AI agents to squeeze AI models onto tiny devices — such as a solar-powered camera that spots elk in the wild — won the Madrona Prize at the Allen School’s annual Research Showcase on Thursday.

Seattle venture capital firm Madrona has awarded the prize since 2006 to Allen School student projects that combine strong research with commercial potential. The winners were chosen from among the student posters presented at the evening event on the UW campus.

Zhihan Zhang, a PhD student in the Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering, presented the winning project. It tests whether AI agents can do a job that experts now do by hand: shrinking AI models and tuning device software to run on small, low-power chips with tight limits on memory, power and heat.

In the team’s tests, leading AI models failed at the task without feedback from real hardware. The team built a system that let the agent load its work onto real hardware, measure the results and try again. With that feedback, the agent beat human experts within seven rounds.

The researchers used the approach on two real-world projects: an elk-detection camera trap, which needed its vision model shrunk by 250 times, and a wearable device that records children’s speech for child development research.

The team released its benchmark, called Embedded Arena, as open-source code. Allen School faculty members Shwetak Patel, Vikram Iyer, Natasha Jaques and Kurtis Heimerl also worked on the project.

Other collaborators: Alexander Metzger, Jiuyang Lyu, Chun-Cheng Chang, Jiayi Shao, Yujia Liu, Emmanuel Azuh Mensah, Edward Wang and Gregory D. Abowd.

The People’s Choice award went to Keisuke Kamahori for VibeSys, a project that uses AI agents to write custom software for a specific chip and task, then keep improving it, instead of relying on general-purpose tools built for common setups.

Its first application, VibeServe, writes the behind-the-scenes software that takes requests from users and runs them through an AI model. On Amazon’s Trainium2 chips, the software it built handled up to 2.7 times as much work as an existing system. Shihang (Vic) Li and Allen School faculty members Simon Peter and Baris Kasikci also worked on the project.

The first runner-up for the Madrona Prize, Tanush Yadav, presented VideoNet, a test of how well AI models recognize specific actions in video, such as a particular bouldering move or a type of surgical stitch. It covers more than 1,000 actions across 38 fields.

Leading AI models struggle with it compared to ordinary people. Shown three examples, people improved their accuracy by about 14 percentage points, while AI models improved by about 3 percentage points.

Allen School faculty members Ali Farhadi, Hanna Hajishirzi and Ranjay Krishna, and former Allen School faculty member Yejin Choi, now at Stanford University, also worked on the project.

Other collaborators: Mohammadreza Salehi, Jae Sung Park, Vivek Ramanujan and Rohun Tripathi.

The second runner-up, Henry Wong, presented work on securing benchtop DNA synthesizers, machines that let users print synthetic DNA.

His project focuses on protecting the screening software meant to stop someone from printing a dangerous pathogen, and concludes that even perfectly secure hardware wouldn’t fully solve the problem.

Allen School faculty member Jeff Nivala and former Allen School faculty member Tadayoshi Kohno, now at Georgetown University, also worked on the project.

All of the presenters are PhD students in the Allen School.

Correction: An earlier version of this story misidentified Sethu Raman of Madrona in the lead photo caption.

#5465. Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon says the best advice he ever got came from his grandmother in his 20s: ‘Don’t be in a hurry’

David Solomon runs one of the most powerful banks on Wall Street, but the best career advice he ever received didn’t come from a mentor in a corner office. It came from his grandmother.

“Don’t be in a hurry,” the Goldman Sachs CEO told NBC News’ Christine Romans in a rapid-fire interview about his daily routine and the lessons that have shaped his career. He said she gave him that advice when he was in his twenties.

The clip came out of Romans’ wider conversation with Solomon for NBC’s Business in America series. That conversation aired Oct. 23, one day after Goldman launched its Small Business AI Institute, part of a new $500 million commitment to its 10,000 Small Businesses program, with Anthropic, Google, Meta, and OpenAI as partners. In the segment that ran on Nightly News, Solomon said he’s excited about what AI could mean for businesses and for people’s longevity.

In the lightning round, though, he talked less about markets and more about how he manages his days and his life.

Asked to name three things he does before 7 a.m., Solomon kept it simple: He wakes up, goes to the gym, and generally has a cup of coffee and a protein shake.

He’s in good company. An early workout is a fixture of many executives’ routines, from the Bupa CEO who trains six days a week with his Gen Z son to the many leaders featured in Fortune’s Day in the Life of a CEO series.

The research suggests the habit matters more than the hour. A 2022 systematic review published in the Public Health Agency of Canada’s journal Health Promotion and Chronic Disease Prevention in Canada examined 35 studies. Eleven found morning activity more beneficial; 12 found afternoon or evening activity more beneficial; and 12 found no clear difference. The authors concluded there is no consistent evidence that exercising at one time of day is better for your health than another, and they rated the evidence quality as very low.

Solomon’s best trick for keeping his day on track is unglamorous: sticking to his schedule.

“The one thing that we can’t…get back is time,” he said, adding that he tries to be very purposeful with how he spends it. That means making commitments and keeping them, because, as he noted, it’s easy to drift off schedule.

The science backs him up, with a twist. A 2021 meta-analysis in PLOS One by Brad Aeon, Aïda Faber, and Alexandra Panaccio found that time management is positively linked to job performance. It was even more strongly linked to well-being, especially life satisfaction. In other words, the payoff from guarding your calendar may show up as much in how you feel as in what you get done.

At first glance, “stick to the schedule” and “don’t be in a hurry” seem to pull in opposite directions. For Solomon, they work on different timelines: Be disciplined with the hours in a day, and be patient with the arc of a career.

He repeats this message often. In August, he told Goldman’s summer interns at a town hall that taking more time can open up more opportunities, urging them to “try not to be in a hurry and enjoy the ride.” He offered small-business owners the same counsel about AI at the institute’s launch last week, telling them that “the important thing is to get it right, not to get it quicker.”

Solomon’s patience has a limit, and it’s the things he cares about. Asked whether he has any obsessions, he said it depends on what has captured his interest.

“If I’m interested in something, I get very obsessive about it. I don’t like to do things halfway,” Solomon said. When something grabs him, he added, he tends to go deep.

Psychologists have found that kind of intensity cuts both ways. In a 2007 study in the Journal of Personality, Robert Vallerand and colleagues distinguished between “harmonious” passion, an activity you freely choose that fits with the rest of your life, and “obsessive” passion, which feels compulsive. Obsessive passion predicted deliberate practice and mastery-oriented goals, which supported performance. But it was also tied to fear-of-failure goals that undercut results. Harmonious passion delivered the upside with less of the downside.

The takeaway: Going deep can fuel success, as long as the obsession serves you, not the other way around.

Not every passion turns into a career, of course. Solomon also named one ambition he’s had to let go of: playing professional basketball. He conceded that one isn’t on the table.

#5462. Sweetgreen managers could earn more than $200,000 a year under a new pay plan, as the salad chain bets higher pay will lift sales

A fast-casual chain favored by the office lunch set is sweetening compensation packages for managers at its restaurants.

Starting next year, Sweetgreen managers will be eligible to earn more than $200,000 a year if they meet certain milestones set by the company. The new offering, which will be paid through a mix of base salary and equity, is intended to empower managers who contribute to the business’s success, and “[share] those wins with those that are driving it,” co-founder and CEO Jonathan Neman said.

Under the new incentive plan, Sweetgreen managers (known as “head coaches”) will see their base pay increase by up to 45% if they work at restaurants with higher sales volume. The company declined to specify how high sales need to be to meet this threshold.

When restaurants outperform their sales goals, managers will get a revenue share bonus from the upside, with the percentage increasing based on their tenure in the business. Managers can also continue to receive equity in the company based on their performance.

Base salary increases will go into effect in Q1 of 2027, while head coaches will start to receive bonuses based on store performance on a quarterly basis from Jan. 1, 2027, according to Sweetgreen.

How Sweetgreen is making the case for higher pay. Higher labor and related costs cut into Sweetgreen’s earnings for the quarter ending in June, accounting for 29% of revenue, up from 28% the year prior. Same-store sales and restaurant profits also declined that quarter compared to 2025. (Sweetgreen will report Q3 earnings on Nov. 5.)

Amid such economic pressures, Neman recognized that investing in additional compensation for managers “is definitely a bet.”“But the data supports that if we’re able to attract, retain, and incentivize better head coaches, that they will drive higher sales and better margins,” he added. Neman noted that while Sweetgreen is investing some money upfront to raise managers’ base salaries, most of the investment is contingent on their stores meeting certain performance targets.

“Typically the company would take more of that upside. Now we’re sharing in that upside with our team, but…we think that’s a good trade,” he said.

Zoom out. Sweetgreen isn’t the first fast-casual chain to bet big on its managers. Chipotle announced in 2021 that workers in its highest general manager position could earn $100,000, on average, as it sought to hang onto workers in a tight labor market. The burrito business doesn’t appear to have taken a financial hit from this move, as its restaurant operating margins have stayed between 23% and 26% in recent years. More than 85% of general managers at Chipotle were promoted internally in 2025, according to its 2026 proxy statement.

Neman said Sweetgreen took inspiration from chains like In-N-Out Burger, which recently confirmed that store managers can earn more than $200,000 on average, and Raising Cane’s, which grants monthly bonuses to managers based on sales, and said in 2024 it paid managers up to $175,000 annually.

In addition to business performance, Sweetgreen will be looking at metrics like team member turnover, “head coach stability” (i.e. whether managers stay in their stores), quality and experience scores, and internal mobility to determine whether this incentive program is working, Neman said.

This report was originally published by HR Brew.

#5461. Washington governor rips Microsoft over TV ad in leaked audio

by Todd Bishop on Oct 30, 2026 at 5:21 pmNovember 2, 2026 at 6:29 am

Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson called out Microsoft for bankrolling a political action committee responsible for a TV ad describing state government as broken, according to newly leaked audio from a Seattle Chamber leadership conference last week.

Remarks at the Seattle Metropolitan Chamber of Commerce’s Regional Leadership Conference, held at the Suncadia resort near Cle Elum, Wash., are supposed to be off the record. But The Washington Observer, an independent newsletter on state politics, published the audio Friday, saying it was obtained from an unnamed source.

In the audio, Ferguson zeroed in on a line near the start of the ad — that in Washington, “it used to be all you needed was an idea, a dream and the guts to chase it.”

The governor repeated the words “it used to be” for emphasis, in a tone of disbelief.

“What’s up with that?” Ferguson asked the crowd of business and government leaders. “First, does anyone else in this room believe that? I sure as hell don’t.”

“I talk to people every day who have that idea, that dream. They’re chasing it and they’re getting it,” he said. He cited the record $3.5 billion that Seattle-area startups raised in the third quarter, more than triple the same period a year ago, according to PitchBook data.

The Microsoft relationship: Ferguson, who noted that he had worked as a lawyer for Microsoft, said he loves the company and respects what it does. But he seemed especially peeved that the ad ran during the Seattle Seahawks game, where it reached people across the state and those from elsewhere who might want to come here and start a company.

“If we’re partners, partners should treat partners like partners, right?” he said.

He asked the room to imagine him running a multimillion-dollar ad criticizing Microsoft. “You guys would think I lost my mind if I did that,” he said.

Ferguson called Microsoft a key partner and a member of his economic roundtable, and said he works well with the company. “But it works both ways,” he said.

Ferguson acknowledged that the state has problems. “Are there challenges? Sure,” he said. But he said he didn’t think the ad was “helpful for where we all want to go.”

He told the crowd he welcomes constructive feedback, but asked business leaders to think about how they communicate, and to talk up the state’s workforce, economy and startup funding along with its challenges.

“What we have here is so bloody special,” he said.

Ferguson, who took office in January 2025, also reminded the room that he isn’t going anywhere. “I plan on being governor for a long time,” he said, adding that he works with all of them, “Microsoft included.”

The Observer noted that $10 million, roughly what the group has left to spend, would be a good start on a campaign to run someone else for governor in 2028.

The newsletter said it stripped the audio from a video of Ferguson’s remarks, to protect its source. Among those in the audience was Michael Mattmiller, who represents Microsoft in Olympia. He and Ferguson “kinda-sorta hugged it out afterward,” the Observer reported.

Who’s behind the ad: The campaign comes from Washington Needs to Compete, a PAC funded in large part by Microsoft and its current and former executives. The group has raised about $13.8 million, according to state campaign finance records, including more than $5 million directly from Microsoft.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and former CEO Steve Ballmer each gave $250,000, and Vice Chair and President Brad Smith gave more than $500,000. Other backers include T-Mobile, F5, Alaska Airlines and Weyerhaeuser.

Washington Needs to Compete has spent about $3 million so far, according to state records. Most of it has gone to state legislative races, the Observer reported, including more than $700,000 backing Rep. Amy Walen, D-Kirkland, in the 48th District, home to Microsoft’s Redmond headquarters.

The group spent $97,000 to air the ad during the Seahawks’ Oct. 15 Thursday night loss to the Denver Broncos on Prime Video and $130,000 during their Oct. 25 Sunday night win over the Kansas City Chiefs on NBC, according to the Observer.

Microsoft referred GeekWire’s inquiry to the group, which the company described as a growing coalition of more than 60 funders that want to keep the state competitive.

A press representative for the group sent a statement from Nick Streuli, an officer of Washington Needs to Compete. Streuli runs the government relations firm Sundial Advocacy and was previously policy and outreach director for former Gov. Jay Inslee.

“Washington Needs to Compete is committed to our state and wants to see it succeed,” Streuli said in the statement. “Rising costs are making it harder for businesses to invest and grow here. We are starting a conversation about our economic challenges and how to solve them.”

What the ad says: The spot opens with a nod to “inventors in garages,” “mom-and-pop shops down Main Street” and farmers “feeding the world,” before declaring, “In Washington, it used to be all you needed was an idea, a dream and the guts to chase it.”

Then it turns: “But today, Olympia is broken, spending more while you get less.” Jobs are leaving, the ad says, and “it’s harder than ever to afford a home and raise a family.”

It doesn’t name Ferguson or any legislation. It ends by saying Olympia needs to “quit wasting money, fix what’s broken and put Washington families first.”

Taxes and the business climate: Ferguson this year signed a 9.9% tax on household income above $1 million, known as the millionaires tax, which takes effect in 2028 and is projected to raise about $3 billion a year. Initiative 645, which would repeal it, is on the Nov. 3 ballot.

In September, Smith joined former Gov. Chris Gregoire and dozens of regional officials to launch a partnership aimed at reversing the Seattle area’s economic slide. “The warning signs are flashing on our economy,” Smith said at the time.

The region lost nearly 7,000 jobs in 2025, according to the group, and Washington has fallen from 32nd to 47th in CNBC’s ranking of states by cost of doing business since 2017.

In the same CNBC study, Washington ranks 11th overall, up from 14th last year, and fifth for its economy. WalletHub ranks Washington’s economy second in the nation, behind Massachusetts.

Washington’s gross domestic product grew faster than any other state’s in the first quarter of 2026, driven largely by its tech sector, according to federal data released in June.

Long-term plans: On its website, Washington Needs to Compete describes itself as businesses and residents building “a modern, permanent political organization” to support leaders and ideas that “strengthen our economy, improve affordability and expand opportunity,” through elections and public education.

The site lists its top five contributors as Microsoft, T-Mobile, the Washington Coalition for Responsible Taxes and Spending, F5 and Smith.

The group is saving most of its money for future campaigns, the Observer reported.

Updated Nov. 2 with comment from Washington Needs to Compete.

#5460. AI Can Build Your Product in a Day —Here’s How Founders Get Someone to Actually Pay for It

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Lessons from 500 first-time founders on how they landed their first paying customer, and how they built momentum.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

This summer, more than 500 people from more than 50 countries joined an eight-week startup camp my company runs. Most had never started a business. Many had never written a line of code, and it didn’t matter. With today’s AI tools, most of them had a working product within the first couple of weeks.

Getting someone to pay was the hard part, and about 1 in 10 managed it.

I spent the weeks after camp asking those founders how they did it. This is what I learned:

Almost none of the first customers were strangers. One founder, a marketing consultant, built a small ad tool for his own use. He showed it to a group of entrepreneurs he met with regularly because he thought it might help them. Those 10 became the first paying customers. Another founder built a language-learning app. Her first customer was a math teacher in Italy, the friend of a friend of a friend. Three introductions away sounds far, but each one carried a little trust, and that was enough.

If you are starting out, write down the 50 people who would take your call. Your first customer is more likely on that list than in an ad audience.

The founders who got paid often sold something that wasn’t really a product yet. A founder working on grief support ran her whole service through Instagram direct messages. She had more than 500 conversations before she built a website, and each conversation was both the product and the demo.

The language app founder did something similar. She got her first user on a video call, set her up personally, and promised to build what she needed. The customer bought an annual plan.

AI makes it tempting to build first because building is so easy now. But a working app doesn’t prove anyone wants it. A person paying for the rough version does. Find the smallest version of your core promise and start figuring out whether someone will pay for that.

I didn’t find a single founder whose first sale came from a stranger on a checkout page alone. The yes came from a text message, a phone call, a video call or showing up in person. One founder who used to run a car collision repair shop found that ads, websites and email never closed a sale for him. Knocking on doors and picking up the phone did. Funnels matter later. For the first customer, you are the funnel.

Many founders put their first few hundred dollars into social media ads. Most learned the same lesson: ads buy attention, not trust. One founder got more than 40 signups and zero buyers. The grief-support founder got clicks and traffic but no customers, because someone scrolling past an ad on a random Tuesday is not someone who needs help right now.

There was one clear exception. A founder with a golf swing app got his first customers through paid ads. My read is that golfers already know they have the problem and go looking for a fix. When your buyer already knows they have the problem, ads can work. When they don’t, you are paying to explain the problem and the product at the same time.

Sometimes the first sale is for something you didn’t mean to sell. The marketing consultant set out to build one business. The side tool he made for himself became the business. Slack was created the same way – as an internal tool in what used to be a gaming company. The former collision shop owner had a lesson from his old business that stuck with me. He closed about 90% of the people who came in, and he was never the cheapest. Many of them didn’t really want the repair. They wanted the insurance money from the claim, and he helped them get what they actually needed. Early conversations will tell you what people will pay for if you listen for what is implied, not just what is said.

AI has taken most of the cost out of building. What it hasn’t changed is that someone has to decide to trust you with their money. That’s why the first $100 matters far more than the amount. It’s the first proof that someone who owes you nothing values what you offer.

So before you build the next feature, ask a different question: Who already trusts me, and what could I sell them this week?

Building is nearly free. Being trusted is not.

This summer, more than 500 people from more than 50 countries joined an eight-week startup camp my company runs. Most had never started a business. Many had never written a line of code, and it didn’t matter. With today’s AI tools, most of them had a working product within the first couple of weeks.

Getting someone to pay was the hard part, and about 1 in 10 managed it.

I spent the weeks after camp asking those founders how they did it. This is what I learned:

#5459. After topping 2024’s donor list, Elon Musk said he’d do ‘a lot less.’ Since then, he’s given more than George Soros has personally in his lifetime

In May 2025, Elon Musk said he was pulling back from political spending.

“I think in terms of political spending, I’m going to do a lot less in the future,” Musk said in an interview with Bloomberg at the Qatar Economic Forum. “I think I’ve done enough.”

He then left room to change course: “Well, if I see a reason to do political spending in the future, I will do it,” he said. “I don’t currently see a reason.”

He had just finished the 2024 election cycle as the country’s biggest political donor, according to OpenSecrets. That year, he gave $291.5 million, all to Republicans. The next-largest donor, Timothy Mellon, gave $197 million.

In the 17 months since, Musk has given $427.5 million to federal political committees, according to a Fortune analysis of Federal Election Commission filings through Oct. 14. That’s nearly $200 million more than George Soros, the man Musk has claimed “astroturfed” anti-Tesla protests. Soros, the Democratic megadonor, has given personally $243.2 million to federal committees in 47 years of FEC records.

Most of Musk’s money arrived after July 1 of this year. SLF PAC, the flagship super PAC for Republican Senate candidates, reported a $75 million check from Musk on Sept. 9 and an $83 million check on Sept. 23. Musk has spent more than $200 million to help elect Ken Paxton, the Texas attorney general, to the Senate, according to a New York Times analysis.

America PAC, the super PAC Musk funds, reported $165.6 million from him between July 1 and Oct. 14, in its October quarterly and pre-general reports. That includes $8 million in in-kind support from United States of America Inc., one of his companies, which America PAC attributed to Musk.

He also gave $20 million on Sept. 4 to the Congressional Leadership Fund, the main super PAC for House Republican candidates. And on Aug. 21, his trust gave $10 million to Lone Star Liberty PAC, which supports Paxton, who is running against Democrat James Talarico.

Other counts put him higher. The Times and OpenSecrets rank Musk as the top donor of the 2026 midterms, at $445.6 million for the full cycle (outside of the FEC, a Fortune analysis of IRS filings found he gave $10 million to the Republican Governors Association and $2 million to the Republican Attorneys General Association on July 6). The Brennan Center for Justice, which counts his company alongside him, puts the total at $483 million.

Soros’s largest personal checks came before July 2026. He gave Democracy PAC II, one of his family’s two super PACs, $125 million in September 2021 and $50 million in November 2022. In the 2024 cycle, he gave $4.2 million personally to federal committees, FEC records show.

Soros has also given $67.8 million to political groups that report to the IRS, including $24.2 million to Justice & Public Safety PAC, according to IRS filings. FollowTheMoney, which compiles state campaign finance records, lists about $70 million more in state and local contributions. Together, that comes to about $381 million, still less than Musk has given since May 2025.

The comparison changes if groups Soros funds are counted. The Fund for Policy Reform, a nonprofit, has given $210.5 million to Democracy PAC since 2020, including $60 million in January 2024 and $50 million in January 2026, but the nonprofit doesn’t disclose its donors. The Times describes it as a channel for Soros family money and notes that Alex Soros, George’s son, is a director. Counting the fund, Soros’s federal total is $453.7 million, more than Musk has given since his remarks.

The Times counts George and Alex Soros together at $103.4 million this cycle and reports that the family’s two super PACs held about $173 million in cash as of mid-October.

Over his lifetime, Musk has given $723.8 million to federal committees, about three times Soros’s personal federal total, according to Fortune’s analysis of FEC filings. Fortune’s analysis counts contributions each man made to federal political committees as reported to the FEC, including in-kind gifts that recipients attributed to them, and excludes duplicate memo entries. Musk’s totals run through Oct. 14, 2026; Soros’s run through Sept. 9, 2026.

Musk’s totals exclude donations to groups that don’t disclose their donors, as well as any money given after Oct. 14.

Catherina covers markets, the economy, energy, tech, and AI.

#5458. A Country Club Built Around a Private Racetrack? Why Exclusive Experiences are the Biggest Trend Among The Wealthy

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

APEX Motorclub is a private motorsports club in Maricopa, Arizona, on a 280-acre facility with race tracks, skid pads and luxury trackside condos, and by offering lifetime memberships to families it taps into the wealthy’s growing interest in passing down passions, not just assets.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Country clubs are an American tradition among those wealthy enough to afford them. But as unique experiences become increasingly coveted, many members are looking for more exciting alternatives to a golf course and some fancy hors d’oeuvres. Enter Apex Motor Club.

APEX Motor Club is a private motorsports club in Maricopa, Arizona, built around cars, community and competition.

As COO, Bill Barba puts it, “We’re similar to a country club, but instead of golf courses, we have race tracks.”

The Club is a 280-acre facility featuring 2 race tracks, a six-acre skid pad, 96 trackside garage condos, a drivers’ lounge and a clubhouse.

The goal is to give motorsports enthusiasts a place to share that passion with others, including their family members. At the same time, the exclusive luxury landscape offers an escape from the pressure of running a billion-dollar company, as some of its members do.

“We’ve got members whose names are known,” Barba says. “They run global companies, plus some local entrepreneurs that built great businesses. Motorsports are interesting because they all share the joy, rather than expecting to be Mr. or Mrs. So and So when they’re out here. That’s part of the culture we’ve created.”

There are two primary membership types: Gold, a $70,000 initiation fee plus an annual $8,000 fee and Platinum, a $90,000 initiation fee plus an annual $15,000 fee. The two are similar, offering 240+ annual track days, transferable membership and family access, with Platinum offering event host days. They also recently introduced a one-year membership for $35,000 and an under-35 membership with a $25,000 initiation fee plus $4,500 annually.

“Motorsports is not a cheap endeavor,” Barba explains. “To run a car for a weekend out here, you go through tires, brakes and maintenance. Depending on the type of car, that cost can go up quite a bit.”

While APEX provides the location and platform, members must maintain their own cars. Some have small teams doing only the necessary maintenance, while others come to the track with five people analyzing the data behind each lap. Some look to shave milliseconds off their cornering, while others just want a place to let the fancy ride they just bought rip.

APEX’s business model includes partnerships with luxury car companies. They have a deal with Lexus, which brought out cars to join the APEX fleet. They also have a relationship with Aston Martin, which has an on-site presence in their garage condos. The local McLaren Scottsdale, one of the country’s highest-volume McLaren dealers, is a corporate member of the club.

Companies will also rent the tracks for events, including Ferrari, Mercedes and Porsche.

“It gives them a chance to put people who aren’t necessarily enthusiastic enough to join a club on a track to understand what the car can do,” Barba explains. According to him, 85% of the engineering in performance cars never shows up on the street. At APEX, someone might own their fourth Porsche 911 but never experience its full power until they get on the course with an instructor.

“The guy who buys or leases a Lamborghini to park at the valet is not a member of a motorsports club,” Barba says. “Our members tend to have more enthusiasm for the vehicles. Then there’s a whole different area of what level of racing they may want.”

While most members are interested in track time, Barba estimates about 20% take wheel-to-wheel racing seriously. For them, APEX runs an 11-race series with 10 to 25 people per race, depending on the car. “Some people love it and thrive on the competition and pushing the car. Others want to enjoy the tracking and their times, but not race,” Babra says.

What sets APEX apart from the competition is its family policy.

“If you join APEX, your spouse and kids are a part of it, and we don’t age them out,” Barba shares. “What we saw historically was that a lot of clubs would age kids out, and then they’d have to buy a membership. We want kids to stay as long as possible because it keeps parents, grandparents and everyone else engaged. So it’s a family membership because we want it to be a family experience.”

This plays into a larger theme among the wealthy: finding the “new inheritance.” Rather than passing down expensive paintings and big houses, rich parents want to give their kids something more meaningful and personal.

One option is their passions. “Members will talk about the first race car they had, the first time they reached a certain speed, or the first time they watched their child drive a car,” Barba says. “It’s a passion that passes down, and it connects back to what I believe is most potent about motorsports: the emotions.”

One example is the Bacon family. Seth Bacon had built a successful logistics business focused on organ donations and sold it. Looking for a way to spend more time with his teenage son Jace as he approached adulthood, he found an unexpected solution: racing.

“He was about to turn 16 and get his driver’s license. He’s getting a job. He was busy in school. He’s about to go off to college, and I thought this is that period where he’s beginning to separate himself from the nest,” Seth says. “I wanted an opportunity for us to still do something tight together.”

The two visited APEX to watch a few races. Before long, they bought a pair of Radical race cars and hit the track themselves.

“Instead of the son ignoring him at 16, they’re working together on racing,” Barba says with a laugh.

At Jace’s first race at another club in Nevada, father and son competed together, with Jace winning.

“It made a real impact on the dad that out there, his son is an equal with guys who are running billion-dollar companies,” Barba says.

The Bacons could take their cars to any track, but few offer the built-in community they’ve found at APEX.

“There’s a lot of senior drivers, a lot of retired professional drivers who are members there, and everywhere we go, they’re always checking in on him, asking about his career,” Seth says of Jace. “It really is more of a community of people who are willing to support one another, not only on track, but also, how did that business of yours go? Did you get that acquisition you were looking for? What do you need next?”

Business connections are great, but at the end of the day, APEX is about cars, community and competition. A hole-in-one is unforgettable, but the average day on the golf course doesn’t necessarily make the lifetime highlight reel. Driving a luxury race car at breakneck speeds on an open track? That’s an experience that’s not only incredible, but repeatable.

Country clubs are an American tradition among those wealthy enough to afford them. But as unique experiences become increasingly coveted, many members are looking for more exciting alternatives to a golf course and some fancy hors d’oeuvres. Enter Apex Motor Club.

APEX Motor Club is a private motorsports club in Maricopa, Arizona, built around cars, community and competition.

As COO, Bill Barba puts it, “We’re similar to a country club, but instead of golf courses, we have race tracks.”
