#5457. What Solana’s Alpenglow Switch Actually Changes at Slot 459,653,000

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

For about 400 milliseconds this afternoon, Solana will stop landing user transactions. That isn't a failure.

It's the scheduled handoff between two consensus systems, and it's probably the only "400 ms" figure that matters today.

Many people heading into the Alpenglow launch still treat 400 ms block times and 12.8-second finality as the bar to beat. Those are the old chain's numbers. They describe TowerBFT, the system Alpenglow is replacing, so Alpenglow shouldn't be checked against them. If you go through Solana's own documentation, you'll find the right benchmarks before the first post-launch numbers arrive.

According to Solana's official Alpenglow page, the upgrade's feature gate activates at the start of epoch 1064 on Wednesday, October 21, at about 13:20 UTC. The Solana Foundation says to treat that time as an estimate and to watch the epoch instead.

The new consensus doesn't take over the moment the epoch begins. TowerBFT keeps running for the first 5,000 slots, and Alpenglow takes control at slot 459,653,000. Anza, the team behind the main Agave client, put that switch at around 14:00 UTC.

That time isn't fixed. Solana Compass calculated that with about 375,000 slots left before the switch, each millisecond of drift in average slot time moves the boundary by roughly six minutes. Using epoch 1062's pace, it estimated the switch at about 14:02 UTC.

The transition itself has a cost. Solana Compass reports a gap of roughly two slots, about 400 ms, during which blocks carry only votes and user transactions don't land. So the 400 ms everyone is watching for will turn up, just as a pause rather than a block time.

This is where much of today's coverage gets it wrong.

Block time first. Solana's page says slots moved from 400 ms to 200 ms in a separate "reduced slot times" upgrade, which finished this month. That change isn't part of Alpenglow. It was already running before today. Solana Compass measured epoch 1062 averaging 217.7 ms per slot over 26.1 hours. Checking Alpenglow against 400 ms would mean grading it against a number the network had already beaten before the switch.

Then finality. The 12.8 seconds is TowerBFT's figure. Under that system, a block became final only after enough votes built up over 32 slots. Alpenglow's stated target is about 150 ms, which Solana describes as 99% faster than TowerBFT.

Solana is careful about that 150 ms figure, and I think readers should be too. The Foundation calls it an expectation, not a constant, and says one-round finality comes in lower. Galaxy's engineers, quoted by Solana Compass, call it a design target rather than a measured result. As I noted when looking at how CertiK verifies a TPS claim, a target is a claim until someone measures it on the live network.

Alpenglow is Solana's first replacement of its core consensus since TowerBFT, and today's launch only covers part of it.

The first phase, Votor, ships in Agave 4.3. Validators now send votes directly to each other and combine them into certificates, instead of submitting votes as on-chain transactions. Per Solana's page, votes are no longer transactions and no longer appear in blocks. A block can finalize in one round if at least 80% of stake notarizes it. Otherwise, a second round uses 60% thresholds.

Proof of History no longer paces block production. Execution stays the same: the SVM, programs, transactions and fees don't change.

The second phase, Rotor, will replace Turbine, Solana's block propagation layer. Solana lists it as "not yet scheduled." If someone credits today's numbers to "Alpenglow" as a whole, half of the design hasn't shipped yet.

The security trade-off is also worth knowing. TowerBFT needed more than two-thirds of stake for confirmation. Alpenglow tolerates 20% malicious stake plus 20% offline stake. Solana Compass notes that slashing for double voting is defined but not enabled in this first version.

Validators also pay differently. TowerBFT voting cost about 1 SOL per epoch in vote transaction fees. Alpenglow replaces that with a flat 0.8 SOL per epoch Validator Admission Ticket (SIMD-0357), which is burned. A validator that can't pay doesn't vote or produce blocks in the next epoch.

In my view, this is the detail most likely to affect today's real numbers.

Alpenglow's fastest finality depends on the one-round fast path, which needs at least 80% of stake to notarize a block. On the morning of October 20, a tracker run by Pumpkin's Pool, cited by SolanaFloor and reported by Solana Compass, flagged 151 validators holding 20.3% of stake as unprepared. The day before, that figure was 45%.

The math is uncomfortable. If 20.3% of stake really couldn't vote, only 79.7% would be left, which is just short of the fast-path threshold. In that case, blocks would need the slower second round, and finality would land above the headline figure.

I expect that number to drop before the switch, since operators have been upgrading quickly. But it's the main reason I wouldn't trust any finality figure from the first hour without also checking how much stake is actually voting. Validators without a registered BLS key, or that miss the required client version, stop voting entirely. Their delegators also stop earning inflation rewards.

There's already one public reference point. Solana's page links to a community cluster explorer run by Valid Blocks, where Alpenglow has been running on Agave 4.3.2.

When I checked this morning, it showed an average finalization time of 131 ms over the past hour, ranging from 111 ms to 156 ms. Average slot time was 215 ms. That's inside Solana's target range.

That cluster had 62 active validators and about 10.2 million SOL staked. Mainnet is far larger, more spread out geographically, and runs under real load. Test-cluster results are a strong sign, but they aren't proof of how mainnet will perform.

You don't need to wait for a press release to know whether the switch happened. Solana's getAgGenesisCert RPC method returns null while the cluster is still on TowerBFT and returns a genesis certificate once Alpenglow is live. Nodes older than Agave 4.3 return a "Method not found" error, which shouldn't be confused with null.

Once the certificate shows up, here's what I'll be watching over the first few epochs:

One caveat for developers: according to Anza's operator notes, the Clock sysvar's unix_timestamp now estimates when the parent block ended, not when the current block began, and should be treated as approximate. Any timing tool that reads block timestamps may need adjusting.

If Alpenglow delivers, Solana goes from finality you wait for to finality you'd barely notice. I'll believe the 150 ms figure once mainnet consistently shows it.

#5456. How Trump’s trade policy is handing Asia to Beijing

Ted Osius is the former U.S. ambassador to Vietnam.

For a decade, Washington urged the world’s manufacturers to move their factories out of China and into friendly Southeast Asian states—only to attack the very countries and companies that answered the call.

Usually, U.S. economic statecraft is designed to help American companies succeed abroad. President Donald Trump’s punitive trade program is having the reverse effect. Broad-based import taxes have jolted manufacturers across ASEAN (the Association of Southeast Asian Nations), including American ones.

Rather than checking China, trade policy is alienating regional partners, harming supply-chain diversification, and eroding America’s influence over the bloc’s trade decisions. The U.S. is engaged in what Evan Feigenbaum, a veteran diplomat and former Republican, terms a “reverse pivot.” Bogged down in foreign crises elsewhere, Washington now projects hesitation and retreat in Asia rather than dynamic leadership.

In the months after President Trump’s April 2025 announcement of “Liberation Day” tariffs, some of ASEAN’s non-tariff barriers fell. A few countries used the exogenous threat to bring about needed reforms.  Deals were done, including Boeing sales and–at least prospective–LNG contracts. It appeared that coercion worked, at least in the short term. In February the Supreme Court struck down much of the initial tariff regime and the administration pivoted to workarounds: 150-day emergency measures under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974, and expansive Section 301 investigations into forced labor, intellectual property violations, and “excess capacity.”

America’s labor, intellectual property, and excess-capacity concerns are really about China, not Southeast Asia. The administration substituted an improvised China policy for a coherent Southeast Asia policy—a strategic blunder. By treating regional partners as collateral damage to show that China isn’t singled out, Washington is undercutting its most reliable partners and allies.

Nowhere is the absurdity of this approach more evident than in the supply chains themselves. For nearly a decade, multinational corporations have redirected capital and manufacturing from China into Vietnam, Malaysia, India, and the Philippines. The goal of these “China plus one” strategies was to insulate critical industries from geopolitical risk and move them into friendly states.

Washington’s tariff regime now undercuts this strategy. Southeast Asian export hubs suffer far more than the United States when Chinese firms attempt illicit transshipment, while subsidized Chinese overcapacity squeezes local producers. The broader reality, though, is not widespread evasion but deep and legitimate supply-chain integration. By imposing blanket punitive duties, Washington is tightening the vise on the very partners helping achieve that diversification.

As Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Hinrich Foundation, has observed, Washington created the incentive structure for alternate supply routes and is now penalizing regional partners for using them.

These tariffs aren’t even achieving Trump’s stated goals. Higher costs and a shortage of skilled domestic labor mean production lines won’t magically shift to U.S. shores. Bilateral trade deficits with Southeast Asian economies remain largely unchanged; regional exporters, U.S. importers, and consumers are simply absorbing higher costs.

ASEAN nations have long been masters of dynamic hedging—exemplified by Vietnam’s “bamboo diplomacy”—balancing China against the United States. None of them want to be dominated by Beijing, making Washington their natural partner. Yet as U.S. policy grows increasingly erratic and punitive, it inadvertently pushes them to hedge elsewhere.

As Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney warned at the World Economic Forum in Davos in January, the weaponization of economic tools forces middle powers to organize: “If we are not at the table, we are on the menu.”

Coercive tactics failed with Canada, and they will fail in Asia. Recently, politically appointed U.S. ambassador to Singapore Anjani Sinha told local and international business leaders that he received orders from the President to “bring home the money,” so they needed to double their U.S. investments.  The demand went over like a lead balloon. Capital flows are not surging into the United States; they are pivoting further into Asia.

This friction runs counter to decades of bipartisan precedent. Since the 1985 Plaza Accord, which catalyzed an era of industrial integration in Southeast Asia, American leaders have recognized that regional partners thrive under predictable, rules-based frameworks rather than blunt coercion. Today’s transactional posture risks creating a durable trust deficit that will penalize American enterprise for a generation.

Since America pulled out of the Trans-Pacific Partnership in favor of country-by-country negotiations, its absence at the table has been filled by others. ASEAN is now building institutional networks that bypass Washington altogether. Member states are working with accords like the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) and the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP).

American companies have not forgotten the benefits of clear rules of the road in a multilateral context. They have worked closely with ASEAN negotiators toward the ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement (DEFA). Spanning 11 nations, nearly 700 million consumers, and an estimated $2 trillion digital marketplace, DEFA would establish comprehensive standards for cross-border data governance, cybersecurity, digital identity, and artificial intelligence.

As Washington retreats behind tariffs and procedural disputes, Southeast Asia—with input from U.S. companies—is writing the regulatory architecture of the 21st-century digital economy.

Washington builds walls while ASEAN builds architecture.

Southeast Asia does not wish to decouple from the United States. Four ASEAN nations—Vietnam, Thailand, Malaysia, and Singapore—rank among America’s top 20 bilateral trading partners. Private enterprise, investment flows, and educational links remain extraordinarily resilient.

But in statecraft, trust is the ultimate currency. U.S. influence in the Indo-Pacific was never sustained through sheer market size or coercive leverage alone; it thrived because Washington offered an institutional vision grounded in mutual benefit and reliable rules. If Washington continues to treat its Asian partners as transactional pawns in a zero-sum struggle with Beijing, it will discover they have other trading partners. America risks economic isolation and strategic diminishment in the century of the Pacific Rim.

#5455. Apple outpaces sales expectations as it continues to battle surging memory chip costs

Apple beat its quarterly financial expectations in Chief Executive John Ternus’s first earnings report since taking over Tim Cook’s post in September, though the company continues to be pressured by a surge in memory chip costs.

The iPhone maker posted revenue of $114.5 billion in its fiscal fourth-quarter, up 12% year-over-year and above Wall Street targets of $113.4 billion. Its profit was $30.7 billion, or $2.10 per share.

Ternus extolled the company’s expanding lineup of products during a conference call with analysts, including the all-important iPhone business, which grew 17%, to $57.58 billion, in the three months ending on Sept. 26.

Apple said that it expects overall revenue to grow between 7% and 10% year-over-year in the current, holiday quarter, seasonally Apple’s strongest quarter of the year. The forecast suggests a range of $153.8 billion to $158.2 billion, compared to the $153.2 billion that analysts were expecting. But the outlook for profit margins seems to have left investors cold.

Shares of the $4.9 trillion company fell as much as 4% in after hours trading on Monday, before recovering some ground to trade down 2.7%.

Many investors have been watching the impact of rising memory chip prices on Apple and how it will weigh on profit margins. To help offset what Ternus described on Monday’s call as an “unprecedented” situation in the memory market, Apple has raised prices across its product line. Apple’s gross margin weighed in at 47.9% in the recently ended quarter, landing near the high end of its forecast range and above the 47.2% gross margin it posted in the year-ago period. But Apple’s chief financial officer, Kevan Parekh, said tariff refunds lifted the gross margin by roughly one percentage point; without them, it would have been lower.

For the current, holiday quarter, Apple said it expects gross margins to decline, ranging between 45% and 46% due to rising memory costs and some costs associated with ramping up its Siri AI service.

Ternus has marked his first couple of months at Apple with a slew of product releases that have helped the engineer savant show off Apple’s latest innovations and ease into the new job. That has included the September launch of the foldable iPhone Duo, followed by new home products, and last week’s unveiling of Apple’s first touch screen MacBook Pro.

Ternus said in a written statement that iPhone revenue reached a September quarter record and Services posted an all-time high, “capping off our best fiscal year ever.”

“We’re closing the year with our most ambitious lineup yet,” he said. “Together with the all-new Siri AI, it’s an incredible lineup to carry us into the holiday season.”

Apple’s Services revenue, which includes iCloud, the App Store, and other services, was $31.57 billion, up roughly 10% year-over-year. But sales in the company’s iPad business and its wearables business both declined.

Apple’s earnings followed financial reports from its Big Tech peers. Meta, Microsoft, Google, and Amazon all revealed their latest earnings in the last two weeks. While the companies generally had positive results, shares in the Nasdaq Composite have sunk in recent days as investors have weighed Big Tech’s positive growth, especially in cloud-computing demand for AI services, against the hundreds of billions Microsoft, Amazon, and others are spending in AI infrastructure.

#5454. Palantir posts ‘highest-ever’ revenue growth rate of 96% as investors’ patience rests on a hair trigger

Palantir Technologies said Monday that third quarter revenue rose 96% year over year to $2.3 billion, surpassing last year’s 63% growth and $1.2 billion in revenue. Chief financial officer David Glazer called it the “highest-ever” reported year-over-year growth rate as well as the highest ever sequential revenue growth rate of 20%. Moreover, quarterly revenue crossed the $2 billion milestone marker for the first time.

It raised its full-year revenue forecast to between $8.53 billion and $8.534 billion, roughly 91% growth, from as high as $8.2 billion a quarter ago. However, investors didn’t seem swayed immediately. In after-hours trading shares began to climb, rising about 1.5% immediately after the figures were published, before dropping 3.6%.

In the third quarter, Palantir reported adjusted and GAAP earnings per share of 44 cents. That compares to third quarter 2025, when adjusted EPS was 21 cents and GAAP EPS was 18 cents. Analysts were expecting revenue of $2.18 billion and adjusted earnings of 41 cents per share.

In his quarterly letter to investors, CEO Alex Karp touted the firm’s results, writing “it would be an understatement” to say Palantir’s results in Q3 “were extraordinary.” He said the company’s growth rate of 96% was “absolutely striking.” Palantir had guided revenue to roughly $2.16 billion to $2.164 billion.

Palantir’s quarterly results came after last week’s bloodbath in certain tech stocks, and served as something of a temperature read on the AI trade. Karp made no bones about the change he sees on the horizon and how it could demolish certain sectors.

“Every industry in the world—from banks to insurers to hospitals and even once-storied law firms—will either be remade or set briskly aside,” wrote Karp. He continued his aggressive optimism about the company he helped found in 2003 with investor Peter Thiel and others as the quarterly call with analysts got underway.

Karp said Palantir’s quarterly earnings calls have grown beyond its financial results to serve as “the focal point of tech, society, and general trends.” He said Palantir’s earnings calls, streamed on YouTube, are “by far the most-watched earnings calls in the world.”

The software maker has become a bellwether for public market confidence in AI software converting into revenue growth. Its latest financials come days after Alphabet suffered its worst one-day drop on record in its 22-year history as a public company. Disappointing reception to Amazon and Intel last week deepened concerns that relentless spending on AI—which is approaching $2 trillion in two years, according to S&P Global research—is sprinting well ahead of returns for investors. Google parent Alphabet lost $505 billion in market value since it published third-quarter figures last week and Intel’s stock dropped about 29% last week. The Nasdaq Composite fell more than 1% Monday and the benchmark is down 4% over the past five days.

At Palantir, investors keep a gimlet eye on U.S. commercial revenue as evidence that companies as well as governments are willing to pony up for AI software. That business grew 148% to $984 million, compared to $397 million a year ago.

And for the first time, U.S. commercial revenue skipped ahead of U.S. government revenue, clocking in at $984 million versus $953 million. U.S. government revenue grew to $953 million, up 96% from $486 million a year ago.

Meanwhile, total contract value rose 6% to $2.9 billion and U.S. commercial contract value grew 11% to $1.5 billion.

For the current quarter, Palantir forecast revenue of roughly $2.64 billion to $2.65 billion, or about 88% growth at the midpoint. Analysts expected about $2.46 billion. Fiscal year 2026 revenue guidance also rose to 91% year over year growth, and U.S. commercial revenue guidance rose to 143%.

The backdrop for Palantir is markedly different from its second quarter results in August even though Karp’s tone this quarter is just as ebullient as he was three months ago. This quarter, as last quarter, the $430 billion tech firm’s own quarterly release to investors said its results were “crushing consensus expectations.”

Karp maintained the same tone throughout the call and in response to a question for tech bull Dan Ives, said potential clients seek out Palantir because they’re concerned about their intellectual property and getting value from it. He compared it in various ways to types of romantic relationships. He said “warm leads” now turn quicker into “hot leads” the way a first date can progress further romantically.

“We’ve gone from being the most attractive person in the physics department to being the captain of the football team kind of thing,” he continued. “I mean, not that I did that.”

Amanda Gerut is the west coast editor at Fortune, overseeing publicly traded businesses, executive compensation, Securities and Exchange Commission regulations, and investigations.

#5453. 4 Reasons Your Homepage Messaging Isn’t Converting (and How to Address Them)

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Why isn’t your homepage converting visitors into customers? Discover four common website messaging mistakes and how customer interviews can help fix them.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Your homepage has one of the most important jobs in marketing: convincing the right visitors that your solution is worth exploring.

Yet many companies struggle to turn website traffic into demos, trials or purchases. They invest in SEO, advertising and content to attract visitors, only to watch most of them leave without taking action.

Having spent more than a decade helping B2B companies improve their messaging as a product marketing executive and consultant, I’ve learned that the problem often starts with a misunderstanding of what buyers need to hear before they’re willing to take the next step.

Companies often explain their products from their own perspective. They highlight what they’ve built, everything their product can do and the benefits they assume customers care about. It often results in messaging like “The AI-native GTM platform powering Precision GTM at scale.”

But buyers have their own priorities, frustrations and concerns. If your homepage doesn’t address those, even a great product can struggle to convert.

Here are four common messaging mistakes and how to fix them.

Many companies want their homepage to communicate everything their product can do. They try to capture multiple use cases, features and benefits in a single headline, hoping to appeal to as many potential customers as possible.

The result is often vague messaging that promises to “streamline operations,” “boost productivity,” “help your business grow,” or vague slogans like “We’ll take care of your accounting so you can focus on your business.”

These statements may have some truth, but they’re unlikely to resonate with someone facing a specific, urgent problem. When you try to communicate everything, you risk saying nothing compelling enough to make a buyer act.

Consider a project management platform for marketing agencies. Its homepage might promise to “streamline projects and improve team productivity” or some version of that. But customer interviews could reveal that agency owners are particularly frustrated by missed deadlines that damage client relationships.

Now the company has a more specific message to lead with: “Deliver every client project on time, without constantly chasing your team for updates.”

That message is more likely to capture the attention of an agency owner who’s tired of apologizing to clients for late work. It connects with a problem they’re experiencing and have a reason to solve.

In my customer research work, I often find that what companies think customers value most differs from what actually motivates them to look for a solution.

To find your strongest message, interview recent customers or prospects. Ask what prompted them to start looking for a solution, what problem they were most eager to solve and why solving it became a priority.

Look for the single problem or desired outcome that most consistently motivates your ideal customers to act. Lead with that message on your homepage. You can use the rest of the page to communicate everything else your product offers.

Your biggest competitor isn’t always another company. Often, it’s the way your prospective customers already do things.

They might recognize the problem your product solves but have learned to live with it. Unless the cost of continuing becomes clear, they have little reason to make a change.

Imagine a software product that automates invoicing for agencies. Its homepage might say, “Automate invoicing and save time.” That’s a reasonable benefit, but it doesn’t fully communicate why the problem deserves attention.

Now consider the agency owner’s existing workflow. Project managers finish work, someone manually checks billable hours, invoices are created at the end of the month, and the finance team follows up on unpaid balances.

The consequences might include delayed invoices, missed billable work, slower payments and unnecessary administrative costs. These are much more compelling reasons to change.

Instead of simply promising automation, the homepage could explain how manual billing creates revenue leakage and cash flow problems.

To make the status quo feel costly, make its consequences visible.

Ask customers what happened before they adopted your solution. How much time did they spend on the problem? What mistakes occurred? What opportunities did they miss? What happened when they delayed fixing it?

Use their answers to communicate the business and emotional impact of the problem. Wherever possible, include real numbers, concrete examples and real-life anecdotes.

Even when visitors recognize the problem, they still need to understand how your solution will improve their situation.

Many homepages fall short here because they emphasize generic benefits or product capabilities without explaining how the product fits into the buyer’s actual workflow.

For example, an AI-powered customer support platform might highlight advanced language models, intelligent routing and automated workflows. But customer research might reveal that support managers primarily want to reduce the number of repetitive tickets their agents handle without compromising customer satisfaction.

They want to know which questions AI can resolve, when a human agent takes over and how the platform will connect with their existing help desk. The homepage should answer those deeper questions or help the reader easily find that guidance elsewhere on the website.

Rather than simply stating that the product “improves support efficiency,” it could walk visitors through a familiar scenario: A customer asks about an order, AI retrieves the relevant information, and the issue gets resolved without an agent getting involved.

A simple workflow illustration can make the value immediately understandable.

I’ve found that understanding a customer’s existing process is one of the most useful parts of customer interviews. It reveals not only which benefits matter but also which details buyers need to see before they can imagine using a product.

Ask customers to walk you through how they handled the problem before finding your solution and what changed afterward. Then build your messaging around those specific improvements.

Even when buyers see the value, they might hesitate because they’re uncertain about what happens next.

Will the product work for their business? Will implementation be difficult? Will their team actually use it? Can they trust your company to deliver? These concerns can prevent otherwise interested visitors from converting.

I frequently see websites use customer logos and testimonials as their main form of reassurance. Those elements help, but they don’t necessarily answer the specific questions making buyers hesitate.

A small business considering a new accounting platform, for example, might be far more concerned about migrating its financial data than whether the software has won an industry award.

Showing how migration works, explaining the support available and featuring a customer who successfully made the switch could do more to increase conversions.

The most effective reassurance addresses the risks your buyers actually perceive.

Interview customers about the concerns they had before purchasing. Ask what nearly stopped them, what reassured them and what information would have made their decision easier.

Use those insights to select the right customer stories, product demonstrations, guarantees, implementation details and FAQs for your homepage.

Improving homepage conversions doesn’t always require a complete redesign, more persuasive copywriting or another round of A/B testing. Sometimes, the most valuable starting point is a handful of conversations with recent buyers.

Ask what problem made them look for a solution, why they couldn’t continue with their existing approach, what convinced them your product was right and what almost prevented them from buying.

Their answers can help you build a homepage that speaks to a real priority, makes the cost of inaction clear, demonstrates relevant value and gives visitors the confidence to take the next step.

That’s a much stronger foundation for conversion than guessing which headline or call to action might perform better.

Your homepage has one of the most important jobs in marketing: convincing the right visitors that your solution is worth exploring.

Yet many companies struggle to turn website traffic into demos, trials or purchases. They invest in SEO, advertising and content to attract visitors, only to watch most of them leave without taking action.

Having spent more than a decade helping B2B companies improve their messaging as a product marketing executive and consultant, I’ve learned that the problem often starts with a misunderstanding of what buyers need to hear before they’re willing to take the next step.

#5451. Fears over $828 billion AI capex spending spree help erase $1 trillion in market value

The richest companies in the history of the world are spending so much on the infrastructure backing AI that they’re burning through billions in cash and threatening a recent AI-fueled stock surge as Wall Street wavers.

The latest financial disclosures by four of the biggest hyperscalers, Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft, and Meta, as well as Elon Musk’s up-and-coming AI player, SpaceX, which includes xAI, revealed that the small group of tech heavyweights is set to invest as much as $828 billion on capital expenditures this year. That spending includes data centers, high-powered chips, and other infrastructure that fuels AI.

Making up the $828 billion in capex spending is an expected spend for 2026 of $220 billion from Amazon, up to $205 billion from Alphabet, approximately $170 billion from Microsoft, up to $145 billion from Meta, and up to $88 billion from SpaceX, according to company earnings releases and calls.

At this point, the massive AI infrastructure bill has surpassed the market value of well-known businesses like energy giant ExxonMobil or payments company Mastercard and is even approaching the roughly $1 trillion America is spending on defense this fiscal year, itself the largest in the world. Several banks, including Evercore and Bank of America, see capital expenditure related to AI hitting $1 trillion in 2027.

Partly in response to this massive spending, stocks tumbled on Friday, leading both the Nasdaq and the S&P 500 to their worst one-day performances since June. The tech-heavy Nasdaq closed down 2.9%, while the S&P 500 fell 1.8%. Nasdaq 100 companies lost more than $1 trillion in market value. Sour guidance for the last three months of the year from U.S. chipmaker Intel also played a role.

Some of the market’s jitters can be drawn to concerns over free cash flow, which has long been a source of strength for Silicon Valley companies but has recently taken a turn. Four of the five tech giants spending hundreds of billions cumulatively on capex had negative free cash flow in the third quarter (Microsoft was the exception), meaning they spent more on buildings, equipment, and other capital investments than they generated in cash from their operations.

As companies that built their fortunes selling software and services increasingly pour money into physical infrastructure they are looking to borrow or raise more in some cases to pay for it. With a handful of technology stocks accounting for an outsized share of the S&P 500, the success or failure of these companies’ investments could have enormous implications for the market and the millions of Americans invested in it.

Aleksandar Tomic, an economist and the associate dean at Boston College, warned that these infrastructure investments could lead to consequences far beyond Silicon Valley if they don’t pan out, especially as companies increasingly rely on debt to finance their expansion. This increased borrowing could raise the cost of capital for other businesses, while a downturn among the tech giants could ripple throughout the broader economy.

“If these tech companies sneeze, the rest of the market would catch pneumonia,” Tomic told Fortune.

Microsoft’s recent financials show how keeping up in the AI race is affecting tech companies’ decisions overall.

For decades, the software giant has been one of the world’s biggest cash-generating businesses. It earned nearly $134 billion in profit during its latest fiscal year and generated almost $183 billion in cash from operations. Still, during the same period, its cash spending on property and equipment rose about 80%.

Microsoft announced a $25 billion bond offering Thursday, its first bond sale in more than nine years. The company said it would use the money for general corporate purposes, which it said could include capital expenditures.

Microsoft remained free cash flow positive last quarter unlike competitors, Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, and SpaceX, but as the costs of infrastructure increase, the company is looking to raise funds.

Meta reported negative free cash flow of $2.1 billion last quarter, compared with positive $10.6 billion during the same period a year earlier. On Monday, it announced it would issue new shares in a plan to raise up to $95 billion that will give it more funds it could put toward AI infrastructure.

Oracle, another major player in the AI infrastructure race, is also relying on borrowing and other avenues to support its expansion. The company told investors this week that it doesn’t expect to return to positive free cash flow until the second half of its next fiscal year, which would run from the six months prior to May 2028. After that, the company said, it predicts free cash flow shooting up to at least $30 billion for the fiscal year ending in May 2029.

For now, some big tech companies can point to the encouraging sign that demand for computing power is translating into record cloud revenue. Google’s cloud revenue more than doubled last quarter to $30.7 billion, while Microsoft’s Azure business grew 48% to approximately $33.3 billion and Amazon Web Services expanded 39.3% to $46 billion. Despite its slower growth rate, AWS remains the largest of the three by quarterly revenue.

Cloud providers make money partly by renting compute to AI providers. As AI demand is also projected to grow in the coming years, these operations could be a welcome source of revenue for hyperscalers. Still, not all cloud revenue comes from AI, and rising sales don’t necessarily validate the giant investments of today.

In other positive news for the AI sector, Claude maker Anthropic filed paperwork for an initial public offering this week, helping to boost the Nasdaq 0.8% on Monday. The filing also drew attention to more than $265 billion in future minimum purchase commitments, mostly for cloud computing and other infrastructure services, which could be a boon for hyperscalers.

Still, overall, companies are betting huge sums of money today to build out the  computing capacity they expect to need years from now, a move that could be prescient but also comes with big risks in the short term.

For investors, the question is increasingly whether AI will become profitable enough to justify the enormous bill. If expensive data centers and chips don’t generate the profits that companies are expecting, the fallout could have consequences that extend well beyond Silicon Valley to the U.S. economy and beyond, said Tomic.

“We do need infrastructure, we do need this capital, but, can they sustain it? I think that’s the big big question,” he said.

Amazon CEO Andy Jassy, whose company on Thursday reported negative free cash flow of more than $42 billion over the past year, made it clear on the company’s third quarter earnings call he sees little choice but to keep spending.

“Would it be more convenient if this type of acceleration and opportunity happened over 25 years and you could spread the CapEx over 25 years,” Jassy asked an analyst during the call. “Yeah, it might be more convenient, but that’s not the world that we live in, and that’s not the opportunity.”

Role: Reporter Marco Quiroz-Gutierrez is a reporter for Fortune covering general business news.

#5449. The Systems Behind Your Business Are Changing Beneath the Surface — and Most Teams Haven’t Caught On

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

The GTM stack is getting an operating system. Most teams don’t know they’re already building on it.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Over the past two years, a subtle transformation has taken place in how go-to-market technology gets constructed, yet most executive teams have not given a name to what they are actually building.

If you audit a modern revenue organization, you will likely find five or six separate systems querying the exact same data source in the background: lead scoring, automated routing, territory assignment, enrichment steps in marketing automation and AI SDRs pulling context before drafting outreach. And what matters is that none of these workflows require a human operator to log into a browser tab or export a spreadsheet.

When multiple systems continuously query a single data source to execute automated tasks unattended, that source has stopped being a software tool. It has become infrastructure — the operating system underneath your revenue stack.

The transition from a point tool to an operating system is rarely a deliberate procurement decision. It happens quietly through a change in operational direction.

A software tool answers a question a human explicitly asked. Core infrastructure answers questions nobody asked, on an automated schedule, without human intervention. When an account executive opens a research tab at 2 p.m. to look up a prospect, they are using a tool. When an automated routing engine queries the same data layer at 2 a.m. to assign an incoming lead based on parent-subsidiary hierarchy and buying signals, that system is running on an operating system.

The simplest way to determine whether a data source has become your stack’s operating system is to examine your failure modes. If that provider goes dark for a week and a few reps lose a research portal, you are using a tool. But if lead scoring drifts, routing rules misfire and automated workflows stall, your organization is running on infrastructure.

For technical builders evaluating their stack architecture today, the critical challenge is avoiding misclassification. Treating infrastructure like a temporary tool leads to casual vendor swaps that break workflows across your ecosystem. On the flip side, treating a basic tool like infrastructure causes you to overpay for software you could easily swap over a weekend.

To determine what you actually hold, run a simple diagnostic: Price the divorce, not the contract.

Instead of reviewing the renewal invoice, write the actual engineering migration plan required to replace your current data provider. Map every workflow that reads from the layer, every AI agent that pulls its fields into context, every scoring algorithm trained on its records and every downstream system storing copies of its truth. Then, estimate the cost of rewiring those connections in engineering quarters rather than software license dollars.

If replacing the provider means simply swapping user logins, you own a tool. If replacing it requires re-architecting how your systems communicate, you have built an operating system.

When an intelligence layer moves underneath the stack, its core function changes. It stops serving up individual contact lookups to human users and starts performing continuous, unattended background operations.

At the center of that is entity resolution: resolving a CRM record, a web form fill and an attendee on a sales call to the same human and ultimate parent company. It handles corporate hierarchy mapping, ensuring automated agents do not prospect a subsidiary while a strategic enterprise team negotiates with the parent holding company. It constantly maps call transcripts, CRM stage changes and external intent signals onto a single, unified record.

We ran this exact transition internally when I stepped into the CMO seat at ZoomInfo. Rather than making external claims, our first move was instrumenting our own marketing organization directly on our platform — wiring scoring, routing, signal-driven plays and AI workflows into one shared context graph.

The immediate lesson was that an operating system requires uncompromising identity resolution first. Automated workflows built on top of fragmented records or stale lists do not create efficiency; they simply distribute confusion at scale. When an AI agent acts unattended, every field requires clear data provenance, accompanied by strict low-confidence rules: If a record is ambiguous, route it to a human, log the exception, and pause execution.

You can copy a stack in a quarter, but you can’t copy three years of context. The gap between organizations that treat data as a point tool and those that build on an underlying operating system becomes impossible to close quickly.

That compounding advantage manifests across two operational dimensions: velocity from signal to touch and marginal unit economics. When a key champion changes jobs, an agentic workflow wired into an intelligence layer catches the movement, links the executive to historical relationship context and routes a relevant touchpoint the same day. On an operating system, every new workflow you build becomes cheaper than the last because the underlying integration logic already exists.

In an AI-native ecosystem, basic contact records are rapidly commoditizing. Long-term defensibility belongs to the continuous, authoritative data graph underneath — the operating system that every agent and workflow defaults to by design.

Over the past two years, a subtle transformation has taken place in how go-to-market technology gets constructed, yet most executive teams have not given a name to what they are actually building.

If you audit a modern revenue organization, you will likely find five or six separate systems querying the exact same data source in the background: lead scoring, automated routing, territory assignment, enrichment steps in marketing automation and AI SDRs pulling context before drafting outreach. And what matters is that none of these workflows require a human operator to log into a browser tab or export a spreadsheet.

When multiple systems continuously query a single data source to execute automated tasks unattended, that source has stopped being a software tool. It has become infrastructure — the operating system underneath your revenue stack.

#5448. A Next-Day ‘Thank You’ Can Do More for Your Career Than You Think

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

When someone gives you a gift, extends a favor or considers you for an opportunity, take the time to recognize their effort.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

The business world presents countless opportunities to make positive impressions that can influence your career trajectory. Whether you receive a thoughtful gift, benefit from a professional favor or interview for a new position, knowing when and how to express appreciation is an important professional skill.

Unfortunately, not everyone recognizes these moments for what they are: opportunities to demonstrate character, emotional intelligence and respect for others.

In my experience as a business owner, you can rarely go wrong by showing gratitude. A sincere thank-you email or text sent within 24 hours can distinguish you from colleagues and competitors who overlook this simple courtesy.

Here are three situations when a next-day thank-you can make a meaningful difference.

As a business owner, I often give team members tickets to concerts, theatrical performances or sporting events. Whenever possible, I personalize these gifts. For example, if I know an employee follows a particular sports team, I may offer tickets to see that team play.

Naturally, I appreciate the initial thank you. That acknowledgment usually arrives through our in-office chat tool shortly after the employee receives my offer.

When an employee sends a follow-up text or email after attending the event, especially one that includes a photo or personal detail, it tells me something important about that person’s character.

Employees often share how exciting the final minutes of the game were or mention that the concert exceeded expectations. These details show that the gift was genuinely appreciated.

More importantly, the message demonstrates that the employee doesn’t consider these experiences to be an expected perk of employment. Instead, they recognize that someone made an effort to provide something of value.

When I don’t receive any acknowledgment after the event, I notice. While people sometimes forget or get busy, a consistent lack of expressed appreciation can create an impression of entitlement.  And entitlement is not a quality that encourages employers to invest in someone’s future career development.

Professional favors come in many forms. Your boss might invite you to sit at the company’s table at a major charity event, introduce you to an influential business contact or offer you an opportunity to attend an industry conference.

These gestures deserve more than casual acknowledgment.

Consider the invitation to a charity event. Your first responsibility is to RSVP promptly. RSVP comes from the French phrase Répondez, s’il vous plaît, meaning “Please respond.”

Yet responding to invitations isn’t something everyone does consistently. According to Greenvelope’s RSVP benchmarks, the response rate for conference and meeting invitations is approximately 66%.

Failing to respond promptly can make you appear disorganized or indifferent.

More importantly, recognize the invitation for what it represents: an opportunity to build professional relationships, demonstrate your interpersonal skills and potentially advance your career.

After attending, send a next-day thank-you message. Mention something specific you appreciated, such as an interesting conversation or a valuable introduction.

The same principle applies when a manager recommends you for a special assignment, provides career guidance or makes an introduction that expands your professional network.

Of course, you don’t need to write a formal note every time your boss buys you a cup of coffee. But meaningful favors deserve meaningful appreciation. When you thank someone immediately and follow up afterward, you have taken advantage of demonstrating gratitude twice.

Our SalesFuel research shows that 36% of B2B decision-makers will not do business with a sales professional who demonstrates poor etiquette. Even if you don’t work in sales, that finding should get your attention. Professional behavior influences how others perceive your credibility and character.

Some managers, particularly those from older generations, likely place considerable importance on traditional expressions of courtesy. Don’t miss these opportunities to show your character.

Job candidates typically have three major opportunities to impress prospective employers.

The first comes through their resumes, applications and assessment results. These materials help demonstrate whether candidates possess the skills and abilities required for the position.

The second opportunity occurs during the interview. Candidates can distinguish themselves by discussing their accomplishments, answering questions thoughtfully and communicating their career aspirations.

The third opportunity arrives after the interview ends. A well-written thank-you message sent within 24 hours can reinforce the positive impression you’ve worked hard to establish. This message shouldn’t be a generic, AI-generated paragraph that could be sent to any hiring manager.

Instead, reference something specific from your conversation. Perhaps you appreciated learning about the company’s growth plans or discussing a challenge the team hopes to solve. Briefly reaffirm your interest in the position and explain why the opportunity excites you.

In an age when AI can produce polished resumes and professional correspondence in seconds, genuine personalization matters more than ever. A thoughtful thank you demonstrates communication skills, attention to detail and an understanding of professional etiquette.

It also suggests something employers value: You recognize that another person invested time in considering your future.

A next-day thank-you doesn’t require elaborate language, expensive stationery or a lengthy message. Often, three or four sincere sentences are enough. What matters is the acknowledgment.

When someone gives you a gift, extends a favor or considers you for an opportunity, take the time to recognize their effort. You never know which professional relationship may influence your next promotion, assignment or career move.

Gratitude costs very little, but failing to express it can cost you opportunities. Make the next-day thank-you a habit that sets you apart.

The business world presents countless opportunities to make positive impressions that can influence your career trajectory. Whether you receive a thoughtful gift, benefit from a professional favor or interview for a new position, knowing when and how to express appreciation is an important professional skill.

Unfortunately, not everyone recognizes these moments for what they are: opportunities to demonstrate character, emotional intelligence and respect for others.

In my experience as a business owner, you can rarely go wrong by showing gratitude. A sincere thank-you email or text sent within 24 hours can distinguish you from colleagues and competitors who overlook this simple courtesy.

#5447. ‘Fastest entertainment property in history’: GTA VI arrives to test a thin November box office

A nearly three-hour documentary about Elizabeth Holmes was the No. 1 movie in America over Halloween weekend. That’s a triumph for A24, and a scary harbinger for theaters heading into a thin November that faces competition from an entirely different corner of entertainment.

A24’s You Can See Everything, directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, took in $11.4 million in its third weekend, narrowly edging DC Studios’ Clayface, according to Monday’s final figures reported by Variety. It had finished second in each of its first two weekends, behind Street Fighter and then Clayface. Its domestic total now stands at $64.7 million.

It is the first documentary outside the concert genre to top the box office since Michael Moore’s Fahrenheit 9/11 in 2004. But its lack of direct competition is telling. No studio opened a wide release, and overall ticket sales came to about $56 million, down more than 40% from the prior weekend and the second-lowest total of the year, according to studio estimates.

Unlike Christmas, Thanksgiving, or the Fourth of July, Halloween doesn’t boost the box office when it lands on a weekend. People don’t get an extra day off, and they’re more likely to spend peak moviegoing hours trick-or-treating or at parties.

The last Saturday Halloween, in 2020, came while most theaters were shuttered. The one before that, in 2015, was the weakest weekend of that year to that point: three new wide releases flopped, and The Martian stayed on top in its fifth week, as Fortune reported.

This year’s quiet Halloween also foreshadows a challenging month. The biggest swing is Lionsgate’s The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping on Nov. 20, the sixth film in the franchise and an adaptation of Suzanne Collins’ 2025 bestseller. Boxoffice Pro’s long-range tracking puts its opening at $55 million to $65 million; the last installment, 2023’s The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes, opened to $44.6 million.

Thanksgiving week brings Disney’s animated Hexed and Universal’s Focker In-Law, both on Nov. 25. Focker In-Law is a greater gamble: the fourth film in the franchise that began with 2000’s Meet the Parents arrives 16 years after Little Fockers, which opened to $30.8 million in 2010.

Warner Bros.’ animated The Cat in the Hat and Searchlight’s Wild Horse Nine open Nov. 6, and smaller titles like Ebenezer: A Christmas Carol and I Play Rocky are sprinkled through the month. But the box office’s most likely competition comes from the video game business: Rockstar Games releases Grand Theft Auto VI on Nov. 19, one day before Sunrise on the Reaping opens.

The sixth game in the series arrives 13 years after Grand Theft Auto V, and anticipation has been building for years. Rockstar confirmed development in February 2022; that September, a hack leaked roughly 90 clips of early footage, and in December 2023 the first trailer leaked hours before its scheduled debut. The game promises a more expansive setting than any previous Grand Theft Auto title.

Grand Theft Auto V generated $800 million in sales in its first 24 hours in 2013 and passed $1 billion in three days, which publisher Take-Two Interactive called the fastest any entertainment property had reached that mark. It has since sold more than 230 million units, according to Take-Two’s August 2026 earnings report.

GTA VI is poised to beat those numbers. Analytics firm Sensor Tower estimates it had drawn 6.45 million digital pre-orders worth about $630 million as of Oct. 20, excluding physical copies. That global, pre-launch haul already tops the roughly $625 million domestic run of Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, the year’s second-highest-grossing film behind Spider-Man: Brand New Day.

It is also more than 11 times what every movie in North American theaters grossed over Halloween weekend. For Take-Two, which reported $6.66 billion in revenue in its fiscal year ended in March, the launch underpins a forecast of $8 billion to $8.2 billion in net bookings this fiscal year.

Video games may draw a narrower audience than theatrical films, but a release this size is bound to occupy the attention of millions later this month. That’s likely to pull some of them away from the big screen for at least a weekend, leaving a notable dent in the fall box office.

#5446. New Apple CEO John Ternus chalks up some early wins, but the honeymoon is over

John Ternus, Apple’s new CEO, has spent the first two months in his new post celebrating a batch of fresh products, particularly the release of the foldable iPhone Duo. On Monday, the 51-year-old executive introduced himself to Wall Street for his first quarterly earnings call.

While Apple beat September-quarter earnings expectations, investors traded the stock down in after-hours trading due to the company’s outlook on margins, which it said will continue to be squeezed by a shortage in memory chips, and slowing growth in its Services segment without a clear answer to how that may rebound. The company has also attempted to tell its AI story through its revamped Siri AI product, but investors don’t seem convinced yet that Apple has the winning formula for the AI age.

On the call with analysts following earnings, Ternus fielded some questions but also delegated answers to Chief Financial Officer Kevan Parekh and Chief Operating Officer Sabih Khan, who Apple said would participate in earnings calls moving forward, something the company hasn’t done for years. Ternus projected confidence on the call, but he appeared to stick mostly to scripted marketing points, such as “Apple is the greatest company in the world,” that subdued the conversation.

By some measures Apple is performing at its best ever (its September iPhone sales set a record), but the more nuanced reality is that the $4.9 trillion company has had to offset surging memory chip prices by raising its own prices, and it is relying on its massive install base to carry it forward. Compounding the pressures are supply chain shortages for products that include the iPhone Duo, with new orders for the phone not arriving until the end of January.

“What we’re seeing with memory pricing right now is unprecedented,” Ternus told analysts on the Monday call. “That has put pressure on our prices.” He added that beyond the December quarter, the company expects the pricing for memory purchases to continue to increase.

Apple said it expects its gross margin for its December quarter to be between 45% and 46% after posting a margin of 47.9% for its September quarter, when tariff refunds provided an approximately one-percentage-point boost. The decline, the company said, reflects the continued cost of memory, as well as costs associated with ramping up Siri AI.

“We’re going into this [holiday period] with more downside than upside,” Apple investor Gene Munster told Fortune in an interview prior to Apple’s earnings. On X, Munster wrote after the earnings posted that, “It’s clear they don’t want to talk about personalized agents. They’re the biggest risk to the Apple ecosystem.”

Ternus and Parekh offered few details when asked by analysts about the roadmap for Siri AI, the company’s revamped assistant. When asked about the industry shift toward consumer AI agents such as Meta’s Muse assistant, Ternus noted that Siri is “primarily request-based today,” though he said the assistant is built on an architecture that makes it possible to substantially expand its capabilities over time

Apple has touted Siri AI, which has been rolling out to users in beta mode, as a key upgrade that is central to new products such as the home devices it recently launched, which included its first smart home display. The new Siri is designed to understand what is on a user’s screen and act on it, help with writing, and search a user’s device for context, among other features.

Reviews have been mixed on the revamp. Some analysts have said they liked the new features, but overall, the assistant has lagged well behind leading chatbots from OpenAI and Anthropic, as well as a wave of personalized agents from Meta and others that have ushered in a new kind of AI assistant capable of shopping, checking bank statements, and other tasks on its own.

“Siri AI is much more capable and functional today, but how do you take it to the next level?” Wamsi Mohan, an analyst at Bank of America, told Fortune.

Asked about Apple’s plans to handle its slowdown in its Services unit, which includes iCloud, the App Store, and other services, and how the company may find new revenue streams, Ternus and other executives on Monday mostly spoke about the company’s active installed base surpassing 2.5 billion devices, which they said will lead to future monetization possibilities. They added that there will be some usage limits on features that rely on AI that does not run locally, and that iCloud tiers historically focused on storage will evolve.

The start of Ternus’ tenure has mostly comprised a new wave of hardware. In early September, at his first public event as CEO, Ternus unveiled the iPhone Duo. The phone has shown strong demand, with orders backed up, but supply constraints have made it difficult to gauge the scale of sales. Some units dealt with cracked screens, which Apple acknowledged and said it was replacing.

When an analyst asked about the rollout of the Duo phones and hinted at “supply chain” issues, Ternus let Khan respond. The product ramp is going well, Khan said. “It’s really hard to predict when supply and demand will be in balance.”

Analysts at Yorkville Ives predict Apple can sell roughly 10 million Duos over the next few quarters.

Apple has moved to a staggered iPhone release, with its Pro, Pro Max, and Duo models now available but the base model and iPhone Air not expected until the spring. The approach, together with the rising component costs and a slowdown in Services growth, could affect its future performance, according to BofA’s Mohan.

Sales in Greater China, a key market for Apple, jumped 21% year-over-year in the September quarter, though the sum was $1 billion short of Wall Street targets, according to Bloomberg estimates. Apple also plans to launch AI features for China-based iPhone customers after working out a deal with Alibaba Group Holding following a long period of negotiations, though the launch is not equivalent to a full Siri AI experience for Chinese customers.

“We have everything we need to be extraordinarily successful,” Ternus said. “With this team, this vision, this mission, and these values, I have no doubt that we will.”
